What about Della Street" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Feminism — Birondo evaluates Della Street through moral psychology and Aristotelian virtue ethics: she is an excellent secretary in the role-specific sense (the Gregg shorthand that traps Robert Caddo's contradiction outside The Lonely Heiress crime scene) and supplies the 'woman's angle' the office needs, while Perry displays Aristotle's practical wisdom in court but a failure of recognition toward her, under-crediting her and kissing her for her 'feminine charms' upon her skullduggery in ways that today would be sexual harassment. The chapter also applies Aristotle on habituation through Mrs. Caddo's 'wildcat' tantrums hardening into character, and asks whether Della's team-playing beyond her duties is admirable, sad, or itself the product of mid-century sexism.
- ch. 23 "IV. Story" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "13. Perry Mason as Greek Tragedy" **·** Aristotle — McCracken reads the show's formula as Aristotelian tragedy from the Poetics: what satisfies us is not the whodunit (we could never deduce Lola in 'The Case of the Silent Partner' or poor Fred Calvert in 'The Case of the Daring Decoy') but the build-up and cathartic release of pity and fear through reversal and discovery, sealed by the guaranteed confession and the lighthearted epilogue that follows the commercial break. She uses Aristotle's plot requirements (beginning, middle, end; reversal; discovery; a hero slightly better than us) to explain why serialized shows like Twin Peaks or Lost fail where Mason's guest-star structure, with Perry, Della, and Paul as uninvolved 'hosts', lets an episodic series deliver complete tragic justice in one hour, even switching our sympathies to the confessing murderer.
- ch. 25 "14. “Yes, I Did It!”" **·** Michel Foucault — Hooke argues the confession, not the evidence, is the TV show's enduring legacy and a pioneer of the modern confession spectacle (Oprah, Dr. Phil, Judge Judy, Jerry Springer): the murderer who lied all episode suddenly avows 'Yes, I did it!' before judge, jury, and millions. Using Foucault's Wrong-Doing, Truth-Telling lectures, he analyzes the confession's three components (public audience, drama, surprise), the epistemic puzzle that a proven liar's self-accusation is nonetheless accepted as true (as when the jealous wife of The Case of the Half-Wakened Wife, innocent in the novel, becomes the TV murderer through sheer dramatic remorse), and Foucault's claim that modern justice demands the criminal's own account, the 'veridiction' that anchors truth where Gardner's beloved forensics offers only objective facts.
- ch. 26 "15. Judge Not, Lest You …" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Hooke uses Nietzsche, the 'pale criminal' of Thus Spoke Zarathustra and the 'valuating animal' of the Genealogy of Morals, to dissect our culture of judgment, in which judge, jury, spectators, and millions of readers assess the accused with an element of self-satisfaction (am I not better than the murderer?), even as Mason's plots ask us to imagine ourselves in the criminal's situation. Working through means/motive/opportunity in The Case of the Mischievous Doll (the client accused of killing her own disguised self) and The Case of the Angry Mourner (the telescope-wielding neighbors who missed the real killer husband), he ends with Mason's maxim that solving cases requires 'sympathy and tolerance for crime', seeing through others' eyes into the soul whose trace of madness Nietzsche says we cannot creep deep enough to find.
- ch. 27 "16. Justice The Master Narrative" **·** Emmanuel Levinas, Jacques Derrida, Hannah Arendt, Martin Heidegger, Aristotle — The Face of the Other; Deconstruction — Christiansen frames justice as our culture's master narrative and tests it through two episodes. In 'The Case of the Substitute Face', Laura Houser's retroactive misidentification of her father going overboard and the fingerprint expert's error illustrate Levinas's face of the Other as first philosophy: the face-to-face call to care and responsibility that Mason answers every time he takes on a client, including the guilty. In 'The Case of the Perjured Parrot', the parrot Casanova's testimony and the imposter-parrot trick let Derrida's deconstruction (meaning by difference, endlessly deferred) and Arendt's public-space dialogue expose how little proof witness testimony really carries, with Heidegger's care-structured Dasein and Aristotle's action-over-character view framing the closing questions about faces and witnesses.
- ch. 28 "Bibliography" *(notes)*
- ch. 29 "The Perry Mason Novels and Novelettes" *(notes)*
- ch. 30 "The Classic TV Episodes" *(notes)*
- ch. 31 "Material Witnesses" *(notes)*
- ch. 32 "Index" *(notes)*

## Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Philip K. Dick and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Praise" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Through a Screen Darkly" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Chapter 01 - Hollywood Doesn’t Know Dick" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Philosophical Skepticism — Ethan Mills opens his 'investigation' of Hollywood's Dick adaptations (Blade Runner, Total Recall, Minority Report, The Adjustment Bureau) by insisting that fan complaints signal something essential lost in translation from print to film, not mere infidelity. He frames the issue as a clash between two philosophical worldviews about free will and knowledge, adopting a bounty-hunter persona to hunt down what Hollywood changed.
- ch. 8 "We Can Conceive It for Ourselves Wholesale" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Philosophical Skepticism — Mills defines the 'Holly-worldview' (good defeats evil, free will secures the triumph of the human spirit, heroes discover truth before the credits roll) and opposes it to the Dickian worldview of paranoia, ignorance and accepted unfreedom, where a 'happy ending' means accepting some inevitable, possibly depressing fact about our place in the universe. He announces the chapter's plan: to test whether the Holly-worldview survives Dick's challenges to its two tenets, free will and knowledge.
- ch. 9 "Free Will at the Box Office" **·** Free Will vs Determinism — Mills contrasts Dick's 'The Minority Report', where Anderton knowingly kills Kaplan exactly as the final Precog prediction foretold and accepts exile contentedly, with Spielberg's film in which Agatha insists 'You still have a choice' and Crow is spared. He pairs 'Adjustment Team', where Ed Fletcher grovels and accepts the adjustments as for the greater good, with The Adjustment Bureau, where Damon's love teaches the Chairman a lesson and wins the couple their freedom. In both cases the story doubts free will while the movie insists the hero's choice secures human dignity, which Mills attributes to the Dickian worldview being box-office poison rather than to mere economics.
- ch. 10 "Determinism’s Bounty on Free Will" **·** David Hume — Free Will vs Determinism; Compatibilism — Mills separates determinism from fate: the film's Chairman and his angels override a free humanity, while 'Adjustment Team' depicts an if-then causal order with nothing supernatural being circumvented. He lays out hard determinism (choices caused by brain states and bad noodles leave you 'no better off than an android with false memories') against soft determinism, enlisting Hume's point that without predictable behavior laws like stop signs would be ridiculous. A free action, he argues, needs no uncaused cause: it is unconstrained and flows from your character, as with Anderton's choice to run.
- ch. 11 "Skepticism for Fun and Profit" **·** Philosophical Skepticism — Mills uses the Blade Runner cuts to stage skepticism: the theatrical happy ending hides the question, the Director's Cut unicorn hints Scott wants Deckard to be a replicant, but Dick's novel has Luba Luft tell Deckard 'You must be an android' and presses him on whether his Voigt-Kampff memories are false, leaving the question unresolved for the reader and for Deckard himself. Since any evidence (empathy, the test's own accuracy) can itself be doubted, the novel is more radically skeptical than the films, because it makes both hypotheses compatible with all the evidence. He then shows Ubik pushing this to the limit, where characters cannot tell what year it is, whether their money is real, or even whether they are alive or dead.
- ch. 12 "What’s So Bad about Determinism" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "What’s So Bad about Skepticism" **·** Sextus Empiricus, Nagarjuna — Pyrrhonian Skepticism (suspension of judgment); Philosophical Skepticism — Mills argues that for the ancient skeptics skepticism was the cure, not the disease: Sextus Empiricus prescribes setting equally strong arguments against each other until judgment is suspended and tranquility follows. He reads Nagarjuna and Jayarashi as more radical, using contradictions to uproot the very impulse to hold philosophical views at all, weaning themselves from attachment even to Buddhist views. Applied to Dick, both approaches would have us stop agonizing over whether Deckard is an android or the Ubik characters are dead: the best way to stop worrying is to stop wanting the answers.
- ch. 14 "A Happy Ending" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "Chapter 02 - A Quintessence of Dust" **·** Aristotle — The Four Causes — Barham breaks down 'what is a replicant' into Aristotle's four causes: efficiently engineered by Tyrell technicians, materially biomechanical, formally modeled on humans, and finally intended for slave labor. Humans can answer the first three causes too, but our final cause, our point or purpose, has no ready answer, and that missing fourth cause is the central theme shared by Blade Runner and Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? as Deckard grapples with his conscience over 'retiring' replicants.
- ch. 16 "Show Me What You’re Made Of" **·** Aristotle — The Four Causes — The chapter runs Blade Runner's replicants through Aristotle's list-style test of essences and rejects each candidate: rationality falls when Roy checkmates his own designer at chess and mocks Deckard's panic, agency falls because the replicants set their own agenda by rebelling, and morality falls by reductio, since if morality defined humanity then Deckard's 'retirements' would unmake his, as Roy's jeer 'Aren't you the good man?' underscores. Even love is withheld as sufficient, from Gaff's 'It's too bad she won't live, but then again, who does?' to the distracting detail of Pris's tongue retracting after Roy kisses her corpse.
- ch. 17 "Have You Ever Retired a Human by Mistake" *(no index entry yet)* — The chapter argues that once Blade Runner has eliminated each candidate essence, 'human' must be treated as an irreducible concept, drawing on Raimond Gaita's example of the racist woman M, who grants Vietnamese people every capacity on the philosopher's list yet remains a racist, and on Simone Weil's claim that every human being is owed obligation simply as a human being. It applies this to Do Androids Dream: Isidore's boss sees past 'chickenhead' prejudice, and Deckard cuts his secretary off before she can label the retired replicants, admitting 'So much for the distinction between authentic living humans and android constructs.' The chapter closes by handing the irreducible concept over to phenomenology and existentialism as methods better suited than necessary-and-sufficient conditions.
- ch. 18 "The Lung-less, All-Penetrating Masterful World-Silence" **·** Martin Heidegger, Friedrich Nietzsche — The Question Concerning Technology; The Absurd — The section reads Do Androids Dream through Heidegger's 'The Question Concerning Technology': mood organs, empathy boxes, Buster Friendly and catalog-bought animals alienate humans from the world, each other and themselves until only the 'silence of the world' remains, which Isidore theorizes as the inevitable kipple-ization of the universe. Byron's 'Darkness' and Nietzsche's parable of the clever beasts frame Deckard's drive into the dead desert after his last retirement, where he confronts a universe of dead stones that perceive and remember nothing.
- ch. 19 "Do You Think Androids Have Souls" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Martin Heidegger — The Ghost in the Machine; The Question Concerning Technology — The chapter sets up strong versus weak AI through Rachael's account of the Rosen Association's strategy of iterating models until one is indistinguishable, then brings in Gaita's 'non-speculative conception' of a soul via Wittgenstein's remark that 'My attitude towards him is an attitude towards a soul.' Heidegger's warning that technology tempts us to treat others as mere means is dramatized in Deckard's realization after meeting the predatory bounty hunter Phil Resch that he had been viewing androids, and hence himself, as means; his half-measure of wishing other androids did the retiring shows how far he still has to go.
- ch. 20 "The Cardinal Mystery of Creation" **·** Martin Heidegger — The Question Concerning Technology; Authenticity — The chapter completes the Heidegger arc: where danger is grows the saving power, so Deckard's first thoughts on finding the toad (U.N. stars and reward money) expose his alienation from any authentic relation to the world, yet he ends 'devoted' to the electric toad because 'The electric things have their lives, too.' Roy Batty's tears-in-rain speech becomes the film's expression of the same saving power: wonder at the mystery of Being is what essentially ensouls humans and replicants alike.
- ch. 21 "Chapter 03 - Dick Doesn’t Do Heroes" *(no index entry yet)* — Weiss and Nicholas center the chapter on Dick's 1977 Metz interview, where he contrasted Flash Gordon and Buck Rogers heroes who 'give all the answers' with his own 'bumbling, coarse, garrulous' protagonists overwhelmed by an inscrutable universe, echoing Faulkner's Nobel speech about man prevailing through compassion, sacrifice and endurance. They argue Hollywood must inflate these ordinary characters into action figures, and that this very distortion clarifies what Dick was doing: spotlighting human weakness and the occasional rise of average Joes above their 'greedy, incompetent, petty selves.'
- ch. 22 "You’ve Been Adjusted" **·** Authenticity — The chapter tracks the Hollywood upgrades: the 'bald and fat and old' administrator of 'The Minority Report' becomes Tom Cruise, the 'miserable little salaried employee' of 'We Can Remember It for You Wholesale' becomes Arnold Schwarzenegger, and real-estate clerk Ed becomes Matt Damon running for Congress. It contrasts The Adjustment Bureau's David Norris, whose defiance of the Chairman's Plan is rewarded with the girl, with Ed Fletcher of 'Adjustment Team', who grovels ('don't de-energize me') and is released only because he is too minor to matter. The upshot: Dick wrote about authenticity, not heroes, and the films swap ordinary endurance for larger-than-life agency.
- ch. 23 "We Can Endorse That for You Wholesale" **·** The Question Concerning Technology — The chapter opposes Total Recall, where Quaid switches on the alien reactor in 'unwavering faith' and benevolent technology terraforms Mars into a paradise, to 'We Can Remember It for You Wholesale', where Quail surrenders because a brain-implanted security device transmits his every thought and 'anything you think may be held against you.' Citing Dick's line that even the most base human schemes are preferable to the most exalted machine tropisms, it argues the films inscribe a faith in technology that Dick himself never held.
- ch. 24 "Nagging Spouses and Robotic Home-Wreckers" **·** Philosophy of Love — The chapter shows Hollywoodization reaching romance: the film gives us a bachelor Deckard and a shy, rescue-worthy Rachael in a classic love story that ends with the couple fleeing together, while the novel gives Deckard a badgering wife Iran and a Rachael Rosen who is a sociopath seducing him precisely so that killing androids like her becomes impossible. Knight-rescues-damsel becomes nebbish-manipulated-by-a-psychopathic-machine, and the chapter insists this wholesale rewriting of Dick's ideas about love and marriage carries philosophical implications that are easy to miss.
- ch. 25 "Scott versus Linklater" **·** Authenticity — The chapter contrasts the directors, Scott's muscular, sensory-assaulting urban noir versus Linklater's quiet, rotoscoped suburban everyday, and their fidelity to the source: quoting Edelstein, Blade Runner misses the novel's empathy-centered psychological complexity, while A Scanner Darkly foregrounds its author with Dick's face appearing in the scramble suit, the closing Author's Note, and Dick's daughters on a faithfully recreated Orange County set. The evaluative criterion throughout is authenticity to Dick, which Linklater preserves and Scott wildly transforms.
- ch. 26 "Deckard versus Arctor" **·** Objectification; Authenticity — The chapter sets Ford's redemptive Deckard against Keanu Reeves's Bob Arctor, the everyman who spies on himself and disintegrates on Substance D, noting the shared scaffolding (lawman, shadowy supplier Tyrell/New Path, nemesis with doubtful humanity, woman in identity crisis) that only highlights the divergence: Deckard is educated into humanity through Rachael while Arctor is progressively dehumanized, with Donna/Audrey betraying rather than redeeming him. It leans on Dick's 'The Android and the Human' definition of becoming an android as being 'pounded down, manipulated, made into a means without one's knowledge or consent', so that Blade Runner imagines androids becoming human where A Scanner Darkly shows humans becoming androids, with even nature (New Path's corn fields) enlisted in the enslavement.
- ch. 27 "From Hover Cars to Substance D" **·** The Question Concerning Technology; The Panopticon (surveillance) — The chapter contrasts the films' technologies: Blade Runner foregrounds gaudy techno-tropes and a Voight-Kampff machine that discloses the truth about replicants, while A Scanner Darkly dwells on mundane devices, Substance D, surveillance cameras, cell phones and Barris's broken contraptions, that obscure reality and help dissolve Arctor's personality. It reads the latter as Dick's fear of the mechanization of humanity made contemporary, mirroring our own self-documentation on YouTube, Twitter and Facebook, and ending with Bruce, 'a dried husk', in the decoy corn field.
- ch. 28 "Through a Screen, Darkly" **·** Authenticity — The chapter argues A Scanner Darkly is consciously about the media itself: rotoscoping inserts a critical break between viewer and screen, exposing our love of scanning and being scanned, an edge that Hollywood, itself invested in media technology, habitually blunts. Against the blockbuster escape it cites Dick's 'How to Build a Universe that Doesn't Fall Apart Two Days Later', where ordinary people's heroism lies in quiet refusals ('they cannot be compelled to be what they are not'), and ends with Deckard's 'unnatural self' and Arctor's 'soul sickness', both of whom endure, which is where their and our heroism lies.
- ch. 29 "Chapter 04 - Ewe, Robot" **·** The Turing Test; What Is It Like to Be a Bat? — Seegert opens with the V-K tortoise scene: Leon knows what a turtle is but cannot feel what it would be like to be one, making empathy the litmus of humanity, even though empathy just is imaginative simulation, so the test ironically demands that humans simulate better than the simulations do. He notes the double irony that replicants show empathy for each other (Roy mourning Pris) while Deckard shoots Zhora in the back without wincing, and that the test's real function is keeping androids enslaveable in an arms race of verisimilitude; the deeper anxiety the chapter sets up is not whether androids can pass for human but whether I might not be human myself.
- ch. 30 "How Animals Make Us Human" **·** Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); Authenticity — The chapter contrasts the novel, where humanity is secured through empathetic relations with scarce real animals (Deckard hating his electric sheep's 'tyranny' because it does not know he exists), with the film, where photographs do the validating: Rachael's 'Look, it's me with my mother' treats the photo as a self-grounding artifact, which the chapter explains via Baudrillard's precession of simulacra, supplemented by Sontag's point that photos act as surrogate relations documenting the loved one's absence. Deckard's piano covered in old sepia photos then reads as overcompensation: abundant evidence, no current relationships, a hint that he may be an android.
- ch. 31 "Narcissism in a “More Human than Human” World" **·** Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — The chapter reads Deckard's longing for a real sheep as a need for his own existence to register on another genuine subjectivity, the electric sheep having no 'there there', as fellow bounty hunter Phil Resch's devotion to his squirrel Buffy implicitly concedes. It then deploys McLuhan's 'Narcissus as Narcosis': technologies like androids, the Penfield Mood Organ and the Empathy Box are a hall of mirrors reflecting humanity back at itself, so Mercerism offers virtual others that 'generate the effects of relationship even if they lack its substance.'
- ch. 32 "Empathy in a “More Human than Human” World" **·** Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — The chapter shows Deckard funding empathy for animals by killing androids, then raises the stakes: since android models keep improving, even close inspection of one's ostensibly 'real' sheep might fail to disclose a clever simulation, which it names as Dick's reconfiguration of the problem of other minds and solipsism. The desert toad, seen 'through Mercer's eyes' and boxed with painstaking care, is revealed by Iran to be electric, so that 'the desert of the real offers safe habitat only for virtual creatures.'
- ch. 33 "The Shock of Being Alive" **·** Martin Heidegger, Jean Baudrillard — The Question Concerning Technology; Deep Ecology; Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — The chapter fuses McLuhan's narcosis with Heidegger's enframing: technology constrains Being to a human-centered 'world picture' in which forests become board feet and animals become production units, and like Narcissus we fall in love with an image we stamped there ourselves. It enlists the deep ecologists and David Abram ('We are human only in contact, in conviviality, with what is not human') to argue that Dick makes human identity essentially relational, and closes on Baudrillard: digital tweets have become more present for many people than birdsong.
- ch. 34 "The Lives of Electric Others" **·** Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); Authenticity — The chapter follows Deckard past despair at universal fakery (the toad electric, Mercer a set) to his muted epiphany, 'The electric things have their lives, too', and his 'Mercer isn't fake... unless reality is fake', asking whether this extends his circle of moral concern to electric beings or merely concedes the inescapability of virtuality. It reads the film's origami unicorn and Deckard's willingness to make a life with Rachael as parallel acceptances, ending with Iran ordering 'one pound of artificial flies that really fly around and buzz' for the toad her husband is devoted to.
- ch. 35 "Identity Crises" *(front)*
- ch. 36 "Chapter 05 - Just Who and How Many Do You Think You Are" **·** Personal Identity — Feist opens with Dr. Wigan's autopsy of a man with half a brain and a full mind, moves through the split-brain experiments (the left hand writing 'PIPE' for a concealed pipe as the hemispheres autocomplete each other), and lands on Joseph Bogen's revived thesis that each of us has two minds that merely feel like one. He shows Dick threading Bogen's actual sentences mid-dialogue into A Scanner Darkly so the reader experiences a voice from nowhere, foreshadowing how Arctor's self explodes under the scramble suit, the Fred persona and Substance D into separate persons, Bob and Fred, who end up unsure who, and how many, they are.
- ch. 37 "The User Illusion" **·** René Descartes — Mind–Body Dualism; Personal Identity — The chapter interleaves a doctor's line-card quiz of Fred with Bogen and Wigan's claims that each cerebrum is 'a distinct and perfect whole as an organ of thought' and that our cherished 'inner conviction of Oneness' is mere opinion. Descartes supplies the target: a partless mind known directly and with certainty, external things known only indirectly through possibly misleading ideas, and Dick, we are told, flips this picture so the inside is messy and the outside clear.
- ch. 38 "In a Mirror, Darkly" **·** John Locke, David Hume — Personal Identity; Bundle Theory of Self; Personal Identity (memory theory); Ship of Theseus — The chapter stages Arctor's bishop's-robe musing ('What is identity? Where does the act end?') against the classic puzzles: the Ship of Theseus with its two reassembled vessels, and the baby photos you share no cells with. Locke gives memory plus a unified 'thinking, intelligent being' with real unity; Hume bites the bullet, finding only perceptions in introspection, never a self, so the self's identity over time is a normal, inescapable delusion like a mountain's. All of it converges on Fred watching Bob and asking 'who am I? Which one of them is me?'
- ch. 39 "You Don’t Always Get Along" **·** David Hume, Plato — Tripartite Soul; Bundle Theory of Self; Personal Identity — The chapter animates Hume's bundle as a 'little republic' of mental citizens without a universal citizen, staging a dialogue between Person-Hume, who cannot believe there is no self, and Philosopher-Hume, who counsels beer and billiards. It traces the view back to Plato's Republic: the tripartite soul (with Freud's id-ego-superego as a modern rerun), the example of desiring and refusing the same cold beer when you must collect your mother from the airport, and Leontius raging at his own eyes before the corpses, cross-chatter as civil strife among inner citizens, exactly what the doctors diagnose as Fred's symptom.
- ch. 40 "The Outer Workings of the Mind" **·** Immanuel Kant — Transcendental Idealism; Phenomena and Noumena — The chapter has Kant complete the flip of Descartes: we know the self only indirectly and external objects directly, because the mind is a car factory that shapes raw material into everyday experience, so you inspect only the finished products, reverse-engineer the assembly line from them, and the thing in itself stays forever outside knowledge. Rotoscoping becomes the visual correlate: reality is partly constructed by the mind but not totally, and the philosophical task is figuring out which parts of the scene are ours.
- ch. 41 "The Scanner-Self" **·** Immanuel Kant, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Look (hell is other people); Transcendental Idealism — The chapter identifies Kant's deeper, non-experiencing self, the pure organizer of data behind ordinary experience, as 'a Kantian scanner', then maps the police scanners planted in Arctor's house onto Sartre's analysis of the gaze: another's look downgrades you from observing-subject to observed object, and God's all-penetrating stare would strip you of subjectivity and freedom entirely. Arctor's relentless surveillance culminates in Bruce, the identity-less pure watcher, the scanner-self incarnate, with a closing joke that Facebook profiles are how 'we see ourselves through a profile darkly.'
- ch. 42 "The Valuable Self" **·** Immanuel Kant — Humanity as an End in Itself; Respect for Persons — The chapter turns from metaphysics to morals: for Kant the self is the most valuable thing in the world, a subject that must never be used as a mere means, since turning a subject into an object is the ultimate immorality. The authorities' plan to hollow Arctor into an unwitting infiltrator, and Donna's lament that he 'didn't volunteer', make the point concrete: what is valuable in us is the self's fuzziness, including its mystery of free will, and to remake a person into a scanner, 'a mere thing that just watches and never chooses', is the ultimate crime.
- ch. 43 "Chapter 06 - Will You Survive a Trip to Rekall, Inc" *(front)*
- ch. 44 "Follow the Psyche" **·** John Locke — Personal Identity (memory theory); Personal Identity — The chapter assembles Dick's survival-of-the-psyche cases: Agneta Rautavaara kept alive as a brain in a nutrient bath, Professor Thomas's conscious brain piloting a spaceship, the wub transferring into Captain Franco mid-execution, and the Rexorian consciousness in 'Human Is', then grounds the pattern in Locke's prince-and-cobbler and detached-little-finger thought experiments: 'consciousness makes personal identity.' Everything is codified as the Psyche Continuity Rule, to keep track of the person follow the psyche, with brains mattering only as convenient storage vessels.
- ch. 45 "The Perils of Rekall, Inc" **·** Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory) — The chapter runs through three incompatible backstories for Total Recall's Quaid, Cohaagen's infiltration plot, Hauser's genuine defection and self-erasure, or a Rekall trip gone live, and shows that in all three no single psyche links the life stages, forcing a Body Continuity Rule and then a Combined Rule that follows the psyche when mental life is unified and the body when it is disjointed. Paycheck's Jennings, who starts referring to his earlier self in the third person, exposes the rule's weak joint: deciding when a mental life counts as sufficiently disjointed.
- ch. 46 "Gotta Have Soul" **·** Gottfried Leibniz, Immanuel Kant, John Locke — Personal Identity; Immortality and the Soul — The chapter tests a Soul Continuity Rule: the wub and Hauser survive because their souls do, though Locke himself denies the soul is the person, and Leibniz's King-of-China bargain, become the richest man if you forget everything, shows why, since it would amount to being annihilated while a King of China is created in your place. Kant's case of one mental life relayed across a chain of souls yields just one person, and the rule's practical failure is evidential: nothing could tell one soul with swapped psyches from swapped souls in the same body.
- ch. 47 "Future Selves and Imposters" **·** Personal Identity — The chapter builds a counterexample from Imposter: suppose the same mind-transfer process makes the alien android an imposter in one story but the dying Olham's chosen future self in another, with identical bodily and mental continuity but opposite verdicts, so the Combined Rule fails. Intention cannot rescue the Soul Rule either, since in a government-forced transfer Olham would absurdly have to say 'I am dead over there across the room' if souls simply went where we wanted.
- ch. 48 "Selfless" **·** Personal Identity; Philosophical Skepticism — The chapter concedes that no rule, psyche, body, soul, or combined, accommodates all of Dick's transformations, and refuses to blame Dick for incoherence: his stories force our own conflicting intuitions about wubs, Quaids and downloaded minds into the open. Pessimist, optimist and skeptic each get a verdict, the skeptic's being the chapter's cliffhanger: if we are none of these things, maybe there are no enduring persons at all.
- ch. 49 "Is It Live or Is It Memorex" **·** Personal Identity; Teleporter Paradox (personal fission) — The chapter supplies the missing detail, transfer versus copying: a 'snapshot' of Olham's brain imprinted on an android leaves Olham where he was, and frying the original destroys him rather than moving him, while the bank-transfer versus copying-money analogy and the question of one psyche imprinted on two androids show why the difference matters. Once the mechanics are filled in one way the alien android is a mere copy and Olham dies, filled in another way he survives bodiless, which restores the Psyche Rule pending a science of how psyches are realized in us.
- ch. 50 "Chapter 07 - Scan Thyself" **·** Socrates, René Descartes, The Buddha — The Unexamined Life; Non-Self (anatman) — Butler frames Dick as the latest in philosophy's self-knowledge line: the Delphic 'know thyself' that Socrates made essential to the good life at the cost of his own, the Buddha who sought himself and found only an illusion at the root of suffering, Descartes whose entire philosophy rests on confidence in knowledge of himself as an immaterial being, and Dick's own 8,000-page Exegesis. The chapter's hook is the stakes of self-ignorance (what if you turned out to be something horrible?) and its Dickian version: how do you know you are not an android?
- ch. 51 "How Do You Know You’re Not an Android" **·** René Descartes, David Hume — The Cogito; Bundle Theory of Self; Philosophical Skepticism — The chapter weaponizes the cogito for Deckard's predicament: the fact that 'the lights are on' for you seems to prove you are human, but Descartes' leap from thinking to an immaterial soul is unjustified, since introspection cannot show whether your thoughts run on a soul, a bundle of neurons, or a silicon chip. Hume's 'I never can catch myself at any time without a perception' supplies the precedent, and the conclusion is that no amount of inner experience rules out being an android, so you will have to go take the V-K test after all.
- ch. 52 "The Art of Knowing Arctor" **·** Philosophical Skepticism — The chapter takes Fred's surveillance of Arctor as a literal solution to the eye-cannot-see-itself problem: split in two, Bob finally observes himself from a detached, evaluative outside, hoping the scanner sees 'clearly' where he sees 'only murk'. Real self-scanning follows, since an fMRI revealing synthetic parts behind your eye sockets would settle the android question and neural correlates might someday sort enduring love from lust, before Alva Noe's Out of Our Heads objection that mental states must be sought in whole organisms interacting with their environments, which would give Arctor's whole-habitat self-scanning the edge over the constrained brain scan.
- ch. 53 "What Does A Scanner See" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Bad Faith; Radical Freedom and Responsibility; Existence Precedes Essence — The chapter answers Arctor's question with Sartre: the gambler cannot observe his way out of deciding again, because consciousness is a nothingness with no determinate essence to be observed, so a scanner used to find yourself 'sees nothing', and Fred watching his own footage is bad faith, hiding from freedom behind presumed facts about himself. Butler then flips the bleakness into Sartre's optimism, reading Dick's 'I myself, I am not a character in this novel: I am the novel' as the author freely remaking his life through the book, his first written without amphetamines, after the break-in he suspected he had staged himself.
- ch. 54 "Phil Chews the Fat" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Bad Faith; Authenticity; Radical Freedom and Responsibility — The chapter closes on VALIS's opening gambit, 'I am Horselover Fat, and I am writing this in the third person to gain much-needed objectivity', and Dick's proliferating self-theories (vitamin C overdose, alien telepathy, past lives, Gnostic revelation) across VALIS, Radio Free Albemuth and the Exegesis. Butler weighs the bad-faith reading, that Dick was nailing down a determinate identity to escape the responsibility to choose, against Dick's own android-human essays, in which the authentic human acts spontaneously and throws off masks, concluding that Dick's refusal to settle on any one theory of himself was his playful, Sartrean way of knowing he is not an android.
- ch. 55 "Chapter 08 - Human or Machine, Does It Mind or Matter" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 56 "Don’t Think about It" **·** Alan Turing — The Turing Test — Reads the Deckard-Rachael sex scene in Do Androids Dream and the unfilmed Hampton/Fancher script, where Rachael says 'don't think about it, just do it,' to argue that the felt intensity of passion makes the real/simulated distinction pointless whenever behavior is indistinguishable. The Voight-Kampff test is presented as a version of the Turing Test, grounded in positivism's view that unverifiable inner consciousness is a meaningless question, with supervisor Bryant's 'skin jobs' sneer voicing the objection that passing behavior may be mere rule-following.
- ch. 57 " . . You Ever Take That Test Yourself" **·** The Turing Test; Personal Identity — Rachael's question to Deckard at the piano ('you ever take that test yourself?') and Luba Luft's suggestion that a human Deckard was killed and replaced put the viewer in the same quandary about implanted memories. The Penfield mood organ lets humans dial numbered moods, so the empathy that supposedly separates humans from androids is itself artificially inducible, while Phil Resch's torment over whether he is an android — compared to Munch's 'The Scream' — shows the human/android line collapsing from inside.
- ch. 58 "I Love You, My Artificial Construct" **·** Michel Foucault — Power/Knowledge — Deckard registers an empathic 4.0 on the Voight-Kampff at the thought of retiring Luba Luft, and Resch's remark that including androids in our empathic range would leave us defenseless leads the chapter to Foucault's claim that true/real distinctions reduce to struggles for power. Bounty hunting is read as a reactionary humanism whose 'barrier' keeps humans and androids distinct because technology has otherwise made them indistinguishable — as Deckard's electric sheep, needing exactly the same care as the real one, and the electric toad ('the electric things have their lives, too') confirm.
- ch. 59 " . . Because My Furnace Believed the House Was Cold" **·** Daniel Dennett — The Intentional Stance — Explains Dennett's physical, design, and intentional stances through a disk drive 'reading' a disk and a thermostat we would never say 'believes' the room is cold, concluding that whether behavior counts as conscious is a choice of vocabulary, not a metaphysical difference. Dick's post-war world of convincing simulacra and economic necessity is the setting in which linguistic conventions shift, explaining Deckard's changed attitudes toward Luba Luft and Rachael.
- ch. 60 "Shaky Theological Foundations" *(front)*
- ch. 61 "The Right Stuff" **·** John Searle, Alan Turing, Ludwig Wittgenstein — The Chinese Room; The Turing Test; Biological Naturalism / Intentionality — Applies Searle's Chinese Room to argue that functional equivalence alone would not make androids sentient, then observes that Dick's androids — biological 'chitinous reflex machines' detectable only by bone-marrow and Boneli reflex-arc tests, unlike obviously mechanical electric sheep — may possess the biological 'right stuff' Searle requires for intentional content. It closes by weighing this against the Turing/Dick behavioral view and the Wittgensteinian choice of which language game to play, calling the latter 'the most humanistic' reading.
- ch. 62 "Soul Against the Archons" *(front)*
- ch. 63 "Chapter 09 - Matt Damon Is a Vast Sinister Conspiracy" **·** Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); The Culture Industry — Argues that 'Matt Damon' is an industrially manufactured person — a simulacrum sustained by executives, marketers, and gossip media that exploits instincts once used to judge trustworthy tribemates. Reading David Norris's tie-choosing specialists in The Adjustment Bureau, Tyrell's 'More human than human,' and the novels The Simulacra and Time Out of Joint, it claims Dick's paranoid fantasy is true: manufactured fake realities keep us docile, distracted, and consuming so we never notice we would rather be lying on a rock in the warm sun.
- ch. 64 "A Variety of Free Will Worth Having" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Alienation; Existentialism — Takes Dick's self-description as a 'fictionalizing philosopher' and reads 'Adjustment Team' — Ed Fletcher stumbling into a world of grey dust animated by an external hidden force — as determinism as we concretely live it: working toward goals we never chose in jobs that are not our own. Thompson's toothpaste line in The Adjustment Bureau becomes the image of consumption-only freedom, while Norris choosing love and politics over the Bureau's plan dramatizes freedom as accepting responsibility for one's own values.
- ch. 65 "Terrible Freedom" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Existentialism — Quotes Dick's A Scanner Darkly author's note — drug misuse 'is a decision,' and the druggie life-style is 'no different from your life-style... only faster' — to argue that dropping out of the plan continues the Sixties' questioning of war, segregation, and monogamy. Dick's refusal of bourgeois moralizing exposes it as part of the social-determinist control system, but a morally neutral natural cause-and-effect is what actually destroyed the druggies, so being free requires taking control, not merely rejecting control.
- ch. 66 "Pre-Crime and Pre-Punishment" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Anselm of Canterbury — Fate and Foreknowledge; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Free Will vs Determinism — Frames 'Minority Report' with Nietzsche's charge that men were considered 'free' only so they could be judged and punished, and with Anselm's De Concordia, where God, outside time, foreknows our choices without determining them. Pre-Crime can punish Anderton and the pre-criminals now only because their not-yet-made choices are treated as absolutely free, and the 1954 context — HUAC, Hoover's anonymous accusations, the Communist Control Act — shows people punished for the present guilt of a future crime.
- ch. 67 "Freedom and Madness" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Authenticity — Updates the McCarthyite stakes of pre-guilt with Michelle Bachmann's 'anti-American' probing and the Guantánamo detainees who are 'too dangerous to transfer but not feasible for prosecution.' Dick's own post-2-3-74 spiral — after the pink light he was writing in his Exegesis about telepathic crab-clawed invaders from Sirius — becomes the case study for the book's closing practical problem: how to free yourself from received social, political, and religious determination without careering into drugs, isolation, or madness.
- ch. 68 "Chapter 10 - How to Build a Democracy that Doesn’t Fall Apart Two Hundred Years Later" *(front)*
- ch. 69 "Rule of the Wise" **·** Plato, Socrates — The Philosopher King; Democracy — Updates Plato's rule of the wise to the pre-cogs of 'Minority Report,' noting that Socrates' 'divine sign' made him a kind of pre-cog. It then argues expertise cannot be operationalized — self-proclaimed authorities from Sarah Palin to Barack Obama disagree, and there is no accepted test of who the experts are — closing with Plato's own comparison of voters to children choosing between the doctor's medicine and the confectioner's candy, which explains why the Founders added the Electoral College.
- ch. 70 "Spinning a Bottle" **·** Democracy — Sets Solar Lottery's Bottle beside the Athenian kleroterion and Madison's fear of factions: because telepaths make any strategy predictable, the Bottle game is a pure game of chance like dice rather than poker. The random twitch that deposes Reese Verrick for Leon Cartwright illustrates the same logic behind Philips and Callenbach's A Citizen Legislature proposal to replace the House with a randomly selected 'portrait of the people in miniature.'
- ch. 71 "Throwing the Rascals Out" **·** Democracy — Uses Joseph Schumpeter's deflationary account of elections — no meaningful popular will, just marketplace competition ensuring rotation in office — to explain Herb Moore's claim in Solar Lottery that the Bottle's random twitch prevents dictators. Since no one can be sure of holding power, a lottery guarantees turnover at least as well as elections, though it introduces the mirror-image danger of simply selecting an incompetent.
- ch. 72 "Checks and Challenges" **·** Democracy — Walks through Solar Lottery's two-part selection machinery — the random Bottle plus the Challenge, an officially appointed assassin who filters out incompetent Quizmasters like the psychotic Robin Pitt — comparing them to Athenian scrutiny of officials and impeachment. It also shows how the unk underclass selling its power cards concentrates any chance of office in the hands of the rich, undercutting the lottery's democratic justification, and asks whether surviving assassination predicts governing any better than winning elections does.
- ch. 73 "How Can Random Machinery Be Rational" **·** Democracy — Answers Verrick's complaint that the Bottle is irrational by distinguishing tools, which are arational, from agents who act for reasons: a lottery is inappropriate for choosing a spouse or career but rational where unpredictability or impartiality is wanted. In Solar Lottery the assassins DeFalla and Keith Pellig randomize their courses against telepaths, just as draft and green-card lotteries ensure equal chances, so random rotation in office is a rational tool for stopping anyone from holding power too long.
- ch. 74 "Giving and Selling" **·** Plato — Democracy — Takes Plato's warning that those who want to rule, like Verrick, will profit from office — true philosophers rule only under compulsion — into the question of whether power cards may be given away or sold. Since we permit donating organs and having sex but criminalize selling them, letting the rich buy up the unks' tickets destroys the equal-chance rationale, the realization that leads Cartwright to see the game as stacked, and that the chapter links to Lani Guinier's smeared electoral-reform proposals.
- ch. 75 "Chapter 11 - We Can Manipulate You Wholesale" **·** Immanuel Kant — Humanity as an End in Itself — Reads Total Recall's opening scenes — Harry's shifty eyes, then the reveal that his friendship, Lori's marriage, and even Benny's cab-driving are all sanctioned deceptions directed at Quaid — as manipulation commissioned by an outside element that sets the agenda of each relationship. Using people this way already troubles Kantian ethics, the chapter concludes, and an outside element directing individuals to do it is 'potentially enough to have Immanuel Kant spin in his grave.'
- ch. 76 "Sure I Deceived You, but What about Me" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Classifies Bob Arctor's undercover drug enforcement, Quail's covert action in 'We Can Remember It for You Wholesale,' and Quaid's HUMINT work as species of spying — one party manipulating or dominating another, as James McCargar's secret-war tradecraft describes. It asks how manipulation is actually done, answering that the manipulator finds weaknesses and links desired behaviors to them, and turns the moral question back on the deceivers themselves.
- ch. 77 "Finding a Lever for Manipulation" **·** Humanity as an End in Itself; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Explains the spy tradecraft acronym MISE (Money, Ideology, Sex, Ego) and walks through 'Fred's' recruitment method in A Scanner Darkly — building trust through drug purchases under false pretenses until the mark must betray another confidant for Fred's benefit. The same template covers Lori, Harry, and Hauser in Total Recall, for whom Quaid 'becomes nothing more than a means': monitoring his return to Mars, or locating the rebel leadership.
- ch. 78 "Categorically, We Have an Imperative Problem" **·** Immanuel Kant — Humanity as an End in Itself; The Categorical Imperative; Utilitarianism — Measures the spying in A Scanner Darkly and Total Recall against Kant's second formulation of the categorical imperative: Benny merely tracks Quaid, while the federal agents sacrifice 'Fred's' entire psyche, devaluing his humanity as a mere means. It then stages the real-world debate the fiction mirrors — the Pike and Church Committees, Godfrey's preference for technological collection, and Langan's utilitarian defense that devaluing a few is justified when society's safety requires it.
- ch. 79 "Utilitarian Doesn’t Necessarily Mean Coveralls" **·** Immanuel Kant — Utilitarianism; Humanity as an End in Itself — Lays out the utilitarian case for the spying in A Scanner Darkly: with New Path immune to inspection and Substance D addiction spreading, sacrificing Bob Arctor — secretly addicted to breakdown point and implanted with the little-flowers trigger — maximizes outcomes for the many. Against this stands the Kantian rebuttal that he should never have been made 'just another means,' likely never again to be 'an able-minded and self-determining person,' and the chapter adds the overlooked victim: the manipulator who violates the categorical imperative.
- ch. 80 "Only Remembered as the Blonde Shot in the Head" **·** Utilitarianism; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Asks whether Total Recall's Lori and Harry — liars, adulterers, willing killers — are immoral people, noting the utilitarian excuse of serving a greater good fails because the Martian government they serve is itself profit-driven and rules by 'the one-way dialogue of the truncheon and rifle.' Following Godfrey, it concludes that an employer who bases jobs on violating individuals' rights will damage the moral frameworks of the employees, whatever their prior calibration.
- ch. 81 "Like People, Like Organizations" **·** Utilitarianism; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Extends the moral-damage analysis one level up: organizations develop their own moral personas, and the LAPD's compartmentalization — where 'Fred' may be spying on fellow detectives and is required to lie to his supervisor 'Hank' — normalizes law-breaking in the name of law enforcement. It argues that society's oversight, the intelligence committees created after the Pike and Church hearings, is the 'bullet-proof vest' allowing risky utilitarian spying to continue without corroding everyone involved.
- ch. 82 "Chapter 12 - Grow, My Dears, the Eugenicist Said" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Opens the eugenics part with Flow My Tears' Jason Taverner — a beautiful, charismatic, fast-healing 'six' from an abandoned government breeding program, 'not a Nexus-Six, but not unlike one either.' Defining eugenics through the dog-and-wolf contrast in selective breeding, it notes that the 'eu' (good) in eugenics smuggles in an ethical judgment, and poses the part's driving question: who decides what counts as a 'good' or 'bad' trait, and by what right?
- ch. 83 "The Bad" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Faces the Nazi elephant in the room — the sixes' program terminated in 1943 'politically,' mirroring real eugenics in California — and dismisses reductio ad Hitlerum as fallacious while conceding eugenics' genuinely darker side in Tidman's sterilization bill, which halves the novel's black population each generation. It tests Nicholas Agar's parent-choice 'liberal eugenics' against sex-selective abortions and the widening rich-poor gap, before asking whether bred children should be seen as competitors or as successors to whom we give every opportunity.
- ch. 84 "The Good" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Übermensch; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Makes the case for eugenics' good side through Jason's uncontroversially desirable traits, invoking Nietzsche's call to 'give birth to a dancing star' and create superhuman successors as a moral philosophy of human improvement. It then probes the limits — beauty is relative (Japan's yaeba), and screening would have lost Van Gogh and Stephen Hawking — before weighing Dick's own compassion for small lives (the electric toad, the avenged cat of 'The Alien Mind,' the potter Mary Anne Dominic) against the blunt statistical claim that healthier, more capable lives go better.
- ch. 85 "The Ugly" **·** The Noble Lie; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Argues eugenics forces us to discard the 'noble lie' of egalitarian democracy we teach children for their own good, and shows the cost in Jason and Heather's contempt for 'ordinaries,' Jason's aging-obsessed narcissism, and the 'aristocratic values' that let him condemn his lover Heather to a labor camp without qualm. Police general Felix Buckman, demoted for compassion toward labor-camp inmates and later assassinated for criticizing the regime, embodies the democratic values the sixes' elitism destroys, with Marvel's X-Men as the analogy for a fractured next-generation humanity.
- ch. 86 "And the Next Step" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Surveys science fiction's next-step humanity — Wells's genetically stratified future, Stapledon's successions of human forms, and the Campbell-era optimism Dick resisted — then turns to contemporary 'posthumanist' theorists like Donna Haraway who want 'human,' 'natural,' and 'gender' fluidly redefined. Dick emerges as the voice of caution in this cross-pollination: expand the definition of what human means, but not at the cost of the compassion and empathy that make us human.
- ch. 87 "The World Is Fake" *(front)*
- ch. 88 "Chapter 13 - Things Are Seldom What They Seem" *(front)*
- ch. 89 "How Are Things in Glocca Morra—or Anywhere Else, for That Matter" **·** Philosophical Skepticism — Opens Gerard Casey's part by asking whether David Norris is really free or governed by an external agency, then argues from perception itself: the stick that looks bent in the fish tank and the rainbow that exists only for an observer positioned between sunlight and raindrops show that ordinary experience is already a construct of sensory limits, expectations, and language. This prepares the radical question of whether everything in our experience is in some way an illusion.
- ch. 90 "Ma or Machine" **·** Authenticity; The Turing Test — Takes Dick's Exegesis self-description ('I am a fictionalizing philosopher') and his twin questions — what is ultimately real, what constitutes the authentic human being — to argue that for Dick the difference between real and fake humans is empathy, not materials. The Adjustment Bureau's emotionally detached bureaucratese ('We are fully licensed to make such corrections') repels, while in 'Human Is' the Rexorian colonizing cruel Lester's body behaves 'more truly human' than the genetic human he replaced.
- ch. 91 "What’s Really Real" **·** Plato, Baruch Spinoza, Parmenides — Theory of Forms; Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura) — Traces the 'veil' theme from Parmenides' dokos and the Indian maya to Ed Fletcher seeing 'the fabric of reality split open' in 'Adjustment Team' and the shadow world of 'Jon's World.' It locates Dick's enduring conviction that the empirical world is not ultimately real in the Plato he was given at UC Berkeley — the archetypal realm of Forms behind sensory appearances — and in his professed affinity for Spinoza's Deus sive natura, alongside the Pre-Socratics he devoured.
- ch. 92 "Alternate Realities" **·** David Lewis — Possible Worlds — Reads the Bureau's adjustments as producing alternate realities — Ed Fletcher's boss as 'a different Douglas. A different version!' — and takes déjà vu, Dick's 'manifold of partially actualized realities,' and Ragle Gumm's haunting sense of having been inside a building he has only seen as a model in Time Out of Joint as clues that variables were reprogrammed in our past. Dick's late speculation converges, the chapter notes, with David Lewis's view that possible worlds are as real as ours, and with Hawking and Mlodinow's M-Theory multiverse.
- ch. 93 "Back to Earth" **·** Zen Buddhism — Argues that any theory denying the reality of the ordinary world must presuppose it: the world of mowing lawns, designing experiments, and going for coffee is where all theorizing starts and the world we never leave. The Zen progression — mountains are mountains, then are not, then are again — frames Dick's fake worlds as places we visit so the everyday world can become strange and new to us again, since, as the Hank Williams song has it, we'll never get out of this world alive.
- ch. 94 "Chapter 14 - Trauma of the Real" **·** Plato — Allegory of the Cave; Theory of Forms — Introduces Paul Livingston's part with Dick's confession that reading Plato in college convinced him the empirical world was not truly real, then retells the cave of Republic Book VII in detail: prisoners bound since birth watching shadows of puppets cast by a fire. The cave becomes the frame for Dick's fiction — the 'reality' our percept-systems report is a show of images, and the philosophical quest is the prisoner's turn toward the archetypal reality behind the scenes.
- ch. 95 "Breakthrough to the Real" **·** Plato — Allegory of the Cave; Theory of Forms; Personal Identity — Details the disorienting breakthrough in which characters learn that they themselves are fakes: Rachael's distress at her implanted memories ('How can it not know what it is?'), Deckard's paper unicorn in the director's cut confirming his own replicant status, and Ragle Gumm's soft-drink stand dissolving into a slip of paper reading 'SOFT-DRINK STAND' in Time Out of Joint. Each case maps onto the freed cave prisoner's discovery, and the disorientation is pressed onto the viewer: how can I be sure my own life and memories are not a fabrication?
- ch. 96 "Reality Is Not Real" **·** Theory of Forms — Contrasts Plato, for whom breakdown leads to a deeper and truer reality, with Dick's characters, whose breakthroughs lead only to another shifting reality — then introduces Jacques Lacan's three registers (the Real, the Imaginary, the Symbolic) as the positive account of Dick's 'sense of the real.' For Lacan, ordinary 'reality' — the accountant's respectable job, even the value of money — is purely Symbolic and Imaginary, and 'reality is not Real'; the Real is encountered only when that symbolic order breaks down, as in psychosis.
- ch. 97 "Procession of Dummies" **·** Allegory of the Cave — Uses Dick's 1972 one-sentence definition ('Reality is that which, when you stop believing in it, doesn't go away') and his claim that absolute reality reveals itself only when our space-time categories collapse, arguing the definition fits Lacan's Real better than Plato's picture of looking away from the cave wall. Through Žižek's readings, Ragle Gumm's objects being literally replaced by their symbolic labels and Deckard's replicant recognition as a 'total loss of the hero's symbolic identity' show the traumatic Real first appearing precisely where symbolically constituted reality fails.
- ch. 98 "Remembrance of Being, Passed" **·** Plotinus, Plato — Neoplatonism (the One); Theory of Forms — Reads Ubik's anti-chronological regressions — rocket to jet to biplane, 1992 decaying into 1939 — through Dick's 'orthogonal time' peeling onion-like layers toward greater Being, which Dick himself compared to Plotinus's concentric emanations from the One beyond all language and comprehension. Dick's 1974 pink-light experience is interpreted as Platonic anamnesis, recovered memory of the forms in a parallel time-stream, shading into the Gnostic conviction that our flawed material universe was created by an imperfect god.
- ch. 99 "Chapter 15 - Lies, Incorporated" **·** René Descartes — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Philosophical Skepticism — Opens Don Fallis's part with an inventory of Dickian deception: Quaid's implanted memories, replicants deceived into believing they are human in Blade Runner and Impostor, the framed Anderton, Ragle Gumm's manufactured town, and the Bureau's constant adjustments. Unlike Descartes' malicious demon or The Matrix, these are not skeptical hypotheticals but the kinds of deception that corporations, parties, and governments actually perpetrate — with us often complicit in our own deception.
- ch. 100 "The Epistemology of Deception" **·** David Hume, Immanuel Kant, Plato — The Noble Lie; On Miracles — Shifts from the ethics of deception (Kant's near-absolute condemnation of lying versus Plato's morally justified governmental lies) to its epistemology, defining deception as intentionally causing a false belief. This definition explains why Cohaagen deceives Quaid, who falsely believes he is a construction worker, while Rekall cannot deceive the Quaid who really is a secret agent, and why the Zoner Cale merely misleads Spencer Olham in Impostor without deceiving him — with Hume's reasoning about miracle testimony modeling when to believe a probable deceiver.
- ch. 101 "How Do We Get Deceived" **·** René Descartes — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Personal Identity — Catalogues the channels of deception: the senses (the nonexistent Martian canals, Quaid's fat-lady disguise and hologram watch, and the Adjustment Team literally remaking the world) and, more worrisomely, memory, with implanted pasts for Quaid, Rachael, and the Impostor replicant 'so that the Tyrell Corporation can control them better.' Real cognitive science backs the threat: Nader's reconsolidation experiments show memory is Read-Write rather than Read-Only, and 'lost-in-the-mall' interviews implant rich false memories without any drug at all.
- ch. 102 "Who Deceives Us" **·** Karl Popper, David Hume — Philosophical Skepticism; The Open Society — Defines the conspiracy through Cohaagen's team — Lori, Harry, Benny, and the turncoat Hauser — with the Adjustment Bureau as 'the quintessential conspiracy' claiming good consequences for humanity. Popper's argument that belief in efficient grand conspiracies is irrational (his 'cock-up theory of society') is tested against the Bureau's own bungled coffee spill that lets David meet Elise, while Keeley's Hume-style critique and the specter of unbridled skepticism about spouses, friends, and memories frame what it would cost to believe in such conspiracies.
- ch. 103 "Circles within Circles" **·** Karl Popper — Falsificationism — Applies Imre Lakatos's 'degenerating research programs' — geocentric astronomy surviving by adding epicycles — to conspiracy theories like Pentagon 'truthers' who must keep patching their account to explain debris, eyewitnesses, and phone calls. But David Coady's rejoinder, voiced through Lies, Inc. where the 'cranks' who doubted Whale's Mouth were right, and the makeshift excuses for Saddam's WMD, show the official story can be the degenerating program, so rejecting conspiracy theories out of hand leaves you easily manipulated.
- ch. 104 "Self-Deception" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Explains Cohaagen's plan — 'Hauser volunteered to become Doug Quaid. It was the only way to fool the psychics' — through Nietzsche's observation that great deceivers are overcome by belief in themselves in the very act of deception, and that one lie obligates twenty more. Against the Impostor replicant and the misled Arctor, the chapter sets the philosophical puzzle that intentional self-deception seems impossible, locating most cases, like Earth's poor clinging to the Whale's Mouth advertisements, in motivated, non-conscious belief maintenance.
- ch. 105 "How Can We Detect Deception" **·** Alan Turing — The Turing Test — Reads the Voight-Kampff test as a Turing Test variant in which the examiner must catch the machine pretending to be human, noting its everyday descendant CAPTCHA and its inversion of the polygraph: lack of emotion, not stress, is the tell that a subject is not human. Dick's characters mostly detect deception the way we do, by inconsistency — Rachmael ben Applebaum's looping audtrack exposes the Whale's Mouth hoax, and Quaid realizes Edgemar must be lying because a man implanted in a dream would not sweat at the prospect of being shot.
- ch. 106 "Chapter 16 - The Blob Necessitates" **·** Baruch Spinoza — Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura) — Matthew McCall's introduction argues that VALIS is about the fuzzy line between delusions, reality, and psychological wellbeing, following Horselover Fat through breakdowns and pink-beam revelations, and that Dick's signature theme is the interplay between metaphysics and emotions. It quotes Dick's own statement of affinity for Spinoza's 'Deus sive substantia sive natura' and promises that Spinoza's system supplies the groundwork for Fat's path to emotional liberation, a path that begins with the pink beam and with blobs.
- ch. 107 "Of Blob" **·** Baruch Spinoza — Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura) — The section recounts Dick's 2-3-74 experience and the eight-thousand-page Exegesis, then uses Fat's Tractatus to teach Spinoza's Ethics through a goo analogy: the blob is substance ('that which is in itself and conceived through itself') while everything in everyday life, including us, exists only as its modes. It concludes that despite what our senses suggest, thinking through the substance-mode distinction shows we are all contained in the blob, so what is true derives from concepts rather than sense experience.
- ch. 108 "The Nature and Origin of the “Mind”" **·** Baruch Spinoza — Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura); Spinozist Necessity — This section reads Fat's cosmology, in which the 'Mind' created the 'Brain' to preserve the memory of its dead sister and left every constituent of the universe partly deranged with grief, against Spinoza's proofs in the Ethics that there is exactly one infinite, uncaused substance, which is why Spinoza calls the blob God or Nature. It stresses Spinoza's necessitarianism: the will is not a free cause, even God had no choice not to create the world, and the actual timeline is the only metaphysically possible one, so on both Fat's and Spinoza's schemes suffering is a built-in metaphysical consequence.
- ch. 109 "The Origin and Nature of Affective Disorder" **·** Baruch Spinoza — Conatus (striving to persist); Spinozist Necessity — Using the opening of VALIS, the section explains Gloria's suicide through Spinoza's account of the passions: imagining we are hated without cause breeds hatred, and Spinoza's lone remark on suicide says those who kill themselves are 'impotent in mind,' overcome by external causes opposed to their nature, since our essence just is the conatus, the striving to persist in being. It then itemizes Fat's three tragedies (Gloria's death, the divorce, losing his son) as accumulating external causes that overwhelmed him into his own suicide attempt, and presents his therapist Maurice's 'take responsibility for your own life' as implicitly Spinozan advice.
- ch. 110 "Of Plasmatic Bondage" **·** Baruch Spinoza — Spinozist Necessity; Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura) — The section explains Fat's plasmate doctrine, with VALIS a Vast Active Living Intelligence System and Sophia the two-year-old who briefly cures Fat by revealing he is an alternate personality of Philip K. Dick before dying of a radiation overdose. It contrasts this failed miraculous cure with Spinoza's intellectual therapy: since 'in so far as the mind understands all things as necessary, so far has it greater power over the affects,' Fat should process Gloria's death as a necessity he could never have prevented, dissolving his guilt.
- ch. 111 "The Power of the Intellect, or of Fat’s Emotional Liberation" **·** Baruch Spinoza — Spinozist Necessity; Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura) — This section argues that although Fat's 'Mind' cosmology, unlike Spinoza's necessitarianism, leaves room for free will, Fat can still borrow Spinoza's therapy: Tractatus entry 29 says we fell through an intellectual error, taking the phenomenal world as real, so he is morally innocent, and Spinoza's concession that we suffer insofar as we are part of nature means suffering can be limited, not eliminated, by understanding its causes. It closes skeptically, noting that monist liberation demands ditching free will, contingency, and self-evident beliefs, so within a monist world 'sometimes it is an appropriate response to reality to go insane.'
- ch. 112 "Chapter 17 - The Gnosis of 2-3-74" *(no index entry yet)* — Ronald S. Green's introduction connects Dick's last novels to the Gnostic texts of the Nag Hammadi Library, where the material universe arises from accidents, mistakes, and the devices of an imperfect architect ignorant of the true creator. It recounts how the 2-3-74 visions began with a delivery woman's fish pendant and bright rectangular images, and argues that the contradictory retellings across VALIS, Radio Free Albemuth, and the Exegesis support one another the way Gnostic myth does, each an imperfect reflection of a higher truth that ordinary terms cannot express.
- ch. 113 "Dick’s Gnosis about Gnostics" *(no index entry yet)* — The section reconstructs the 1945 discovery of the Nag Hammadi codices and retells the cosmogonies of The Hypostasis of the Archons and On the Origin of the World: Sophia's experiment produces a veil of darkness, the aborted watery chaos, and Yaldabaoth, the blind ruler who declares himself God and shapes Adam from mud as a reflection of a reflection. It shows that Horselover Fat cites Yaltabaoth to a baffled psychiatrist and treats the Library, available in English only from 1977, as confirming rather than shaping his belief that his private insanity mirrors humanity's collective forgetting that we ourselves are divine.
- ch. 114 "Dick’s Twins" *(no index entry yet)* — This section explains the Gnostic doctrine of syzygy, necessarily co-existing male-female pairs, including the Gospel of Thomas's claim that Thomas and Jesus are identical twins, and reads Dick's lifelong mourning of his twin sister, dead five weeks after their premature births, as its biographical echo. It then traces syzygic pairings through the VALIS trilogy (Emmanuel and Zina, Herb Asher and Linda Fox, the strangely real-and-unreal Rybys) and argues that per Exegesis entry 32 the unfolding of the world narrates the death of half of a divine syzygy, the tragic motif Dick perpetually re-enacts.
- ch. 115 "Results of the Primordial Rape" *(no index entry yet)* — The section retells the Gnostic rewrite of Genesis in which the rulers, lusting after the luminous Zoe, defile only the clay replica she secretly substituted, while the real woman becomes the Tree of Knowledge; the instructor reveals the fruit grants gnosis rather than death, and Yaltabaoth's prohibition was itself engineered by the true God to draw attention to the tree. It draws out the consequences (expulsion, toil and childbirth as deliberate burdens, the undefiled bloodline of Seth and Norea) and notes a Gnostic parallel to Deckard's sexual aggression in Blade Runner.
- ch. 116 "Pink Light" *(no index entry yet)* — This section argues that Dick's handling of the pink light enacts the Gnostic conviction that salvation comes from direct inner revelation rather than faith, sacraments, or church, cataloguing his competing theories: transmissions from a VALIS satellite that may itself be Yaldabaoth, mere ruler of the material realm, possession by Elijah, or his being Thomas the twin of Jesus. It weighs Dick's answers to why the true God permits the blind ruler (self-reflection, God's love of games, or our own labyrinth built to see if we could not escape) and the Gospel of Thomas's warning that the divine within will destroy us if we do not bring it forth.
- ch. 117 "Ay, There’s the Wub" *(front)*
- ch. 118 "Chapter 18 - Replicating Morality" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — John Sullins's introduction frames evil in Dick as the absence of empathy, noting that in Blade Runner the Voigt-Kampf test exists only because the Tyrell Corporation's replicants mimic every human trait except empathetic response. It argues that Roy Batty and Rachel cross a threshold that puts them in moral parity with humans (Roy's love of life extending to his would-be killer, Rachel and Deckard in love) while many human characters devolve, and poses the chapter's question: what gives a human, robot, or alien moral personhood?
- ch. 119 "Beyond Lies the Other" **·** The Ethics of Care — The section reads Dick's first published story, 'Beyond Lies the Wub,' as the origin of his career-defining theme: the jovial, philosophic wub survives the captain who sees only fresh meat because its empathy is so total it can exchange minds with the man about to slaughter it. Defining empathy as seeing the world from another's viewpoint plus sympathizing (which the cornering cat, predicting the rat's moves, lacks), it ends with Dick's Exegesis: an evil magician-deity occludes our minds until a savior in trash form restores them, and without such a revelation you, the reader, are 'nothing but a robot.'
- ch. 120 "How to Tell if You Are Really Just a Robot" **·** Philosophy of Love; The Turing Test — Using Imposter's Spence Olham, Rachel in Blade Runner, and 'The Electric Ant,' the section asks how anyone could verify they are not a machine with implanted memories and drives, noting that Dick wrote himself into Garson Poole and re-enacted Poole's drastic self-experimentation in his decades of drug use. It then argues Dick's real criterion is agape, the spontaneous, unconditional love of ancient and Christian philosophy, which robots can simulate but never experience since they love only because programmed: 'You are a robot if you cannot experience empathy.'
- ch. 121 "Can a Blade Runner Love a Robot" **·** The Ethics of Care; Philosophy of Love — The section contrasts Dick's bleaker novel, where J.R. Isadore's love for the androids dies when they cut the legs off his rare spider and Deckard's union with Rachael is the 'summa of falsity and mechanical motions' that fuels his resolve to destroy them, with the film's redemptive romance built on Rachael being 'more human than human.' It argues the movie preserves Dick's thesis anyway: Roy Batty's final act of saving the enemy who hunted him shows the empathy that makes the replicants persons, perhaps more than human.
- ch. 122 "How to Build a Moral Robot" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); The Ethics of Care — This section draws design morals from Dick's warnings: machines built as ersatz humans deny the value of being human, robotic sexual partners are doomed deceptions (the novel's Deckard-Rachael encounter is the case study), and a genuine artificial moral agent needs empathy 'logically equivalent to agape,' though a machine reasoning on sound moral principles could still count as a limited moral agent with proportionate rights and responsibilities. The Three Stigmata's Palmer Eldritch, returned from deep space as a machine treating humans as resources, shows that the netherward pull toward machinehood threatens humans themselves.
- ch. 123 "PUBLIC RELATIONS GUIDE FOR NEW OFFICERS DIVISION OF PRECRIME" *(front)*
- ch. 124 "01. Don’t We Arrest Innocent People" **·** Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Writing as a Precrime PR manual, the section answers the charge that arresting people who have broken no law punishes the innocent: pre-criminals genuinely lack mens rea, so punitive blame would be inappropriate, but their detention is justified as prophylactic quarantine, like isolating an infant with a dangerous contagious disease, under a non-punitive containing attitude. It cites Dick's own 'Minority Report' language of 'neutralizing' Anderton and 'the prophylactic pre-detection of criminals,' plus the film's Hall of Containment, as evidence the system is preventive rather than punitive.
- ch. 125 "02. But Is It Really Inappropriate to Punish Pre-criminals" **·** Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — The section defends punitive attitudes toward pre-criminals through a 'pre-punishment' thought experiment: if Walter Wrath credibly announces tomorrow's wrongful harm and will escape all future blame, punishing him now is better than never blaming him at all. Precrime cases are analogous, it argues, because being stopped by others is no credit to the offender and not the right kind of fact to exculpate him; the person who would have done it 'remains on the hook.'
- ch. 126 "03. What Evidence Establishes Guilt" *(front)*
- ch. 127 "Philip K. Dick and Philosophy" **·** Falsificationism — The section argues Precrime needs no evidence of an actual murder, attempt, or plot because pre-criminals are charged with future-murder, which, unlike plots that fizzle or attempts that bungle, always succeeds absent intervention. Using Anderton's demonstration of Witwer's caught ball, it distinguishes a person's NA-future (if not arrested) from the A-future (if arrested), concluding that what happens after an arrest cannot falsify an NA-prediction, since the prediction only ever described the uninterfered-with path.
- ch. 128 "Philip K. Dick and Philosophy" **·** Reliabilism — This section rebuilds the evidential case for the precogs from their verified early track record, which was free of errors of commission (predicting murders that never happened) and omission (missing murders that did). The still-zero present-murder rate rules out omissions, and cases like Howard Marks, caught mid-attempt, form a random and representative sample of the precogs' predictions showing commissions have not crept in, since arrest-timing delays correlate with nothing systematic about guilt.
- ch. 129 "Philip K. Dick and Philosophy" **·** Reliabilism — The section concedes that Precrime techs erred in the Anne Lively case, failing to notice that some previsions showed ripples moving toward the shore and others away. But it argues this is only the general problem of interpreting any evidence, from confessions to forensics to eyewitness reports, and that human fallibility does not imply unreliability, any more than fallible traditional policing meant murders should go uninvestigated.
- ch. 130 "04. What about Leaks" **·** Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Fate and Foreknowledge — The section weighs leaking predictions to pre-criminals so they can reroute (the I-future), and rejects it for three reasons: the precogs' predictions are accurate only for people who never learn of them, standing by to catch a forewarned killer is costly, and would-be murderers have no right to know, since unlike a citizen facing contaminated water they could have avoided their path by not choosing it. It closes the guide's case that Precrime arrests people who deserve arrest, with appropriate attitudes and compelling evidence, without violating rights.
- ch. 131 "Chapter 20 - If the Universe Isn’t Real, How Should We Treat Other People" **·** Martin Heidegger, Emmanuel Levinas — Philosophical Skepticism; Authenticity — Andrew M. Butler's introduction opens with the ambiguous endings of Total Recall, Minority Report, and Blade Runner (the fade to white, the too-neat reunion, the improbable sunset) to pose skeptical doubt about whether any of Dick's realities are real, surveying Eye in the Sky, Flow My Tears, Time Out of Joint, and Next. Against the thought that if nothing is real nothing matters, it sets Eric Sweetscent returning to his failing wife, and introduces Dick's aim to fuse Hebrew monotheism with Heidegger's philosophy of thrownness, noting that Levinas made the attempt first and that for Dick the authentic human is the one who cares for others.
- ch. 132 "To Be or Not To Be—Is That the Question" **·** Emmanuel Levinas, René Descartes, Edmund Husserl — Phenomenology; The Cogito; Philosophical Skepticism — The section introduces Levinas (Heidegger's student, Nazi internment camp survivor, Talmudic scholar) for whom ethics outranks ontology ('To be or not to be?
