## Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike

- ch. 1 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Elizabeth Anscombe — Anthropocentrism — John Huss's introduction frames the franchise as mirroring successive revolutions: Taylor before the ape tribunal recalls Galileo's heresy trial, the Darwinian revolution that toppled humans from evolution's pinnacle is taken to its logical extreme from Boulle's 1963 novel on, and Rise of the Planet of the Apes stages a 'Molecular Revolution' whose wake-up call is addressed to 'human chauvinists' who forget we share the planet with other species. He reads the cover's interspecies erotica through the Sexual Revolution, quoting Elizabeth Anscombe on contraceptive intercourse and asking whether her argument can get us over the species line, and closes with President Morsi's Tahrir Square allegory of the films: 'We are human, we did do this to ourselves.'
- ch. 9 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 10 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes, John Stuart Mill — The Extended Mind — Kristin Andrews uses Taylor's silent attempts to show Zira he has a mind - mouthing answers, wiggling his fingers when she mentions the Hopkins Manual Dexterity Test - to stage the problem of other minds, pushing against Descartes's claim that language is required for thought and Mill's argument from analogy, while Dr. Zaius can always redescribe it all as 'a definite gift for mimicry.' Drawing on her fieldwork with the orangutan Cecep (the leaf-wiping pantomime, guiding the frightened Aldrin home from the turtle scare), she argues against reducing mindreading to false-belief tasks and for knowing minds through shared interaction, inductive overhypotheses, and natural context. She ends with an extended-mind point - 'when you're in a cage, you act caged,' and we offload thinking onto our homes and tools - so lab studies can show what apes can do but never what they can't.
- ch. 12 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** W.V.O. Quine — Indeterminacy of Translation; Speciesism — Sara Waller argues the films show language operating as a tyranny that measures minds and withholds moral standing: Dodge mocking signing Caesar as a 'stupid monkey,' Zaius dismissing Taylor's speech as mimicry, 1894 literacy tests used to disenfranchise Black voters, and IQ tests whose vocabulary sections double-count language skill. She surveys the non-linguistic tests the apes face - the Hopkins dexterity test, the Wisconsin Multiphasic, Kohler's banana-and-boxes task ('Because I loathe bananas'), the Lucas Tower, Caesar's cookie-jar deception - and then deploys Quine's 'gavagai' inscrutability of reference to argue that speech cannot be the ultimate measure of intelligence or moral worth. Nova's hand over Taylor's mouth and Zira and Cornelius's 'be clever... be quiet' suggest that under oppression, silence is the smart play.
- ch. 13 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Daniel Dennett, René Descartes, Ludwig Wittgenstein, William of Ockham — The Intentional Stance; Second-Order Desires (personhood); Ockham's Razor — Don Fallis proposes deception rather than language as the personhood test: following Dennett, a deceiver must be a second-order intentional system who can want someone else to have a false belief, as when General Thade lies to Senator Sandar about Ari's kidnapping, Zira and Cornelius feign muteness before the Presidential Commission, and Caesar fakes his own electrocution in Conquest. The roles' reversal makes this a test for the films' mute humans too, while Descartes's beast machines, Wittgenstein on dogs that cannot simulate pain, and Lloyd Morgan's canon voice the skeptical reading of fake alarm calls and Koko's 'Cat did it.' Against them Fallis invokes Occam's Razor over Hare, Call and Tomasello's food-competition experiments: apes track who sees what, but they fail the misinformed false-belief version, so real apes may not be 'sneaky enough to be people.'
- ch. 14 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes, Ludwig Wittgenstein, David Hume, Heraclitus — Anthropocentrism; Falsificationism — Bernard Rollin reads Dr. Zaius's tribunal as 'scientific ideology' in action - 'human see, human do' refuses to believe its own eyes, just as bishops refused to look through Galileo's telescope. He traces the ideology from Newton's 'hypotheses non fingo' through logical positivism's verifiability criterion (which validates the Hasslein Curve prediction while rendering 'there are intelligent beings in Heaven' meaningless) and Wittgenstein's point that 'killing is wrong' is not a fact of the universe, to the 'science is value-free' dogma that left animal pain untested and untreated - as he documents from his own campaign: the empty analgesic literature search, the 1985 federal legislation, and the pain physiologist whose dog research refutes his own denial. Zira's neurosurgery on mute humans repeats what Descartes's beast-machine doctrine licensed, and IASP's language requirement for pain collapses into a Cratylus-grade confusion of necessary and sufficient conditions ('You can't step into the same river once').
- ch. 16 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill, Michael Sandel — Virtue Ethics (arete); Humanity as an End in Itself; Utilitarianism; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Massimo Pigliucci reads Rise as a Greek tragedy of hubris and asks whether Will Rodman dosing his father with ALZ-112 was wrong, first dissolving the 'it's unnatural' objection and probing the cure/enhancement border with Daniels's Peter-and-Johnny growth-hormone case, vaccination-as-enhancement, and Eubulides's bald-man paradox. He then runs the decision through three ethical theories: Millian consequentialism condemns it by its results (his father dies and humanity goes extinct, though chimp happiness might outweigh that), Kant's humanity formula condemns using his father as an unconsenting experimental subject, and Aristotelian virtue ethics vindicates Will's compassion and courage - Pigliucci's own view, since sometimes our best is just not enough. He closes by rejecting Baylis and Robert's technological-inevitability thesis (we abandoned the Concorde, CFCs, and nuclear weapons before) and lets Jacobs's plunge into San Francisco Bay stand as the penalty for market hubris.
- ch. 17 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Peter Singer, Jeremy Bentham, Plato, Martha Nussbaum, John Locke — Speciesism; Animal Liberation; Euthyphro Dilemma — Travis Timmerman argues the series dramatizes Singer's equal consideration of interests: Zira frees Taylor once he writes 'My name is Taylor' because like interests must count equally regardless of species, while Dr. Zaius's erasing the writing, lobotomizing Landon, and destroying the cave artifacts is pure speciesism in Bentham's 'Can they suffer?' sense. He rejects the crude 'humans are smarter' argument (it would strip severely cognitively disabled humans of standing) and Nussbaum's species-normal version (it would permit caging Zira and Cornelius since normal apes are mute), then deploys Plato's Euthyphro dilemma against Locke-style God-given rights: a deity bellowing that human interests outrank ape interests is arbitrary unless grounded in independent reasons. Since farming severely cognitively disabled humans is obviously wrong and species membership is morally irrelevant, it is equally wrong to factory-farm and experiment on animals - so, like Caesar in Battle for the Planet of the Apes, become vegetarian.
- ch. 19 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Peter Singer, Bernard Williams — Speciesism; The Ethics of Care — Jonas-Sebastien Beaudry defends a 'moderate speciesism' built on relationships rather than individual capacities: Taylor's trial strips him of clothes, name, and speech - the symbols of ethical community - showing how institutional speciesism rationalizes domination behind the Sacred Scrolls' Declaration-of-Independence-style self-evidence. Against Singer's anti-speciesist challenge that any distinctively human capacity is shared by some animals or missing from some humans, he argues both camps wrongly pedestal intrinsic traits, and reads Taylor's love for the mute Nova together with the failed Project Nim as showing that within-species bonds of love, care, and family are genuinely and justifiably valuable without licensing mistreatment. Bernard Williams's 'The Human Prejudice' - should we surrender to superior invading aliens? - marks where impartial anti-speciesism leads, while Zaius's 'Man is evil' and the doomsday-bomb ending show extreme speciesism as self-fulfilling prophecy.
- ch. 20 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 21 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Possible Worlds — David Morgan separates the franchise's two kinds of time travel. Forward travel is physically respectable: special-relativistic time dilation (Taylor's six months against nearly 700 Earth years implies 99.99997 percent of light speed) and gravitational dilation near black holes, confirmed daily by muon lifetimes and GPS satellite corrections. Backward travel, as when Cornelius, Zira, and Milo flee the doomsday blast to 1973, invites the Grandfather Paradox - Hasslein killing the apes would erase the future they came from - but the films resolve it through a closed causal loop in which Hasslein's killings set Caesar's rebellion in motion. Morgan then reads the Aldo-versus-Caesar continuity clash between Escape and Conquest through Hasslein's freeway-of-time speech as a multiple-timelines model aligned with the Many Worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics, which also lets fans file the Burton and Rise reboots as parallel-universe futures.
- ch. 22 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Free Will vs Determinism; The A-Series and B-Series of Time — Ralph Shain argues forward and backward time travel are categorically different: relativistic time dilation is conceptually harmless (in Boulle's novel Merou could not return to Soror for a thousand years), but Escape from the Planet of the Apes' backward jump is conceptually impossible because it treats the open future as fixed like the past - Hasslein's plan to kill baby Milo is the Grandfather Paradox, checked against presentist, possibilist, and eternalist ontologies of time. The real philosophical engine is Aristotle's sea-battle argument from the law of excluded middle: since Cornelius's story of the takeover is past for the apes and future for 1973 humans, the film's causal loop (Milo saved at the circus) enacts the fatalist conclusion that the ape takeover will necessarily occur. Hasslein's freeway image of time defeats itself - switching lanes means landing in the past of a different, parallel universe, so the apes' jump would be travel between worlds, not times.
- ch. 23 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Plato — Justice in the Republic; The Philosopher King; The Noble Lie; Tripartite Soul — Greg Littmann maps Ape City onto Plato's Republic class by class: orangutan rulers who legislate, censor, and propagandize; gorilla warriors who enforce; chimpanzee producers who do all the work - including, pointedly, the science Plato made no provision for; and humans as the 'barbarians' Plato says may be enslaved or exterminated. The overlaps are detailed: the Sacred Scrolls' first article of faith functions as the noble lie's myth of the metals, orangutan funerals promise heaven to keep gorillas unafraid of death, and Zaius's erasing of Taylor's dust-writing and blowing up of the archaeological cave enact the rulers' duty to supervise stories. But the films also refute Plato: hereditary orangutans show that power corrupts philosopher kings, Dr. Honorius's 'reason' is dogma serving the faith, the gelding threat that finally breaks Taylor cracks the tripartite-soul analogy of justice, and democracy's rough virtue is that it lets us remove rulers 'without sticking anybody with iron spears.'
- ch. 25 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Plato, Jean-Jacques Rousseau — The State of Nature; The Social Contract; Ring of Gyges (why be moral?) — Leslie Dale Feldman reads the 1968 film's blasted opening as Hobbes's state of nature - 'solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short' - with the Lawgiver's 'Beware the beast Man' scroll echoing Hobbes's three causes of war (competition, fear, glory) and Plato's Ring of Gyges explaining why even the 'just' man acts rightly only under compulsion, both grounding the social contract's origin story. She then casts Dr. Zaius as Alexis de Tocqueville's tyranny of the majority - erasing Taylor's writing, lobotomizing Landon, and sealing Cornelius's cave 'to spare them all the care of thinking' - with Rousseau's man 'born free; and everywhere he is in chains' behind it. The chapter also traces Rod Serling's Twilight Zone fingerprints (nuclear-war twist endings like 'Time Enough at Last,' the cave of 'The Old Man in the Cave,' Adam-and-Eve survivor pairs, the beauty reversals of 'Eye of the Beholder') and reads Taylor and Nova's westward ride through Turner's frontier thesis and Kennedy's New Frontier, holding Serling's Hobbesian pessimism and his hope in tension.
- ch. 26 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Existential Risk; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Michael Ruse reads the 1968 film as a study in forbidden knowledge: Dr. Zaius has sealed the cave of human artifacts because he knows a prior human civilization destroyed itself and fears the knowledge could cause a repetition. Weighing nuclear weapons, recombinant DNA, bird-flu research, and data-driven political manipulation, Ruse argues Zaius's censorship is both impossible and undesirable, since the search for knowledge is intrinsically valuable and containment only increases the need for research. The film's deeper lesson is evolutionary: intelligence and sociality co-evolved only to the level 'good enough,' so any species that acquires weapons of mass destruction will likely destroy itself, meaning the Planet of the Apes scenario would recur across the universe.
- ch. 27 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Harry Frankfurt — Second-Order Desires (personhood); Animal Rights (subjects-of-a-life); Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Lori Gruen uses Taylor's cage and Caesar's confinement in Rise to examine real chimpanzee captivity in research labs and sanctuaries, asking whether captivity wrongs apes even when it causes no physical or psychological suffering. Against the view that autonomy requires language-grade self-endorsement, she argues chimpanzees are autonomous: they make choices, deceive (Tristan's false alarm call among the vervets), follow social norms, and set things right (Sheba returning Sarah's book), so denying them freedom is itself a wrong, as Caesar's 'Am I a pet?' moment shows. Since wild habitat is vanishing, she concludes the best we can do is captive care that respects apes' wild dignity and lets them come as close to feeling at home as captivity allows.
- ch. 29 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Thomas Hobbes, Plato, Jean-Jacques Rousseau — The Categorical Imperative; Ethical Egoism; The State of Nature — John Wilkins treats Caesar, who spares the neighbor he has beaten, as a Kantian exemplar whose reason lets him adopt the Categorical Imperative, contrasting him with the rational egoism of the film's human keepers and executives. He argues the film trades on the outdated Great Chain of Being, which Darwinian tree thinking dissolves: with no higher or lower species, only branching homologies, human nature must be continuous with ape nature, and talk of innate species essences must allow for statistical variation and dispositions rather than determination. Caesar's morality also needs more than reason, namely the primate dispositions of deference and empathy scaffolded by his human family, though Buck's instant moral conversion after enhancement shows the film is ambivalent about whether scaffolding alone explains it.
- ch. 30 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 31 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Socrates — Socratic Method (elenchus); Paradigm Shifts — John Huss asks whether Andy Serkis deserved an Oscar nomination for playing Caesar through performance capture, and argues that 'What is acting?' is a Socratic-style definitional question (like stumping Euthyphro on piety) of the sort Wittgenstein diagnosed as a language confusion, since the definition of movie acting is in flux. Using the seeing-as debate, Kuhnian theory-ladenness of observation versus Fodor's Muller-Lyer point that belief does not dictate sight, he explains why animators and fans see such different things in the identical raw footage. He concludes, with James Franco, that acting is an emergent ensemble property of actors reacting to one another on a shared stage, which performance capture enables rather than threatens, and a coda notes PETA's hope that CG performers will end the use of animal actors.
- ch. 32 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, G.E. Moore, Plato — Language Games; Philosophical Skepticism; The Noble Lie — Tom McBride reads the film through Wittgenstein's On Certainty: Dr. Zaius's certainties (flight is impossible, humans come from the forests) are hinge or riverbed propositions that cannot be doubted within the ape form of life, so Taylor's true story sounds not false but insane, like claiming to have slept on the moon. Speaking and able to prompt empirical investigation, Taylor fractures a foundational principle where G.E. Moore, facing a 'wild tribe' playing a different language game, could only confess that things 'stand fast' with him; and Zaius's explicit origin myth, a parallel to Plato's Myth of the Metals, is flimsy precisely because rulers who must insist on rules are not potent and are reduced to destroying the cave evidence. The genre's appeal is Margaret Atwood's 'controlled hallucination': crazy doors that swing on safe hinges, rivers that still have stable beds.
- ch. 33 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Theodor Adorno, Charles Sanders Peirce — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; Binary Oppositions — William McGinney argues Jerry Goldsmith's modernist score, with its twelve-tone themes, ostinati, cuica, slide whistle, and ram's horn, carries no inherent meaning but acquires it through learned associations: its dissonance recalls Cold War modernist concert music promoted as the high art of Western freedom, while its Stravinsky-like rhythms and 'primitive' timbres mark the apes as other and feed the film's deconstruction of the human-ape, advanced-primitive, civilized-barbaric oppositions. Because Taylor is given no heroic music, the score undercuts identification with him as an anti-hero, and its modernist associations implicate the technocratic, militarized West he represents in Earth's self-destruction. The chapter's machinery is the semiotic view of Kant, Adorno, Cage, Peirce, and Saussure: music modifies a film's images the way adjectives modify nouns.
- ch. 34 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 35 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes — The Cogito — Chad Timm reads Caesar's arc, from 'Am I a pet?' to 'What is Caesar?', through Lacan: the mirror stage fixes an alienating ideal-I (his reflection, the human children he watches), entry into sign language inducts him into the symbolic Other, and the over-stuffed signifier 'pet' confronts him with the real, precipitating an identity crisis that deepens when the shelter chimps also reject him. Against Descartes's cogito, an unconscious structured like language means the self can never fully know itself, and Zizek's ideological fantasy explains how the new master signifier Freedom quilts Caesar's ape liberation, with humans cast as the savage oppressive Other. His closing 'Caesar is home' completes the Zizekian Act, traversing the ideological fantasy and retroactively redefining the coordinates of his identity.
- ch. 36 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Charles W. Mills, Kwame Anthony Appiah — The Racial Contract; Epistemic Injustice — Jason Davis opens with Sammy Davis Jr. thanking the white producers for the best film ever made on black-white relations, and their cluelessness, to show that white privilege rests on an epistemology of ignorance, paralleled by the human enjoyment of ape slavery in Conquest. He reads the ape castes through the ontology of race: the films first stage race as biological realism and essentialism (warrior gorillas, chimpanzee scientists, orangutan priests), but Battle for the Planet of the Apes shows biology is not destiny, and human genetics (race accounts for about 0.012 percent of human variation) discredits biological racial realism altogether. Via Charles Mills's social ontology of race and Kwame Anthony Appiah's racial skepticism, the chapter treats ape racism as a mirror of anti-miscegenation-era America whose racial categories are social constructs, down to the dropped ape-human hybrid child.
- ch. 37 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Martin Heidegger, René Descartes — Dasein (being-there); Authenticity — Shaun May uses Heidegger's being-in-the-world to mark off the human: Caesar correcting Charles's fork grip shows a grasp of the unspoken norms governing equipment, and the apes of the 1968 film, surgeons with scalpels and years of training, inhabit the same world of projects, skills, and tools that Heidegger says other animals lack. Language seals the difference: Taylor's syntax, Zaius's carefully ordered 'The Almighty created the ape in his own image,' and socially learned practices like pointing and map-reading stand against Nim Chimpsky's syntax-free signing and chimps' failure to understand pointing. Caesar's foresight in stealing the ALZ-113 before leading the escape extends this to Heideggerian temporality, and the ape uprising becomes a move toward authenticity, lives owned as a meaningful narrative whole.
- ch. 38 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 39 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** John Locke, Tom Regan — Anthropocentrism; Speciesism; Animal Rights (subjects-of-a-life) — Norva Lo and Andrew Brennan set Richard Routley's 'last man' thought experiment beside Taylor's triggering of the doomsday bomb in Beneath the Planet of the Apes: both ask whether wiping out every living thing would be wrong once no humans remain to be harmed, which basic human chauvinism cannot condemn. The chapter argues the act is wrong from both sides: non-anthropocentrism counts the apes, mutants, and horses as intrinsically valuable beings, and even human-centered standards condemn it, since the talking apes and mutants are Locke's rational persons and Nova's people are biologically human, making Taylor's outburst 'you damned dirty ape' a form of speciesism. Taylor emerges not as simply mad or evil but as the Cold War logic of mutually assured destruction made flesh, a warning that excessive self-interest, personal or species-level, is itself the danger.
- ch. 40 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" **·** Charles Sanders Peirce, Ralph Waldo Emerson, Friedrich Nietzsche — Anthropocentrism; Pragmatism; Deep Ecology — Eugene Halton retells human history as the fable of Peirce's 'degenerate monkey': a neotenous, instinct-weak blunderer (Homo errans) whose gift for abductive guessing and attunement to the intelligence of the wild was inverted by agriculture and civilization into Narcissistic self-mirroring, anthropocentric religion, and the worship of the machine. The telepathic, rubber-masked mutants of Beneath the Planet of the Apes who worship the Alpha-Omega bomb ('I reveal my Inmost Self unto my God!') become a prophecy of our own screen-mediated, empathy-poor life, from Facebook to Botox, in Huxley's pleasure-conditioning rather than Orwell's pain. Against this, the chapter holds up Armando's Franciscan empathy for Caesar and the hope of a 'planet of the regenerate monkeys' re-attuned to the community of wild life.
- ch. 41 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 42 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 43 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings

- ch. 1 "Poker and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Poker and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Poker and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Poker and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Poker and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Poker and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Poker and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Poker and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 9 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Friedrich Nietzsche, Blaise Pascal — The Leap of Faith; Pascal's Wager — The editor's introduction stages poker and philosophy as twin crafts of risk: 'philosopher' was once slang for a card cheat, Socrates and Wild Bill Hickok both died for keeping villainous company, and the Buddha's six years to enlightenment are measured against the Birdcage Theater's eight-year poker game. It recruits Nietzsche's 'live dangerously' and Kierkegaard's leap of faith to defend the all-in as the only meaningful way to live, then traces probability from Cardano's Book on Games of Chance to Pascal's wager that believing in God is the smarter bet — the ancestor of today's pot-odds reasoning. Chris Ferguson's PhD, Annie Duke's psycholinguistics, and Jesse May's 'the trick to poker is mastering the luck — that's philosophy' set up the book's Texas Hold'em focus.
- ch. 10 "Poker and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** William James, Plato, Henry David Thoreau, René Descartes, Herbert Spencer, Ralph Waldo Emerson, Charles Sanders Peirce, Immanuel Kant — The Will to Believe; Tripartite Soul; Social Darwinism; Walden (deliberate living) — Ventimiglia mines No-Limit Hold'em for seven lessons philosophers also teach: we lack certain knowledge (Descartes' cogito is the famous quest for certainty, but philosophy's own history of disagreement proves uncertainty is the human condition), and like William James against Clifford we must still believe and act without the nuts — waiting for pocket aces while the blinds eat you alive is no strategy. Risking everything echoes Thoreau's escape from lives of quiet desperation, trusting hunches over arithmetic follows Thoreau and Peirce's sentimentalism, and the Darwin-and-Spencer competition of tournament poker hides a deeper cooperative social contract: get caught cheating and you are out of the game. It closes with Plato's four classic virtues from the Republic — wisdom, courage, moderation, and the justice of a balanced soul — as the perfection of a poker player.
- ch. 12 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** Karl Marx — Alienation; Ideology and False Consciousness; Historical Materialism — Belliotti tells of busting 'Pickle Puss' with flopped queens and of tight 'Howard the Vest' paying off his flopped full house to ask whether Marx's diagnoses — alienation in four forms, exploitation of surplus value, and false consciousness spread through the ideological superstructure by the economic base — condemn poker. He argues no: unlike coerced factory labor, poker is freely chosen creative activity that energizes our species-being like an absorbed artist, as Doyle 'Texas Dolly' Brunson's road-gambler career and his famous ten-deuce full-house call against Jessie Alto at the 1976 WSOP (and the 1980 loss to Stu Ungar's gutshot) show. Poker may still launder capitalist ideology — antes that lure investment, zero-sum rivalry, rugged individualism — but the owner-worker exploitation Marx feared has no equivalent at an equal-buy-in table.
- ch. 13 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Edmund Husserl, Socrates — Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Virtue Ethics (arete); Phenomenology; Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — Young reads David Sklansky's fundamental theorem of poker — play as if you could see all the cards — through Aristotle and Husserl. Aristotle's phronesis and virtue-as-habituation explain how excellent players come to perceive the particulars (pot odds, opponent tendencies, the best possible hand) and stay unharmed even when losing with the best play, while Husserl's Cartesian Meditations, translated hand-by-hand into poker terms, supply analogical appresentation for knowing the other minds seated across the table. Chris Moneymaker's 2003 'Bluff of the Century' all-in with nothing against Sammy Farha shows how bluffing randomizes play and lets you shape the truth you seek, until a slow-played quad aces ends the night in Socratic humility about the limits of knowledge.
- ch. 14 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Søren Kierkegaard, Gottfried Leibniz, Albert Camus, Blaise Pascal, Karl Popper — Existence Precedes Essence; The Leap of Faith; Principle of Sufficient Reason; The Meaning of Life — Sanders splits poker into two philosophical styles. The Rationalist — Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason, Pascal's domestication of chance into probability — plays like Sklansky, Chris Ferguson, and Howard Lederer, whose temptation is the paralysis of analysis; the Existentialist — Sartre's existence precedes essence, Camus' scorn for the absurd, Kierkegaard's leap of faith taken without decisive evidence — plays like Gus Hansen calling Antonio Esfandiari's $334,000 all-in re-raise with ten-high. A Russell-and-Popper-style regress of predictions (knowing a prediction changes its outcome) becomes the tournament 'hall of mirrors' of intentions read in Phil Ivey and Johnny Chan, and the chapter lands on Richard Taylor's existentialist point that meaning comes from committed doing, at the table as in life.
- ch. 15 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus, Søren Kierkegaard — Existentialism; The Absurd; The Myth of Sisyphus; Existence Precedes Essence — Vernezze uses Dostoevsky to make gambling existential: Notes from Underground's insistence that will trumps reason ('what do I care for the laws of nature and arithmetic?') and The Gambler's portrait of the calculating gambler — who loses like everyone else and worships money with a 'German' soul — prefigure existentialism's three traits: lost confidence in reason, despair as part of the human condition, and the willed overcoming of absurdity (Camus' Sisyphus happy, Sartre's condemned freedom). Dostoevsky's own roulette addiction fuels the reading, with Amarillo Slim and Brunson's side bets as heirs. The Cincinnati Kid's climax clinches it: Lancey Howard 'making the wrong move at the right time' by chasing a straight flush proves poker's essence lies beyond reason — a truly Dostoevskean activity.
- ch. 16 "Poker and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** W.V.O. Quine, Gilbert Ryle — Indeterminacy of Translation; The Web of Belief — Ellis analyzes expert poker as thought attribution, spelling the iterations out to the sixth order in a Big Slick hand against T.J. Cloutier, then argues via Quine's 'gavagai' rabbit and Davidson's interpretationism that attributing thoughts to opponents requires assuming deep shared belief — which explains why pros misread novices whose minds they cannot model. The centerpiece is Dan Harrington's reconstruction of Daniel Negreanu's 2004 river raise against Freddy Deeb as a set of fourth-order-or-below attributions (Deeb will read a small raise as a lure bet and fold the best hand), not one towering thought. It ends asking how anyone ever learns what an opponent thinks from actions that are a vector of beliefs and desires, and notes poker forces rare deep agreement among strangers worldwide.
- ch. 18 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Bassham and Marchese catalogue seven critical-thinking traps that cost even good players money: self-serving bias (Rochester Ricky donating $10,000 to Brunson's Texas road gamblers), short-term thinking (aimed at Aristippus' live-for-today hedonism), the availability heuristic (Brunson's red eights on a four-flush board), the fundamental attribution error (crediting wins to skill and losses to luck), loss aversion (which breeds tight-passive 'rocks'), superstitious thinking (Alexander ripping the pockets off his shirt for luck), and the gambler's fallacy (Ken Warren's bogus 'rush' theory of streaky cards). The moral is psychological self-knowledge: great players must know their own cognitive frailties, because — as Clint Eastwood says — a man's got to know his limitations.
- ch. 19 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** David Lewis — Fallis asks which probability should guide a poker decision, working one Big Slick hand ($20,000 call into a $160,000 pot) through four candidates: objective chances (already 100% or 0% under the dealt river card — useless without cheating), the TV viewer's WPT-cam probability, Sklansky's Fundamental-Theorem probability given the opponent's exact cards, and Beebee and Papineau's relative probability given what you actually know (9.5%, under the 11.1% pot-odds threshold, so fold). David Lewis's Principal Principle frames the first option, and Jack Good's value-of-information theorem explains why Sklansky's ideal remains worth approximating: additional information can never hurt your expectation.
- ch. 20 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** David Lewis, David Hume — Possible Worlds; Free Will vs Determinism — Northcott loses his first casino tournament to a fluky inside straight and mines the bad beat for philosophy of science: objective odds collapse into knowledge-relative probabilities (a card-tracking magician would assign different numbers to the very same draw), Laplacean determinism versus quantum chance bears on whether decision theory presupposes free will, and bad-beat counterfactuals — 'I'd have won the tournament but for that hand' — get David Lewis's possible-worlds closeness analysis and Hume's counterfactual account of causation, with no settled verdict. Even game theory cannot deliver a perfect system: a Nash-equilibrium strategy is only optimal against other optimal players, so the mindless all-in 'Stupidus' beats it. Conclusion: no can't-lose system exists, and poker will never be a game for robots.
- ch. 21 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** Gilbert Ryle — Lucey opens with the ultimate bad beat — four aces losing a $180,000 jackpot share to two straight flushes — to ask what poker knowledge could have told you, and answers with Ryle's distinction between 'knowing that' and 'knowing how' from The Concept of Mind. Knowing-that is a priori and internalized: hand rankings and five conditionals for spotting the best possible hand (board pairs, three flush cards, three-to-a-straight spans, diamond threats). Knowing-how is dispositional — folding 2-9 'Montana bananas' despite the rare flopped full house, adjusting value between limit and no-limit — and with Israel Scheffler's vertical spectrum from competence to mastery it explains why poker skill is endlessly refinable, which is why the game is so addictive and so frustrating.
- ch. 22 "Poker and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** Harry Frankfurt, Immanuel Kant — On Bullshit; The Categorical Imperative — Huss tests four models of bluffing on one K-9 all-in: it is not lying, because everyone at the table expects deception, so the victim is never Frankfurt's 'twice deceived' (and Kant's argument that lying fails where everyone lies applies); it is not bullshit, because Frankfurt's bullshitter ignores the facts a poker player cannot afford to ignore; it is not pure acceptance in Jonathan Cohen's sense, since bluffing adds deception to acting-as-if; and it is not full self-deception, since nobody can make themselves believe that 2+2=5 or that 4-7 offsuit is pocket aces. Good bluffing is an art blending all four: deceiving about hand and beliefs, prying attention away from your cards, acting as if, and trying — and necessarily failing — to fool yourself.
- ch. 24 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Barnhill and Solomon use Robert Varkonyi's staged five-minute 'agony' over pocket aces — pure theater that lured Ralph Perry into an all-in at the 2002 WSOP (and later busted Phil Hellmuth's A-K with Q-10 suited) — to ask when poker deception is morally acceptable and when it crosses the line: the towed-car lie, the fake-Marine claim, racist goading, and collusion are wrong. Their answer is an implicit-permission theory: by sitting down, players waive the right not to be deceived, but only where deception tests poker skills, so bluffs, disguised strength, and silently reading exposed cards are fine. The underlying order of the implicit rules — the game must test only poker skills — also explains everyday white lies and what you may tell a mugger.
- ch. 25 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** John Searle — Koepsell applies Searle's method from The Construction of Social Reality — picture the game, subtract an attribute, ask whether what remains still counts — to decide whether online poker is really poker. After tracing poker's lineage from Brag and primero through the 1830s draw to Texas Hold'em's communal cards, he argues poker's essence includes the artful, theatrical bluff carried by physical tells, mystique, and etiquette, so the disembodied online game, where only bets and chat remain, is 'a subset of the game' lacking the social institution that makes poker poker. His father's farm-purchase negotiation shows the same non-liar's bluff at work off the felt.
- ch. 26 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** Niccolò Machiavelli, Sun Tzu — Virtù and Fortuna; Strategy Without Conflict; The Ends Justify the Means — Hahn reads Doyle Brunson's Super System — 'I go into a Poker game with the idea of completely destroying it' — as applied Machiavelli: The Prince's fox and lion become the bluffer and the bully chip leader, 'better to be feared than loved' justifies cutting even old friend Sailor Roberts's throat at the table, and swift decisive attack (Tex Barch stomped out of the 2005 WSOP) avoids sowing the seeds of vengeance. Fortune rules half our events — the river card that fills an opponent's inside straight — so virtù means building dikes against the flood, as Cesare Borgia failed to do when his papal patron died. Sun Tzu's 'when able, seem to be unable' supplies the same disguise of strength in poker and in war.
- ch. 27 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill — Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Hamilton, unsettled that his seventeen-year-old daughter Tess has taken up poker, sorts the game's motives three ways. Competition is morally justified as a mutual quest for excellence with respect for worthy opponents (Robert Simon; Phil Hellmuth's tilt as the counterexample to Brunson's class); fellowship is Aristotle's three friendships — utility, pleasure, and the virtue friendship that shapes character — enacted in his father's VFW games and in Louise and Sailor Roberts keeping vigil when Brunson had four months to live, with Kant's rare moral friendship and C.S. Lewis's side-by-side companionship filling it out; but profit-playing invites the three-phase slide into pathological gambling addiction. His verdict: the motive decides the morality — poker is justified for competition and friendship, not for profit.
- ch. 28 "Poker and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 29 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** Emmanuel Levinas — The Face of the Other — Lindholm retells Stu Ungar's 1981 WSOP repeat — the 'Jews' (Ungar, Perry Green, Jay Heimowitz) against the 'Texans' (Ken Smith, Gene Fisher, Bill Smith) — through Levinas's Talmudic lecture 'The Temptation of Temptation.' Philosophy's sin is wanting to know before doing, while the Jews at Sinai accepted the Torah before knowing what it contained; the gambler's decision under risk, like Ungar's triple all-ins and final A-Q call against Green, enacts the same ethical priority of doing over knowing, so to lose is still to win if you dared to decide. Ethics as first philosophy — responsibility to the Other prior to comprehension, born of Levinas's Holocaust losses — closes the loop: unlike poker, life is not zero-sum, and deciding to decide lets everyone win.
- ch. 30 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Hobbes — The State of Nature; The Social Contract — Stoehr finds Hobbes in the saloon: poker in classic Westerns — Hatfield's farewell game in Stagecoach, and the cheating scene where Wyatt Earp first crosses Doc Holliday in My Darling Clementine — dramatizes the tension between the lawless state of nature ('solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short') and the rule-governed community built by an implicit social contract, with caught cheaters (Chihuahua signaling hole cards) marking where play reverts to primal vengeance. Poker itself is a Hobbesian paradox: a communal social event built on winner-takes-all competition, exercising both logic and intuition within luck's hard limits. The morally ambiguous Fordian hero — Doc Holliday above all — lives at the same crossroads of civilization and wilderness as the card table.
- ch. 31 "Poker and Philosophy" **·** Epictetus, Carol Gilligan, Friedrich Nietzsche, Sun Tzu — The Ethics of Care; The Dichotomy of Control; Feminism; The Male Gaze — Housel surveys a century of poker on screen — from the Tombstone Birdcage Theater's 'bird in a gilded cage' through Maverick, The Gambler, Rounders, and ESPN's Tilt with its brothel-break 'Matador' — to show women cast as eye-candy, damsels, or flukes (Joanne Woodward winning a high-stakes game without knowing how to play). Against the myth stands Annie Duke, who beat her brother Howard on the way to the 2004 Tournament of Champions title. The argument: poker rewards reading and projecting emotion, so women socialized into emotional intelligence hold an edge over macho men who suppress it — a retooled Stoicism fusing Epictetus's 'make the best use of what is in your power' with Gilligan's care ethics, backed by Nietzsche's trust in the senses and Sun Tzu's 'pretend inferiority and encourage his arrogance.'
- ch. 32 "Poker and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Hamblet, a violence scholar, asks why the 'cheating game' fascinates us, weighing Charles Lamb's Mrs. Battle (cards as dream-fighting that harmlessly dissipates aggression) and Georges Bataille's 'unproductive expenditure' before concluding that no-limit hold'em amplifies rather than vents hostility. Poker's history is soaked in blood — Mississippi riverboats, Bugsy Siegel's Las Vegas, and twice-indicted killer Benny Binion founding the WSOP from his Horseshoe ('I never killed anyone who didn't deserve it') — because a game whose core skills are lying and aggression attracts and rewards criminals. Lou Krieger's claim that poker mirrors capitalism and democracy is tested against David Callahan's cheating culture: Martha Stewart condoned because everybody does it, and the model poker-playing politician was Nixon.

## Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo

- ch. 1 "Psych and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Psych and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Psych and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Psych and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Psych and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Psych and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Niccolò Machiavelli — The Ends Justify the Means; Consequentialism — Robert Arp's introduction argues Psych is perfect for philosophy because Henry's games train observation and inference exactly as philosophers hone them, while Shawn's ruse shows how clever people abuse those powers to deceive - quoting Machiavelli's line that one who deceives will always find those who allow themselves to be deceived. It sets up the book's recurring ethical question about lying: lies for the liar's profit (Shawn avoiding jail in the pilot), paternalistic lies for the hearer's own good (Henry telling seven-year-old Shawn he 'blacked out' about his mother's death), and lies to benefit many (promising a terrorist freedom to find his bomb). Since Shawn's lies solve cases and save lives, the introduction suggests they may not be so bad in the end, though it admits wishing he would just come clean as a talented honest detective.
- ch. 8 "Psych and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Socrates, Plato — Socratic Method (elenchus); Consequentialism — Michaud argues that Shawn's whole psychic career runs on fallacies of relevance - the red herring of claiming to be psychic to dodge arrest, plus ad hominem mockery that deflects Lassiter's fraud accusations - so the show's comedy turns on bad logic being used to lead people to true conclusions. Socrates supplies the opposing voice: like the Sophists who argued any side for money, Shawn reasons for convenience and amusement, and his deception is an inconsistency of the kind Socrates refused in Plato's Crito, where he would not bribe his way out of a death sentence. An invented Platonic-style dialogue has Socrates question Shawn until he concedes that lying breeds more lying and harm - 'her name is Truth!' - before Shawn escapes the elenchus by spotting lipstick on Socrates's collar. The chapter leaves the verdict open: Shawn saves lives and raises the world's happiness, but his trickery also trains Santa Barbara to reason badly and trust con artists.
- ch. 10 "Psych and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Muniz plays narratologist, arguing that what matters in Psych is not the story but the storyteller: the 1980s prologues, alias gags, pineapples, and Lassie feuds are recurring formula elements, while Shawn's eidetic-memory sequence - the raised eyebrow, the chime, the highlighted detail - is the one necessary element around which every episode's rising action, climax, and denouement are arranged. Asking whether Gus chatting at the aquarium dolphins or the characters' comic pauses break the fourth wall, he answers no: the eidetic sequences only produce a 'projective illusion of cinematic image' that makes viewers feel they see through Shawn's eyes, so the wall is never actually broken - the show simply 'psychs you out in the end.' The chapter even structures itself like a Psych episode, prologue to climax, to prove the point that structure is function.
- ch. 11 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Ockham's Razor; The Web of Belief — Jones argues that Shawn's 'psychic' act is really hypersensory perception (HSP) - noticing cat fur, fine print, blood spatter - feeding inference to the best explanation (IBE), the natural abductive method Sherlock Holmes mislabels deduction, with Clever Hans and Ilga Kirks as real-world parallels. Applying IBE with Ockham's Razor to the two hypotheses 'he's psychic' versus 'he's hyper-observant,' she concludes the natural explanation should win for everyone: Lassiter's skepticism tracks the evidence, Gus knows better despite believing in ghosts, and Chief Vick shouldn't buy the supernatural story either. Juliet's belief survives only through background supernatural beliefs, a psychic-friendly culture, and ignoring the clues Gus feeds Shawn, which the chapter diagnoses as the same public misunderstanding of the scope and limits of science that keeps most Americans believing in ESP.
- ch. 12 "Psych and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "Psych and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Yim argues that what onlookers mistake for psychic power is thin-slicing, Gladwell's rapid pattern-recognition, the same skill behind John Gottman's ninety-percent-accurate marriage predictions and Paul Ekman's involuntary micro-expressions, which is how Shawn acquits the telenovela actor in 'Lights, Camera,... Homicidio' by reading genuine surprise on the tape. Criminals deceive by staging a context - a gun by the suicide's hand - that biases investigators the way thinking 'forest' biases us toward 'black bear,' while Shawn's two-stage slice, gut instinct plus conscious interpretation, isolates the telltale detail (a marinated steak in the fridge) that the staging was designed to bury. Henry's flashbacks - the cereal box opened from the bottom, young Shawn reading poker tells in the locker room - are boot camp that trains him to think outside conventional frames, producing the 'tint on the windows to the soul' certitude he invokes in 'Cloudy... with a Chance of Murder.'
- ch. 14 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Edmund Gettier — Reliabilism; The Gettier Problem — The Senors use Psych to separate true belief from knowledge: Shawn's hunch that Shabby the sea lion was murdered is true but shabbily evidenced, and his justified, true belief that a Clayton family member sabotaged the plane fails to be knowledge when the killer turns out to be a son-in-law he had no reason to think existed - a textbook Gettier case from 'He Dead.' They then weigh the two main theories of justification, evidentialism (with its base rates and prior probabilities) and reliabilism, and both vindicate the careful, methodical work of Lassiter and Juliet while Shawn's trigger-happy belief-forming habit strikes out twice. Shawn is redeemed only as an evidence-generator whose disregard for priors takes 'impossible' suspects like a murdered sea lion seriously, so that pairing his talents with the detectives' rigor yields the complete detective.
- ch. 15 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** William of Ockham — Ockham's Razor; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Guidry-Grimes treats Chief Vick's hiring of Shawn as a genuine problem in applied ethics rather than a joke: the Psi hypothesis fails Ockham's Razor and no controlled study supports paranormal ability, yet Vick - unlike viewers who know Shawn is a fraud - must weigh her obligations to victims, the department, and taxpayers on the evidence she has. The chapter argues that hiring Shawn is ethically defensible given his record of solving over fifty unsolvable cases, but it catalogues the costs: false hope for distraught families (Marc Klaas's resentment of psychic tipsters), damage to Lassiter's morale, wasted resources, and the fragile public trust bound up with taxpayer money. The conclusion is a compromise: Vick is ethically required to use every tool in the arsenal, including a successful 'psychic,' only in desperate high-stakes cases where the victim's family does not object, and otherwise merely permitted.
- ch. 16 "Psych and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Übermensch; The Last Man; Ressentiment — Malloy maps Nietzsche's three metamorphoses onto Shawn's life: the camel who carried Henry's burdensome training and the expectation he become a cop, the lion who slew the dragon 'Thou shalt' by stealing a car at eighteen and ending Henry's dream, and the child who creates his own values of fun, laughter, and silliness - defended as genuinely Nietzschean since the Overman must overcome the 'spirit of gravity.' Gus and Lassiter figure as last men, the herd animals Shawn manipulates and pities (Lassie's literal crap list a study in ressentiment), while only Pierre Despereaux and Mr. Yin count as true rivals because only fellow Overmen, forging values beyond good and evil, can genuinely challenge Shawn. The chapter closes on the Overman's dilemma - loneliness, backsliding into the herd, or trying to make Overmen of others - which explains why Shawn treats his friends and enemies the way he does.
- ch. 18 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, G.W.F. Hegel — Master and Slave Morality; Ressentiment; Will to Power — Ruiz casts Lassiter as Nietzsche's slave - his worth defined reactively against Shawn, his advice that 'all romance ends in despair or death' reproducing the Judeo-Christian slave revolt in morality that turned weakness into virtue - and Shawn as the master, a self-propelled wheel who bakes a pineapple cake in an Easy Bake oven for nineteen hours whether or not anyone is watching. Shawn's generosity (helping the wrongly accused, the ghost-struck, and the deluded, once even crediting a cat with solving murders in '9 Lives') is read as the noble overflow of superabundant power rather than pity, and his hostage-saving risk-taking as will to power understood as self-mastery. Even the central lie gets a dialectical reading - like art, pretending to be psychic reveals the truth hidden behind appearances - though the chapter concedes Shawn's slavish moments, from daddy issues to his obsession with one-upping Declan in 'Shawn 2.0.'
- ch. 19 "Psych and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** David Hume, Thomas Reid — Common Sense Philosophy; Philosophical Skepticism — McCraw turns the question 'should we trust Shawn?' into the philosophy of testimony: Lassiter's policy of never believing without independent evidence embodies Hume's demand that testimony be backed by evidence of the speaker's reliability, while Buzz McNab's instant faith embodies Reid's innate principles of veracity and credulity, and both extremes fail the department - Lassiter solves too late, McNab chases every early false lead. Juliet's developing, flexible trust - suspicious at first, convinced by results, never naive - models the circumstantial middle path that no hard-and-fast Humean or Reidian rule can capture. The verdict: treat Shawn's testimony as both psychic and psychotic, trusting the track record in some cases and discounting the wilder 'visions' in others, because when to trust is unavoidably vague and case-by-case.
- ch. 21 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Karl Popper — Falsificationism; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Mahon and Ceballos read the pilot through the big-lie principle credited to Hitler and Goebbels: the truth - hyper-observation plus a photographic memory - is too mundane to be believed, so only the biggest possible lie, 'I am a psychic,' saves Shawn from jail, exploiting the reverse psychology by which hearers assume no liar would say something so implausible. The lie's durability is then explained with Karl Popper's falsifiability criterion: like horoscopes and psychoanalysis, Shawn's psychic claim is unfalsifiable, so the ex-con's finger-counting 'tests' in 'Woman Seeking Dead Husband' can confirm it but never refute it - a virtue for a liar, and precisely what makes a claim unscientific. Finally the chapter shifts blame to the victims: like Madoff investors who 'kind of saw it coming,' the SBPD is self-deceived, complicit in a lie it half knows is a lie because the gift horse keeps closing cases.
- ch. 22 "Psych and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — King argues that memory is only generally reliable and hence a limited evidential tool, sorting procedural, episodic, semantic, and flashbulb memory before cataloguing Psych's failure modes: Shawn's source confusion that has him chasing Frenzy when the Yin killer follows Psycho, Abigail's accurate pier memory feeding the false conclusion that Shawn stood her up, and Lassiter's implanted recollections after Shawn feeds him 'remembered' clues in 'From the Earth to the Starbucks.' The fake FBI psychic Lindsey's suggestive questioning of the Home Depot cashier shows how easily vivid 'recovered' memories are manufactured - even though the show conveniently makes them true every time. The upshot: only Henry-trained, near-eidetic recall approaches Shawn's feats, ordinary memory needs physical corroboration before it sends anyone to jail, and everyone else should train recall like a muscle.
- ch. 23 "Psych and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant — Humanity as an End in Itself; Deontology — Rocha argues Kant is not the absolutist of legend: in 'On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy' Kant denies only a right to lie - Gus could be held responsible if his lie to Shawn's pursuing murderer goes wrong - and in The Metaphysics of Morals Kant openly leaves questions like polite untruths unanswered, to be judged by agents in their concrete circumstances. The deeper ground is Kant's duty to oneself: lying shows disrespect for the honest communication through which social beings sharpen their rationality, and so 'throws away and annihilates' the liar's dignity, which is why Uncle Jack's gold-hunting lies in 'The Greatest Adventure in the History of Basic Cable' are beyond rescue. On Rocha's reading even Kant could endorse the one lie to rule them all - claiming to be psychic - because it respects rationality and human life in a society that irrationally esteems the supernatural, while Shawn's Gus-alias gags and bunny fabrications remain immoral.
- ch. 25 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Immanuel Kant, Karl Popper — The Noble Lie; Utilitarianism; The Open Society; The Categorical Imperative — Stephenson tests Shawn's ruse against the major theories of justified deceit and finds it wanting: Plato's Myth of the Metals excuses paternalistic noble lies for social harmony that Shawn's self-aggrandizing motives cannot claim, utilitarianism collapses on the long-term costs of exposure (Gus, Juliet, Henry, and the SBPD condemned by association; clients betrayed; trust in law enforcement eroded), Kant's universalizability test sinks maxims like 'lie whenever a career opportunity is at stake,' and Popper's open society condemns just the deceit on which the psychic brand runs. Even the mutual-deceit analogy to poker and Sissela Bok's reasonable-person publicity test fail, since no public forum of reasonable people would bless duping paying private clients. The escape is extra-moral: Shawn's mischievous hokum is the socially necessary boundary-pusher, whose lesson against unreflective occult belief lands best when delivered with a laugh.
- ch. 26 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Augustine of Hippo, Niccolò Machiavelli, Friedrich Nietzsche — Deontology; The Ends Justify the Means; Utilitarianism; Ethical Egoism — The Bock brothers ask whether Shawn's fake-psychic lie is morally permissible, testing it against Augustine's and Kant's absolute prohibitions on lying, Nietzsche's claim that all language is metaphorical (the 'Lights, Camera . . . Homicidio' acting-as-lying scene), and Machiavelli's ends-justify-the-means deception from The Prince. Using Sissela Bok's three-question test they contrast justified police undercover work - Juliet infiltrating the sorority in 'Scary Sherry' and the roller derby team in 'Talk Derby to Me' - with Shawn's ruse, which fails because it protects Shawn's own interests rather than others. They end by weighing Sorensen's bald-faced lies (Shawn's 'I know you know I'm not telling the truth') and conclude Chief Vick's genuine belief shows these are real, indefensible lies.
- ch. 27 "Psych and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Edmund Gettier, Plato — The Gettier Problem; Reliabilism — Ronda Bowen argues that because Shawn delivers true conclusions under a false justification (psychic power), the SBPD's beliefs are Gettier-style justified true beliefs rather than knowledge, using Plato's Theaetetus (perception and true judgment fail as definitions) as the frame and Gettier's Smith/Jones and Ford/Brown cases to model episodes like 'Spellingg Bee,' where the police infer Miklous's guilt from Shawn's staged psychic demonstration. John Hawthorne's lottery propositions explain why Lassiter's 'Shawn isn't a psychic' certainty can never be fully justified, and the chapter closes on internalism versus externalism and the reliability of testimony, concluding the detectives become internally justified only when they re-derive Shawn's conclusions through their own reasoning.
- ch. 29 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** William James, John Dewey, Charles Sanders Peirce — Pragmatism; The Pragmatic Method; Democracy as a Way of Life — Amanda Lusky argues Shawn is a model pragmatist in the lineage of Peirce, James, and Dewey: he treats ideas as tools judged by consequences, is tough-minded about facts over theory (James's temperament distinction), and applies the pragmatic maxim from the squirrel-and-tree dispute to his loosely formed but working hunches. His co-operative inquiry with Gus and the SBPD - Gus's safe-cracking knowledge in 'Sixty Five Million Years Off,' passing Lassiter's polygraph in 'Shawn Rescues Darth Vader' - enacts Dewey's democratic community solving problems together, and the chapter reads his tolerance of Gus's paranormal leads ('The Devil's in the Details') as pragmatic openness that enriches Santa Barbara's democratic life.
- ch. 30 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Edmund Gettier — The Gettier Problem; Reliabilism — Courtland Lewis replays Plato's Theaetetus with Shawn and Henry to show that perception and true judgment fail as accounts of knowledge, then recasts both Gettier cases with Psych material: Chief Vick's justified-but-lucky belief about the chief-of-police job, and Juliet's disjunction 'Shawn is a psychic or Gus is in Mazatlan.' Since justified true belief is not knowledge, he argues Shawn's trained senses fit reliabilism - distinguished from lucky predictors like Leonard Koppett and probed through Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp against Gus's super sniffer - and closes by combining reliabilist-foundationalism (Alston's two levels of knowledge), coherence theory, and Klein's infinitism into Shawn's observe-eliminate-conclude method.
- ch. 31 "Psych and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 32 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** David Hume, Daniel Dennett — Bundle Theory of Self; Personal Identity — Dena Hurst reads Shawn as the mythological trickster - the fool who fools fools - who brings disorder to order by overturning hierarchies (Henry's ring-in-the-box lesson in '9 Lives'), taunting Lassiter, and inventing Gus's nicknames, while using his convenient psychic act to surface clues when found and excuse blunders. She argues people buy the act because we crave patterns and motivated narratives (Alfred Mele's work on seeing what we want to see), and closes with Hume's and Dennett's view that the self is a loose narrative we star in: Shawn literally invents himself as psychic detective, an exaggeration of the identities we all construct.
- ch. 33 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Falsificationism; Philosophical Skepticism — Courtney Neal explains that Santa Barbara believes Shawn is psychic because pseudoscience offers easier, more appealing explanations than the truth: in the pilot, 'he's psychic' beats 'he's the killer' as a narrative that fits the facts, and psychic claims are worded so they cannot be disproved. She shows how Shawn's real observational deductions are packaged through cold reading (the comic-convention scene in 'Shawn vs. the Red Phantom'), Robert Cialdini's social-influence principles of liking, social proof, and commitment/consistency, and the self-fulfilling prophecy of his reputation - so even Lassiter's skepticism cannot dislodge a belief the city keeps confirming.
- ch. 34 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Karl Marx — Ideology and False Consciousness; Alienation; Class Struggle — Jeff Ewing applies Marx's critique of religion - the supernatural as ruling-class ideology, 'the opium of the people,' behind which priests and shamans hide real material processes and prop up hierarchy - to Shawn, who likewise masks his genuinely material observational talent as psychic gift to escape arrest in the pilot and keep access to SBPD cases. But the comparison inverts: unlike Marx's priests, Shawn serves ordinary people rather than the ruling class, and the chapter concludes he is better understood as an alienated worker - forced by a repressive state's threat of prosecution to sell a false product, defined by what he is not, and never credited for his true skill.
- ch. 35 "Psych and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 36 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Laozi, Zhuangzi — The Tao (the Way); Wu Wei (effortless action); Yin and Yang; Zhuangzi's Perspectivism (butterfly dream) — John Thompson argues Psych embodies the Daoist Way of reversal from the Daodejing and Zhuangzi: every episode begins with a death that triggers Shawn and Gus's irreverent, backwards-tracing investigation, their untrained spontaneous 'gifts' exemplify wu wei like Cook Ding carving an ox, and their bickering partnership is yin-yang interplay (as when Gus leads the joking in 'An Evening with Mr. Yang'). Zhuangzi singing at his wife's funeral parallels the Shabby the Sea Lion and 'Dust in the Wind' funeral parodies, the show's blurred TV-versus-fandom reality echoes the butterfly dream, Lassiter succeeds when he relaxes into wu wei ('Feet Don't Kill Me Now'), and the closing bloopers enact Dao's endless reversal - though the chapter ends by conceding Dao defies the very label 'Daoist show.'
- ch. 37 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); The Golden Mean; Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Patricia Brace maps Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics categories of friendship onto Psych: Shawn's first-season ties to the SBPD are friendships of utility, the shared hobbies and bar nights (tap dancing in 'Feet Don't Kill Me Now,' 'Neil Simon's Lover's Retreat') build friendships of pleasure, and Shawn-Juliet matures from utilitarian boundaries into erotic friendship. Lassiter's lie-detector threat to protect Juliet in 'Shawn Rescues Darth Vader' and the lifelong Shawn-Gus bond ('Gus Walks into a Bank') approach complete friendship grounded in virtue, while the Henry-Shawn paternal friendship heals as Shawn develops the golden mean, and the vicious Mr. Yin and Yang - full of regret, incapable of complete friendship - show the life without it.
- ch. 38 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, René Descartes, Augustine of Hippo — Platonic Love (the ladder of love); Theory of Forms; Autonomy of the Will; Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — C. Scott Sevier argues Henry deliberately recreated Shawn as Aristotle's 'another self' - Lassiter's 'which one?' joke in the kidnapping episode makes the identity explicit - and reads this through Plato's Symposium: via Diotima's ladder of love and the doctrine of forms, Henry achieves immortality by reproducing beauty in his son's educated soul, not just his body. The chapter then frames Shawn's fierce independence against his constant recourse to Henry's voice as the collision between medieval deference to authority and the modern ideal of autonomy in Descartes and Kant, showing that both thinkers quietly borrowed from Augustine (the causal adequacy principle, the good will), so Shawn's 'autonomy' is itself the product of his father's training - an internalized authority indistinguishable from his own.
- ch. 39 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Feminism; Epistemic Injustice; One Is Not Born a Woman — Mona Rocha asks whether Psych is sexist given Shawn's eighth-grade-girl caricature of Juliet in 'Spellingg Bee' and the secret knowledge kept from the show's women, then argues it is not: the women's inferior epistemic position is a byproduct of the con, not misogynist gatekeeping, because Shawn works collaboratively and non-hierarchically, shares credit (solving Lassiter's Back Bay Killer case for him in 'From the Earth to Starbucks'), gives the Chief the glory in 'There Might Be Blood,' and confronts the oilrig chauvinist outright. The contrast is The Mentalist, where Patrick Jane's withholding of deductions from Lisbon - going behind her back in 'Red Hair and Silver Tape' and getting evidence thrown out in 'Blood Money' - enacts patriarchal paternalism that undermines female leadership.
- ch. 40 "Psych and Philosophy" **·** Philosophical Skepticism; Falsificationism — This chapter is a skeptical debunking tour of real-life 'psycho psychics' - Babylonian astrologers, the Delphi oracle that set Socrates testing the claim he was wisest, Nostradamus's hindsight-friendly quatrains, Blavatsky, Cayce, spoon-bender Uri Geller, and Sylvia Browne's failed Shawn Hornbeck prediction - arguing that no repeatable, peer-reviewed evidence of ESP has ever existed and that figures like cold-reading psychic detective Peter Hurkos thrive on gullibility. It ties to Psych through Gus's credulity about UFOs and werewolves and the real police practice of consulting psychic detectives that Shawn's con parodies, while Houdini's congressional testimony and James Randi's Million Dollar Challenge model the evidence-demanding skepticism the show's fake psychic gets away from.
- ch. 41 "Psych and Philosophy" *(notes)*
