## Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Table of Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "ii" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "iii" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "iv" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Cast Members" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "Cold Open The Introduction" **·** The Unexamined Life — The editors introduce the volume by arguing that SNL, like philosophy, trains viewers to regard the world with a critical, questioning eye: four and a half decades of parody and satire wired generations of fans to think philosophically before they could articulate why. Land Shark, Spartan Cheerleaders, and Trump-era Update bits are cited as the shared generational memory the book will now analyze.
- ch. 8 "Part I THE OPENING MONOLOGUE" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "When the Subject is Not the Butt Schmitts Gay Beer" **·** Plato — Objectification; Heteronormativity — Tallman asks why SNL may mock presidents (Chase's pratfalling Ford, Carvey's Bush) and Clintons but not unchosen groups, framing the question with the aesthetics debate among radical autonomism (Bell), radical moralism (traced to Plato and Tolstoy), and moderate moralism. Sketches from Samurai Futaba to Farley's Lunchlady Land show jokes can punch up, punch down, or elevate a low-status group. The Schmitts Gay beer sketch, she argues, ridicules not gay men but beer-ad conventions: swapping the usual female sex objects for men in speedos exposes the objectification and heteronormativity viewers had stopped noticing, so the butt is the advertising industry.
- ch. 10 "Responsibility" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Karl Marx — Existence Precedes Essence; The Look (hell is other people); The Absurd; Alienation — Christiansen reads SNL's first head writer Michael O'Donoghue ('Mr. Mike') through Sartre: the Least-Loved Bedtime Tales (Brer Rabbit skinned alive, 'there's no moral... just random acts of meaningless violence') dramatize a world where existence precedes essence and narratives lie; 'Sartresky and Hutch' stages the absurd via a Vietnam veteran with PTSD; and the needles-in-the-eyes impressions embody Sartre's vulnerability to the Other, which Mr. Mike's dark glasses shut out. The chapter ends with Sartre's Marxist turn in the Critique of Dialectical Reason, arguing O'Donoghue's angry 'Police State' sketch shows that scarcity, alienation, and organized state violence are contingent and can be fought, which is where his nihilism leaves room for hope.
- ch. 11 "Robust Social Critique" **·** John Stuart Mill — The Harm Principle; On Liberty — McGowan asks how SNL gets away with offensive material, from Larry David's concentration-camp monologue to the Chase-Pryor 'Word Association' and 'Nude Beach.' He argues censorship fails because offense is historically relative and slippery-slope prone, and that on Mill's On Liberty the harm principle never licenses suppressing speech SNL viewers can freely avoid, a point he sharpens with Feinberg's Volenti maxim and the offense principle. He closes by defending offensive comedy as robust social critique: Mill's fallibilist case that free speech drives human progress, with Baldwin's Trump and Tina Fey's Charlottesville bit as comedians speaking truth to power.
- ch. 12 "And Now, Deep Thoughts…" **·** Socrates, Plato — Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know); Socratic Method (elenchus) — Reynolds places comedy on a spectrum from philosophy to satire to smart-assery and argues SNL mostly sits at the silly end: Gumby, Mr. Robinson, Hermione's cleavage, and Hobbit Office are parody with an absurd twist but no constructive target, unlike genuine satire such as Mr. Bill. He develops the comparison through Aristophanes' Clouds, whose caricature of Socrates at the Thinkery helped send him to his death, and through the 'Playboy Philosophy' sketch with Belushi as Socrates. Socrates himself emerges as a satirist: the oracle of Delphi, his claim to know only that he knows nothing, and his elenchus that unmasks the supposedly wise are read as comedy in the service of seriousness, before the chapter concedes SNL's absurdism is philosophical mainly in mocking an absurd world.
- ch. 13 "Part II SOME POLITICAL SKETCHES" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "Live from Omaha" **·** John Stuart Mill, Alan Turing, Socrates — The Turing Test; On Liberty — Irwin argues that SNL's caricatures (Fey's Palin, Baldwin's Trump, Aristophanes' Socrates in the Clouds) misrepresent their targets and that learning politics from comedy traps viewers in ideological bubbles, since satire flatters rather than informs. He introduces the Ideological Turing Test, adapted from Turing's test: state your opponent's view so accurately and sympathetically that a neutral observer cannot tell it is not yours, and grounds the duty to learn the other side from its own partisans in Mill's On Liberty. The 2016 'Bubble' sketch passes the test, he says, but SNL's liberal bias (gentle Sanders, untouchable Obama) rarely challenges its audience, and a conservative 'Live from Omaha' alternative would just rebuild the bubble on the other side.
- ch. 15 "“We Always Have Something To Do”" **·** Michel Foucault — Power/Knowledge — Engels uses Foucault's Archaeology of Knowledge, authorities of delimination, and power/knowledge to show that SNL now produces rather than merely reports political truth, as when the Fey-Palin sketch shifted media blame for the Couric interview from the McCain campaign onto Palin herself. The 2016 sketches (McKinnon's Clinton as the inevitable winner, David's Sanders as a fringe idealist, Baldwin's Trump as a self-sabotaging loser) are read as discursive framings that confirmed and shaped mainstream narratives. Like Foucault's doctors defining madness, comedy writers now set the boundaries of political truth, which spotlighted sexist double standards but proved dangerous when SNL's detached writers misread working-class voters; following Foucault's 'everything is dangerous,' she concludes we always have something to do.
- ch. 16 "Where in the Hell is Chris Rock" **·** Charles W. Mills, W.E.B. Du Bois, Kwame Anthony Appiah, Kimberlé Crenshaw, Frantz Fanon — Double Consciousness; The Racial Contract; Intersectionality — Wisnewski reads SNL's race comedy as applied philosophy of race: the Chase-Pryor 'Word Association' sketch shows Mr. Wilson's counter-slurs as an assertion of personhood against Mills's racial contract, Eddie Murphy's Mr. Robinson's Neighborhood and 'White Like Me' expose implicit bias and white privilege, and 'The Day Beyonce Turned Black' illustrates Du Bois's double consciousness. Appiah's racialism explains why Leslie Jones playing Trump strikes audiences as outrageous while white women play men routinely, and Appiah's biological anti-realism about race undercuts that reaction. 'Black Jeopardy' with Tom Hanks's MAGA-hatted Doug finds common ground across race that the 'Lives that Matter' ending sharply limits, Fanon's violence route is raised and set aside, and Crenshaw's intersectionality frames why cast diversity is more than skin-deep.
- ch. 17 "And in the End" **·** Socrates, David Hume, Friedrich Nietzsche — On Bullshit; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Irwin and addictions specialist Lombardo ask where comic inspiration comes from, using Socrates' discovery that poets do not know the meaning of their own work, Hume's account of creativity as recombining materials of experience, and Nietzsche's point that inspiration is really continuous production sifted by judgment, to explain why Belushi and Farley treated cocaine and alcohol as muses. They contrast Belushi's fatal 'I use drugs' hubris, which no one around him challenged, with Farley's genuine twelve-step recovery, three sober years, and relapses. Stuart Smalley's affirmations, which bullshit himself into feeling 'good enough,' spoof recovery culture's cliches while Farley's story shows what actual recovery demands, ending with the advice to look elsewhere for the muse.
- ch. 18 "Part III SOME SKETCHES FEATURING YOUR FAVORITE RECURRING CHARACTERS" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "All Human Experience is an Impression" **·** John Dewey, William James — Experience and Education; Stream of Consciousness — Ruetenik argues the best SNL impressions are not 'spot on': Carvey's Bush ('Not gonna do it. Wouldn't be prudent') and the Tom Brokaw pre-tapes sketch created new experiences rather than faithful copies, while Darrell Hammond's exact impressions made him a 'tribute band' without Carvey's artistry. Dewey's Art as Experience and James's selective attention, in which every perceiver is an impressionist ignoring the blooming buzzing confusion, ground the claim that all experience is creative re-presentation rather than tribute to reality. He then turns the point political: SNL casting Amy Poehler over a spot-on Black impressionist as Michael Jackson tells us something about the audience's own selective, and possibly racist, experience.
- ch. 20 "Fighting the Real Enemy" **·** Plato, Friedrich Nietzsche — The Problem of Evil; Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Justice in the Republic — Johnson asks why Sinead O'Connor tearing the Pope's photo ended her career while SNL's own religion sketches drew little fire: 'DJesus Uncrossed' targets Tarantino's gratuitous violence rather than Jesus, the Tebow sketch ridicules prayers for football wins that Nietzsche said cheapen God into a servant of chance, and 'God's a Boob Man' satirizes the God's Not Dead films' strawmanning of atheists. Louis C.K.'s God monologue, he argues, raises the burden of proof and the problem of natural evil, best answered by Carlin's joke of a God subject to physical laws. The Church Lady embodies Warmke and Tosi's moral grandstanding, whereas O'Connor's protest does not, and the chapter ends on Plato's Republic: better to be a virtuous person scorned as a villain, like O'Connor, than a celebrated villain, though her tragic life strains Plato's promise that virtue pays.
- ch. 21 "“We’re Not Worthy”" **·** Bertrand Russell, Ludwig Wittgenstein — Language Games — Holt reads Wayne's World as applied philosophy of play: Wayne and Garth's basement show is intrinsically motivated leisure in Huizinga's sense, free, rule-bound, absorbing, and outside ordinary life, and Russell's 'In Praise of Idleness' supplies the play ethic against the work ethic. Against Wittgenstein's claim that games cannot be defined, Suits's definition of games as the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles is applied to 'A-sphincter-says-what?', the '...not!' game, and one-on-one hockey with Gretzky. The dark side of play closes the chapter: Wayne and Garth exclude and mock outsiders, and the leisure of their magic circle rests on unacknowledged labor like Wayne's mom's laundry.
- ch. 22 "It’s Good to Be a Fan if …" **·** Aristotle — The Golden Mean; Virtue Ethics (arete) — Barrett uses Bill Swerski's Super Fans to map a spectrum of fandom from casual to moderate to Super Fan, then applies Aristotle's doctrine of the mean to the virtues and vices of fandom: knowing trivia is a virtue (the Trekkies sketch), admiring athletic excellence is noble, but excess becomes licentious obsession, Shatner's 'Get a life!', heart attacks at Ditka's, and spending Thanksgiving with da Bears instead of family. Deficiency appears in bandwagon fans who lack commitment and loyalty, and the Red Sox fans' hospitalized heartbreak shows misplaced priorities in grief. Moderate fandom, loyal to people first and teams second, is the virtuous mean.
- ch. 23 "Part IV AND NOW FOR OUR MUSICAL GUEST" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Andy Kaufman Lip‐synchs" *(no index entry yet)* — Gracyk argues that SNL's liveness lies in real-time broadcast rather than co-presence, rejecting the performance-studies claim that televised audiences see only simulations: a performance is whatever the performer frames for audience attention (Sparshott's isolating act of attention, Thom's for-an-audience condition, Davies's framing), and mediated viewing counts. On that basis Eminem's contested 'Mosh' and 'Bezerk' appearances either were not performances or were badly framed ones, since he failed to signal that his prerecorded vocal was meant as intentional doubling. Andy Kaufman's Mighty Mouse lip-synch on the 1975 premiere, by contrast, openly framed its own fakery as 'Foreign Man,' a Warholian act that made lip-synching itself the philosophical subject and so a great live performance about what performance is.
- ch. 25 "Part V WEEKEND UPDATE" *(front)*
- ch. 26 "We’re Here to Pump ‐clap‐ You Up! The Goal of SNL and “Weekend Update”" **·** Sigmund Freud — Fried recasts Norm Macdonald's firing from Weekend Update as a philosophical dispute about the goal of comedy: NBC executive Don Ohlmeyer wanted wall-to-wall laughter and applause, guaranteed by recurring characters and celebrity walk-ons, while Macdonald hated applause as a cheap voluntary 'we agree' and aimed only at involuntary laughter he could not pander his way to. Eastman's play theory of laughter as an instinctive, uncontrollable response supports Norm, while Freud's relief theory, humor as release of pent-up tension, fits Ohlmeyer's comfort comedy. Fried concludes that if SNL is merely a comedy platform Norm was right, but as a shared cultural ritual that also comforts after tragedy, SNL may legitimately aim at more than involuntary laughter.
- ch. 27 "A New Holiday Album A Lesson Is in the Lyrics" **·** John Dewey — Democracy as a Way of Life; The Public Sphere — Sudnick and Garrett stage the Dewey-Lippmann debate through Weekend Update's citizen journalists: Drunk Uncle and Girl at Party exemplify Lippmann's propagandized pseudo-environments and echo chambers, while Stefon parodies the expert gatekeeper his technocratic 'machinery of knowledge' would install. Dewey's The Public and its Problems answers that democracy needs public education, a free and publicly funded press, and wide participation, with Point/Counterpoint and Cathy Ann's plea to log off and meet face-to-face as comic images of deliberative citizenship. The chapter ends with Dewey's hope that artists, from Opera Man to Sandler's Chanukah Song, are the real purveyors of news in a democracy consummated by artful communication.
- ch. 28 "That’s the News. Good Night and Have a Pleasant Tomorrow" *(no index entry yet)* — Erion reads Weekend Update as comic media theory built on Postman's Amusing Ourselves to Death and McLuhan's 'medium is the message': television's entertainment bias shapes what its content can be, and SNL's fake newscast has demonstrated the 'Now...this' incoherence of TV news from the 1975 premiere's disaster teasers, Blaine Hotel slashings report, and Goggles-and-Pip feel-good story onward. Later sketches parodying Morning Joe, Dateline's Pervert Hunters, and CNN's animated reenactments keep the same critique alive for cable and social media. Because Postman himself proposed parody along the lines of SNL as television's only self-critique, the chapter closes asking whether comedy can expose TV from inside TV or is inevitably co-opted by it, leaving education as the last hope.
- ch. 29 "Dysfunctional Family Feud The No Special Obligations View" **·** Confucius — Xiao (filial piety); Philosophy of Love — Southworth and Tallman use David Spade's 'falling star' joke about Eddie Murphy, and Murphy's twenty-year SNL boycott, to test three theories of familial obligation against the show's self-described 'family.' The role-based Just Because View, identified with Confucian filial piety, condemns Spade's disrespect toward an SNL elder but also forbids Murphy's divorce from the family; the contractarian Reciprocity View says Spade owes Dennis Miller but not Murphy, unless Murphy's saving the early show counts; and Jane English's No Special Obligations View, on which family should work like friendship, love rather than debt, clears Spade entirely. Sketches from the Vogelchecks' kissing family to Dysfunctional Family Feud supply the counterexamples.
- ch. 30 "Part VI THE ABSURD STUFF THAT HAPPENS NEAR THE END" *(front)*
- ch. 31 "Live From New York" **·** Plato, Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); Allegory of the Cave — Perez sorts SNL's realities using Plato's cave and Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation: Kate McKinnon's Bieber Calvin Klein ad is a first-phase reflection, Natalie Portman's raps a masking second phase, Ferrell's commodified Bush a second-order copy, and Maya Rudolph's Donatella Versace a third-phase simulacrum with no reality behind it that Versace herself protested. The Church Lady's 2016 Update appearance and the Palin-meets-Palin and Hillary-at-the-bar sketches show characters substituting for the real, while the May 2018 cold open where the real Stormy Daniels tells Baldwin's Trump 'a storm's a-comin',' live-tweeted by @nbcsnl, achieves Baudrillard's hyperreality where fiction and reality are abolished as distinct. Studio 8H becomes a Plato's cave viewers willingly re-enter each Saturday to glimpse the real through simulation.
- ch. 32 "Getting the Joke" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus, Simone de Beauvoir, Martin Heidegger — The Absurd; The Myth of Sisyphus; Existence Precedes Essence; Authenticity — Gray reads Jack Handey's Deep Thoughts and Fuzzy Memories as packaged existentialism: Sartre's existence precedes essence grounds Handey's responsibility for self-made meaning ('if you're robbing a bank and your pants fall down... life is funny'), Camus's absurd and Sisyphus's happy perseverance match 'sometimes I think the world has gone completely mad. And then I think, Aw, who cares?', and Beauvoir's ruts of inferiority warn against the ease of 'just sitting there' wanting money. Heidegger's authenticity and mortality appear in the parachute-swimming gag, dying laughing rather than in dread. The chapter also explains why the deadpan delivery over serene stream imagery makes morbidity funny, and worries that Handey's 'truth is... unreal' anticipated post-truth politics.
- ch. 33 "Where Do We Go from Here – Buh‐Bye!" **·** Aristotle, John Stuart Mill, Bernard Williams — Moral Luck; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Southworth asks whether SNL's dumb characters, the Ladies Man, Celebrity Jeopardy's Burt Reynolds, Ferrell's Bush, can be too stupid for moral responsibility. Aristotle's capacity for decision grounds moral agency; the Merit View, sharpened by Williams's constitutive moral luck and the Control Principle, blames Ferrell's deliberately nasty Connery but not the hapless Reynolds; and Mill's consequentialist view of praise and blame as nudges for 'progressive beings' explains Stuart Smalley's affirmations and Gilly's scoldings. Strawson's reactive attitudes finally resolve the puzzle: pitiable Bush is no proper target of blame, which is why we love him, though making him so lovable may have helped the real Bush escape accountability.
- ch. 34 "Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 35 "End User License Agreement" *(notes)*

## Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "i" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "ii" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "The Reality of Scott Adams" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' introduction sets up the book: in 2016 Scott Adams, a left-leaning Mensa member trained in hypnosis, predicted a 98-percent Trump landslide on the ground that Trump is a rare Master Persuader whose outrageous statements were calibrated weapons-grade persuasion aimed at irrational, emotion-driven voters who rationalize after the fact, and that the victory would rip a hole in the fabric of reality, producing cognitive dissonance and mass hysteria among Hillary supporters. It then profiles Adams's path from bank teller and 4 a.m. cartoonist at Pacific Bell to Dilbert creator, business guru (The Dilbert Principle and the Logitech gibberish mission-statement prank in a false mustache), fiction writer (God's Debris, The Religion War), talent-stack theorist of How to Fail at Almost Everything and Still Win Big, and author of Win Bigly, framing the volume as philosophy's examination of this gadfly.
- ch. 8 "I. In Front of Your Eyes" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "1. How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Tolerate the Master Persuader Hypothesis" **·** Socrates, Plato, Aristotle — Man Is the Measure (sophistic relativism) — Wolfe reads Adams's Master Persuader hypothesis through the ancient quarrel between Socrates and the Sophists: Derren Brown's deflation of hypnosis into one personality dominating another leads to Gorgias's Encomium of Helen, where persuasive words are magic spells that steal free will, and to Plato's Gorgias, where Socrates condemns rhetoric as cookery and cosmetics that flatter the ignorant while his disciple Polus covets its tyrannical power. On this mapping Trump's plain-talk style is simply Aristotle's available means of persuasion for a particular audience, and Adams is mostly a Sophist who treats words as programming code for moist robots, though he keeps a Socratic sliver in his stated aim of exposing readers to different ideas rather than converting them. Wolfe closes by refusing both readings of Adams as pro-Trump troll or alt-right hero, urging each side to see how persuasion actually worked on them.
- ch. 10 "2. Persuade Me Once, Shame on You . ." **·** David Hume, Plato, Immanuel Kant — Problem of Induction; Phenomena and Noumena; Philosophical Skepticism — Greene dismantles both phases of Adams's case that Trump is a Master Persuader. The trait-list phase (opening with big demands, the Intentional Wrongness Persuasion Play, never apologizing, exuding confidence, recruiting the reciprocity instinct, and the talent stack) fails because doing what master persuaders do is not being one, by the Tom Brady versus Archie Manning point that we never define good quarterbacks by wins alone and by the Kantian thought that an act must be done for the right reason. The reality phase borrows Plato, Hume, and Kant to deny us access to an objective world, but the chapter replies that the experts' predictive failures illustrate Hume's problem of induction rather than proving there are no facts, notes Adams even misreads Plato, and observes that nothing links the Persuasion Filter's one success to Trump's skills rather than to a one-off political climate.
- ch. 11 "3. How I Could Have Made Hillary President" *(no index entry yet)* — Taking Adams at his word that persuasion is learnable technique, Steele dissects Trump's linguistic kill shots (Low-energy Jeb, Crooked Hillary, Lyin' Ted, Pocahontas) as visual, confirmation-bias-proof forever names that killed Jeb Bush's candidacy in half a second, and contrasts the Clinton campaign's committee flops (Donald Duck, Dangerous Donald, Drumpf, and slogans like Love Trumps Hate and Stronger Together). He then practices what Adams preaches by drafting his own kill shot, The Don, a mafia frame built on offers that cannot be refused, omerta, and sleeping with the fishes, plus the slogan A Win-Win for America, engineered for positive repetition and the slightly-off meaning Adams calls intentional wrongness, concluding the election was winnable with commonsense marketing touches. An Orwell aside about whose victory a wartime poster really celebrates supplies the only classical rhetoric on display.
- ch. 12 "II. Comic-Strip Kafka" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "4. Scoundrels, the Lot of Us" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Søren Kierkegaard, Socrates — The Dialectic; The Stages on Life's Way; Socratic Method (elenchus); Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — Karavitis finds a Hegelian dialectic in the three-panel Dilbert strip (thesis, antithesis, synthesis) delivered through irony, then tests that irony against philosophy: Socrates' feigned-ignorance questioning that leaves interlocutors in aporia, Hegel's complaint that irony is vanity withdrawing from objective reality, and Kierkegaard's dissertation on the concept of irony plus Either/Or, where irony is the bridge from the aesthetic to the ethical life. The punchline is that after nearly three decades of Dilbert the white-collar workplace has not changed, so readers who feel superior to their bosses and co-workers have taken the vain, narcissistic, aesthetic reading Hegel warned against, making the joke a scoundrelly way of avoiding responsibility. A Leo Strauss aside casts Adams as an esoteric writer whose irony preserves him from the powerful.
- ch. 14 "5. The Serious Point of Scott’s Humor" **·** Aristotle, Socrates — The Golden Mean; Virtue Ethics (arete); Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — Guerra and Barkman argue that Dilbert's humor is doing serious philosophical work: strips like the Pointy-Haired Boss's scheme to strip app users of free will, rebranded by Dilbert as marketing, distill manipulative corporate practice to its absurd essential core, and humor serves as a logical tool that, when it preserves the target's integrity rather than straw-manning it, exposes the equivocation in earnest arguments about getting something from nothing. They ground the practice in Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, where wittiness is the virtuous mean between the vices of buffoonery and boorishness, read Adams's catalogue of failures and his luck-first, passion-is-bullshit account of success as a Socratic acknowledgment of ignorance that deflates the American Dream, and treat Win Bigly's persuasion lessons (visuals, repetition, intentional mistakes, the Hitler counterexample) as further proof that Adams has the virtue of wit.
- ch. 15 "6. The PowerPoint Conspiracy Theory" **·** William of Ockham, Immanuel Kant — Ockham's Razor; Utilitarianism — In a sustained deadpan parody, Ketcham builds a conspiracy out of Ockham's Razor: William of Ockham's minimalist principle explains PowerPoint's big-type bullet points, but the slide deck (secretly engineered by DARPA with Microsoft, exported via Siberia to Putin) becomes a weapon that breeds stupidity, conditions Trump to tweet-length simplicities like fake news and crooked, and finally rigs him, not the voting machines. The chapter also wields the Razor correctly, insisting that a minimalist explanation must still be good and complete, as when little Jill's one bullet point tells us too little. Testing moral realism, Kant's absolute prohibition on lying, and utilitarianism's greatest happiness against the conspiracy's missing facts, it concludes we lack the information to render any moral verdict, which is exactly what the conspiracy-minded minimalists want.
- ch. 16 "III. It Tastes Better if We All Do It Together" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "7. Scott Adams’s Joy of Logic" **·** William of Ockham, Francis Bacon — Ockham's Razor — Bilsker turns Adams's Joy of Work catalogue of irrational co-workers into a critical-thinking syllabus: faulty analogy (from dogs fetching sticks to potatoes dancing, and Francis Bacon's body-politic passage praising war as exercise), huge-pants faulty causation, the Reinhart-Rogoff debt paper that drove austerity policy on mere correlation until Herndon, Ash, and Pollin exposed it, complex and objectionable cause, the overapplication of Occam's Razor to moon-landing hoaxes, misplaced authority, begging the question, and egocentric biases like I Am the World. He then contrasts the classroom view that confirmation bias is an unconscious background program with Win Bigly's claim that bias is the operating system itself, worrying about the implication that reasoning with anyone is futile, and concludes that Adams overstates how incapable we are of overcoming our biases.
- ch. 18 "8. Is It a Fact that Facts Don’t Matter" **·** Karl Popper, Aristotle — Falsificationism; The Web of Belief — Steele distinguishes facts as mind-independent reality from facts as expert-certified statements to show that Kellyanne Conway's alternative facts and Adams's own slogans trade on this ambiguity, and that Adams performatively contradicts himself every time he insists his predictions are true and matter. Analyzing the cognitive-dissonance hallucinations of Trump-is-Hitler and then Trump-is-incompetent, he argues that on Adams's own account brute facts proved irresistible, and that such belief revision is rational Popperian conjecture and refutation, plus the conservative strategy of saving fundamental theories (Coulomb's law) and dropping minor ones when the fuse blows. Against the claim that humans are irrational he recalls Aristotle's Rhetoric as persuasion's legitimate complement to the Prior Analytics, and leans on Percival to show propaganda fits a rational-reader model, citing the slow, fact-driven shift on gay marriage.
- ch. 19 "9. But Women Can Vote . ." **·** Simone de Beauvoir — Feminism; Objectification; Woman as the Other — Hansmann and Jones set Adams's gender posts against the four waves of feminism and the men's rights movement: his March 2011 Men's Rights post telling activists to get over it while lumping women with four-year-olds and the mentally handicapped, his Global Gender War matriarchy in which any country where women can vote counts as female-ruled, his framing of sex as a woman's currency for extracting male strategy (sacrifice a pawn to nail the queen), and his serial interrupting of women. They show the rhetoric eerily echoes anti-suffragists like Mrs. William Force Scott and Senator Sanford and the Goldilocks Dilemma, note the red-pill fantasy borrowed from The Matrix, and conclude that calling America a matriarchy defies scholarly consensus, with Beauvoir's The Second Sex marking why the vote never delivered the balance of power.
- ch. 20 "10. Intelligence and Duh-mocracy" **·** Plato, John Stuart Mill, Martha Nussbaum — Democracy; The Philosopher King — Saunders uses Adams's induhviduals and a hundred-voter dilution example in which smart people's votes are swamped to stage the classic case against democracy: Plato's physician analogy against Athenian rule by the ignorant and his philosopher-kings, Jason Brennan's hobbits, hooligans, and Vulcans with voter licensing, Mill's plural votes for the demonstrably wise, and Nussbaum's claim that humanities education breeds empathetic democratic citizens. Each fix fails on Dilbert's own terms, since competence tests demean the labeled, the Pointy-Haired Boss would amass extra votes while Dilbert-grade engineers lack political judgment, Asok's degree would not help, and the more educated are demographically skewed toward men. He concludes that equal votes win as a pragmatic default and muses that workplaces, not polities, might be the truer target of democratization.
- ch. 21 "IV. Comic-Strip Camus" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "11. Dilbert’s Absurd World" **·** Albert Camus, Jean-Paul Sartre, Friedrich Nietzsche — The Absurd; Rebellion and Revolt; The Myth of Sisyphus — Christian contrasts Camus's absurdity, the futile collision between our demand for meaning and a silent world whose only exits are suicide, a leap of faith, or Sisyphean revolt (an active defiance he takes partly from Nietzsche's rejection of resignation), with Adams's office absurdities. In Dilbert the absurd is contained and epistemic rather than pervasive and metaphysical: the battery-dead LED request, Dadaist mission statements, Catbert's evil HR policies, Wally's self-congratulatory Wally Reports, and Alice's harpoon all trace to people being idiots about different things, and could be fixed by honest credit and realizable plans. Dilbert's Business Dorky acceptance therefore looks Camusian but is not: it is recognition minus revolt, bewildered amusement where revolt and reform remain genuinely available.
- ch. 23 "12. Dilbert Is an Asshole and That’s Why He’ll Never Be Happy and Nobody Loves Him" **·** Aristotle, Jean-Paul Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Bad Faith; The Ethics of Ambiguity; The Golden Mean — Elsby and Luzecky argue Dilbert's unhappiness is chosen: from 400 rejections he concludes the women lack quality, he calls insult-bombing gentle kidding, and when Dogbert cites man's rational essence he chooses to watch all-star wrestling, each a textbook Sartrean bad faith where he glimpses the truth and flees it. Measured against Aristotle's eudaimonia he lacks every virtue of the Nicomachean mean (courage as the midpoint of fear, rightly scaled ambition, wit), and since one swallow does not make a summer his whole life, not a day of it, could earn the name happy. The December 2017 addictive-app strips complete the verdict: Dilbert monetizes a zombie-making app for a raise, making him Beauvoir's serious man from The Ethics of Ambiguity, the intelligent sell-out who subordinates human value to a hierarchy he knows is hollow.
- ch. 24 "13. The Essence of Dogbert" **·** Aristotle, David Lewis — Possible Worlds — Knuths asks whether Dogbert is essentially a dog and only accidentally white, importing Aristotle's Metaphysics distinction between essential and accidental properties and its modern modal gloss: essences are what an object has in all possible worlds, with David Lewis's concrete-constructionist reading noted against the standard view of worlds as abstract sets of propositions. The puzzle is that Dogbert's 2014 stint as CEO, combined with his canine essence, would prove dogs can be CEOs, threatening absurd conclusions about the real world unless we choose an ontology of fiction. Three candidates are weighed without a verdict: possibilism (Adams discovered a possible world), Meinongianism (Dogbert has being without existence, at the cost of square circles), and creationism (Dogbert is Adams's abstract artifact, troubled by the Not-Adams duplicate-creator case).
- ch. 25 "14. Of Course It Sucks—It’s Work" **·** Immanuel Kant, Karl Marx, Aristotle, Plato — Humanity as an End in Itself; Alienation; The Myth of Sisyphus; Respect for Persons — Wible stages three theories of work against Dilbert strips: the Greek view of Plato and Aristotle that labor is freedom-sapping and leisure is the civilized ideal, Marx's capitalist critique in which workers become objects and machines (Wally gives off no human vibe, and robots are coming for the engineers), and Desjardins's human-fulfillment model built on Schumacher's creativity, challenge, development, honesty, and beauty, with Wells Fargo's fake accounts showing how jobs that force lying corrupt character. He endorses instead a Kantian middle ground anchored in Norman Bowie's moral minimum: never treating workers as mere means, so the CEO making intern Asok drink industrial sludge on stage is a violation of respect for persons, not just bad management. Sisyphus supplies the image of pointless labor, though even he might be redeemed if he loved the rock.
- ch. 26 "V. Golden Age, Ready or Not" *(front)*
- ch. 27 "15. Bias Is Rational!" **·** Karl Popper — Falsificationism; Stoicism — Percival, whose Myth of the Closed Mind Adams cites, rebuts the Moist Robot Hypothesis that visual, emotional, repetitive anchors make us ninety-percent irrational. Against Kahneman's fast-and-dumb System 1 he sets Gigerenzer's ecological rationality (the gaze-angle heuristic that catches fly balls, the recognition heuristic that lets ignorant German students beat Americans on Detroit versus Milwaukee), then goes further with Popper's critical rationalism: babies as little scientists conjecturing and refuting, experience always theory-laden (the duck-rabbit), and Newton's boy on the seashore facing an infinite but navigable ocean of error elimination. The Stoic insight that all emotion is thoughtful and all thought emotional (the falling-tiles misperception that flips anger to relief) shows feelings track beliefs, so a free battle of the biases, not fact-free affirmation in the lineage of Le Bon and Pavlovian conditioning, is how rationality actually works.
- ch. 28 "16. Why Scott Adams Is Stupid" **·** Karl Popper, Paul Feyerabend, Ludwig Wittgenstein — Falsificationism; Anything Goes (epistemological anarchism) — Miori audits Adams's science talk through epistemology: warrant for belief, empiricism versus rationalism, Wittgenstein's demand for unambiguous clarity, and Clifford's epistemic responsibility, that it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence, which condemns sampling television news while blogging on climate science. Popper's falsifiability, learned from Einstein's willingness to be refuted against Freud's confirmation-seeking, exposes Adams's double standard in waving confirmation bias at critics while crediting his own predictions, and Feyerabend's epistemological anarchism is the view Adams most resembles, except that Feyerabend took responsibility and retracted. Cipolla's Basic Laws of Human Stupidity (the stupid person causes losses to both self and others) frames the closing charge: Adams suggests and retreats, sells product, and shirks the epistemic duty that experts in climate science and medicine shoulder.
- ch. 29 "17. Sweeping Up God’s Debris" **·** Socrates, René Descartes — Socratic Method (elenchus); Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Category Mistake; Philosophical Skepticism — Robison-Greene reads God's Debris as a Socratic dialogue on speed: the Avatar, like Socrates after the Delphic oracle, guts the Postman's confidence so he can unlearn, and the whole book functions as a Cartesian skeptical hypothesis in the dream-and-evil-demon lineage, here that we are the dust of a self-destructed God and perception is illusion, with gravity re-described as probability. Her counterattack is that the cosmology commits category mistakes, since probability cannot cause dust to reappear any more than Joe can consist of tallness, and that God made of probability is incoherent even for an omnipotent being. The five levels of awareness collapse too: level-four skeptics are just people who trust reliable methods, and the Avatar's claim that the mind is an illusion generator is self-defeating, since his own omniscience presupposes objective truth.
- ch. 30 "18. Scott Adams and the Pinocchio Fallacy" **·** Nick Bostrom, Karl Marx — The Simulation Hypothesis — Steele attacks Adams's embrace of the simulation hypothesis with the Pinocchio fallacy: a wooden boy cannot even hanker to be real, because hankering is conscious and wood is the wrong kind of stuff, and likewise no amount of code yields experience, since a simulation of weather wets no one and Deep Blue never knew it was playing chess. Bostrom's careful argument is distinguished from its popularizers, whose substrate-independence slide smuggles possibility into actuality (by the same logic a block of wood could be conscious), and the Matrix storyline, read as an allegory of Marx's exploitation and ideology, is judged as untenable as its energy-harvesting plot. Consciousness remains a property of living bodies, replication rather than simulation, and even if software minds were possible, trapping them in a fabricated world would be immoral.
- ch. 31 "Bibliography" *(notes)*
- ch. 32 "Author Bios" *(notes)*
- ch. 33 "Index" *(notes)*

## Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Seinfeld and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Preface" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Monologue" **·** Martin Heidegger, Socrates, Friedrich Nietzsche — The Unexamined Life; The They-Self (das Man) — Editor William Irwin's introduction explains why Seinfeld is philosophical: 'Seinfeld' sounds like German for 'field of being,' echoing Heidegger's Sein und Zeit, and he tells students to picture the four at Monk's coffee shop when Heidegger describes the 'idle chatter' of the inauthentic mode of being, while George's 'what is the opposite of what I would normally do?' shows the courage of changing one's way of seeing. He frames the whole book with Socrates' claim that the unexamined life is not worth living - the Seinfeld characters examine their lives constantly, though Socrates would approve of neither their lives nor their examinations - and with Nietzsche's 'A Book for None and All' subtitle, then lays out the volume's four-act structure.
- ch. 8 "Act I - The Characters, aka “The New York Four”" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "The Fates of Socrates and Seinfeld" **·** Socrates, Plato — The Unexamined Life; Allegory of the Cave; Theory of Forms; Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — William Irwin compares Jerry and Socrates: the 'Jerry problem' of whether the fictional Jerry is the real Jerry (complicated by Seinlanguage) mirrors the Socratic problem of separating Socrates from Plato's dialogues. Jerry, like Socrates the gadfly, provokes his circle with questions that hunt for essences - the black-and-white cookie, 'is soup a meal?' - and shares Socrates' irony (the 'War: What Is It Good For?' gag in 'The Marine Biologist' works exactly like Socratic shamming ignorance). But where Socrates died serenely per the Apology and Phaedo, Jerry is self-absorbed and ends the series convicted under the Good Samaritan law, doing his stand-up 'gadfly' routine for prison inmates - an examined life, but not an exemplary one.
- ch. 10 "George and Virtue—Like Oil and Water" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing); The Golden Mean; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Daniel Barwick runs George through Aristotle's function argument and finds him wanting: a paradigm of 'the many' who thinks happiness is fortune and momentary victories over others (free parking, perfect airport pickups) rather than activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. His 'do the opposite' epiphany in 'The Opposite' embraces the more extreme vice rather than steering toward the rationally chosen mean, and his self-hatred, laziness, and pleasure-seeking fail all three of Aristotle's tips for hitting the mean. Since George will never practice virtuous action until it becomes habit, Barwick concludes George is doomed to his miserable existence - which is, conveniently for us, why he is funny.
- ch. 11 "Elaine’s Moral Character" **·** Carol Gilligan, Nel Noddings — The Ethics of Care; Caring as the Ground of Ethics; Feminism — Sarah Worth asks whether Elaine is a feminist icon or 'just one of the boys.' Elaine passes every liberal-feminist benchmark - a Tufts education, the only steady career (Pendant Publishing, then the J. Peterman catalogue), financial and emotional independence - but fails the ethic of care: her dating ethics run on pettiness (dumping men for not offering pie, for dirty bathrooms, over Puddy's high-fiving), the 'spongeworthy' episode commodifies her own relationships, she shows no maternal instinct toward the ugly baby, and she secretly resents George's engagement. The conclusion: being one of the boys does not a feminist make, though Elaine still models an independence the women of Friends and Frasier lack.
- ch. 12 "Conclusion" **·** Søren Kierkegaard — The Stages on Life's Way; The Leap of Faith; Despair (sickness unto death); Teleological Suspension of the Ethical — William Irwin argues Kramer is Kierkegaard's aesthete par excellence: his endless abandoned schemes (make-your-own-pizza, beach-smelling cologne, Kramerica Industries), his aliases (H.E. Pennypacker, Dr. Van Nostrand), and his 'Kavorka' revolving door of women enact Either/Or's 'crop rotation' method and the Diary of the Seducer, all flight from the despair hinted at in 'The Switch' ('All this time I'm trying not to be me'). His brief office job in 'The Bizarro Jerry' - 'structure... TCB, taking care of business' - is a flirtation with Judge William's ethical stage of commitment, and Irwin closes with a thought experiment: could Kramer ever make the leap of faith to the religious stage, performing his own teleological suspension of the ethical like Abraham?
- ch. 13 "Act II - Seinfeld and the Philosophers" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "Was it a Show about Nothing" **·** Plato, Laozi, Parmenides — Wu Wei (effortless action); The Tao (the Way); Being and Changelessness — Eric Bronson takes George's NBC pitch for 'a show about nothing' as a live philosophical problem: Parmenides argued we cannot meaningfully speak of what-is-not (so Art Vandelay is unsayable), but Plato's Sophist answers that nothing is 'otherness' with real power - the puffy shirt is something other than beautiful, and 'The Parking Garage' is doing something other than what is interesting or useful. Lao Tzu's Tao Te Ching goes further: the nameless Tao begets the ten thousand things, and wei wu wei (action through non-action) conquers, as in 'The Chinese Restaurant', where a whole episode of standing in line doing nothing is itself something happening.
- ch. 15 "The Seinfeldians as Fixed Essences" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato, Parmenides — Eternal Recurrence; Theory of Forms; Being and Changelessness — Mark Conard notes the show's relentless recurrences - Kramer sliding through the door, 'Newman!', George's firings, the Puddy on-again-off-again loop - and asks whether this is Nietzsche's eternal recurrence. It cannot be, since Nietzsche's cosmos is a flux of recombining centers of force; things recur in Seinfeld precisely because nothing changes. The Seinfeldians are instead fixed Platonic Forms or essences: 'The Bizarro Jerry' proves it, since only an unchanging archetype can have an exact opposite (Kevin, Gene, Feldman, Vargas), and the backwards episode 'The Betrayal' works only because characters exempt from time and change cannot develop.
- ch. 16 "No Exit and The Vault Sartre and Seinfeld on the Inescapability of Others" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — The Look (hell is other people); Existentialism; Existence Precedes Essence — Jennifer McMahon defends the heretical reading of Sartre as a relational theorist of the self: in Being and Nothingness consciousness is a nothingness, not an essential ego, and only the Other - 'the Other accomplishes... to see ourselves as we are' - lets us grasp ourselves as objects. Seinfeld illustrates this better than Sartre's own suspicion of others: Jerry's identity exists only through his entanglement with George, Kramer, and Elaine (change them and you get a 'bizarro-Jerry'), and the finale's prison cell ('The Vault') replays No Exit's locked room with the trial's parade of wounded minor characters - except that Seinfeld's chattering foursome shows friendship as a positive, not hellish, dependency.
- ch. 17 "Finale" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein — Language Games — Kelly Dean Jolley reads Seinfeld as the sitcom twin of Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations: both are 'albums' - remarks, vignettes - that refuse the normal form (the finished essay, the developed plot), and both try to make us notice the commonplace hidden by its very familiarity (PI sections 118, 129, 596 on feelings of familiarity and the attack on meaning as a mental act). Jerry's 'It's a show about nothing' is the show's version of Wittgenstein's destroying houses of cards: the plot was the illusion, and the vignettes nag, repeat, and transpose the commonplaces until we hear what he calls the 'tune of our lives.'
- ch. 18 "Act III - Untimely Meditations by the Water Cooler" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "[Cue Bass]" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Jason Holt asks whether it is rational for George to 'do the opposite' and answers no. Distinguishing minimal, medial, and maximal rationality, he argues the Costanza Maneuver is neither reliable (its .800 batting average in 'The Opposite' is dumb luck - insulting Steinbrenner into a job and cowing movie thugs should not work) nor feasible: George's akrasia and impulse problems betray him, and the opposite of an action is usually indeterminate (Jerry: 'chicken salad is not the opposite of tuna... salmon swim against the current'). Since George knows all this, betting on the Maneuver is irrational - its success is precisely the joke, 'not as good, works better.'
- ch. 20 "Mr. Peterman, the Wicked Witch of the West, and Me" **·** Karl Marx — Ideology and False Consciousness; Commodity Fetishism — Norah Martin uses J. Peterman to explain ideology through irony rather than cynicism: we know the catalogue's 'pointless drivel' is fiction, yet we buy anyway - Žižek's 'fetishists in practice, not in theory' - so that laughing at the absurd narratives is the catalogue's best advertising. Peterman himself, who must buy Kramer's life stories because his own life is only what Elaine writes, is the most realistic character: like the Wicked Witch of the West (not the Wizard with a humbug behind the curtain), there is literally nothing beneath the costume, showing that the unified Cartesian subject is a 'primordial lie' and that Jerry's superficiality ('I'm being as superficial as I possibly can') is the honest response.
- ch. 21 "What’s so Funny about That" *(no index entry yet)* — Jorge Gracia proposes that we laugh at the significance of the insignificant and cry at the insignificance of the significant, then reads 'The Outing' nearly scene by scene: the eavesdropped 'just because you two are homosexuals' joke, the washed pear, the whiny voice on tape, Kramer's 'I thought we were going to take a steam,' and the refrain 'not that there's anything wrong with that.' The episode is funny because it lays bare society's stereotype of the gay man (thin, single, neat) and its duplicity - everyone disavows bigotry in exactly the breath with which they panic at being thought gay - turning an insignificant coffee-shop prank into a mirror of well-intentioned bigotry.
- ch. 22 "Act IV - Is There Anything Wrong with That" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "Conclusion" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Virtue Ethics — Robert Epperson defends the show against the 'no hugging, no learning' charge by arguing Seinfeld is about the pursuit of the moral life: the four constantly consult each other on right conduct (gift-giving, break-up timing, obligations to friends and parents), distinguishing the moral life from mere integrity. He grades each character - Kramer is Plato's man of right opinion without knowledge whose one maxim is 'listen to your little man,' George means rightly but is the man of wrong opinion, Elaine is undone by indecisiveness, Jerry is the moral axis whose flaw is vanity - and argues with Aristotle that it is precisely their imperfect characters that make their concern with acting rightly possible.
- ch. 24 "Elaine, Kramer, and Newman Not Wise" **·** Aristotle, Socrates, Immanuel Kant — Virtue Ethics (arete); Practical Wisdom (phronesis); The Golden Mean — Aeon Skoble argues Seinfeld explicates Aristotelian virtue ethics against utilitarian and Kantian rivals: Jerry's 'I don't want to be an orgy guy' and George's fear of becoming 'one of those guys' ask what sort of person to be, not which rule to follow. George's 'do the opposite' in 'The Opposite' is an update of the Delphic oracle - only he who recognizes his own idiocy (Socratic ignorance) can act well, with Jerry deducing the logic and serving as his phronemos, alongside Superman. Elaine's rule-worship and Jujyfruits utilitarianism backfire, Kramer lacks the social dialectic virtue needs, and the ironic appeals to Newman as arbiter expose the paradox that choosing a role model wisely already requires the wisdom one lacks.
- ch. 25 "Crime and Character" **·** Judith Jarvis Thomson, James Rachels — Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Theodore Schick uses the Latham Good Samaritan law to argue that doing nothing can be something: against Jackie Chiles' bystander defense he sets the French bad-Samaritan statute, Thomson's Henry Fonda cases (distinguishing supererogatory aid from the duty of the 'minimally decent Samaritan'), and Rachels' Smith/Jones pair - Jones lets the child drown and is exactly as culpable as killer Smith - to show a duty of easy rescue exists, so the gang's failure to dial 911 on Jerry's cell phone deserved punishment. But in the 'Crime and Character' section he argues the trial itself was rigged: character evidence was inadmissible, and the four are not bad people, just people who failed their duty once.
- ch. 26 "EPISODE GUIDE" *(notes)*
- ch. 27 "A CHRONOLOGY OF SOME BIG-TIME PHILOSOPHERS" *(notes)*
- ch. 28 "NOTES ON THE SCRIPT WRITERS, AKA THE CONTRIBUTORS TO THIS VOLUME" *(notes)*
- ch. 29 "Index of Everything" *(notes)*

## Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "AN EXTRAORDINARY GENIUS FOR MINUTIAE" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "The House that Holmes Built" **·** Baruch Spinoza, Socrates — Conatus (striving to persist); Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura) — Kate Rufa reads Holmes as Spinoza's 'just man': Watson's 'calculating machine' verdict in The Sign of the Four, his unshaken calm while baiting Moriarty before the Reichenbach leap in 'The Final Problem', and the geometric 'Book of Life' of A Study in Scarlet all show passion mastered by reason into adequate ideas and true freedom. The twist is the cocaine: shooting up between cases means Holmes sacrifices his conatus (the striving to persist in being) to keep his mind at a godlike pitch of activity, a God-complex no finite mode can sustain. Moriarty, equally rational but ruled by passive affects, is the shadow of this ideal, echoing Socrates' Apology point that harming others inevitably harms oneself.
- ch. 7 "His Work Is Its Own Reward" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Übermensch; Will to Power; The Death of God — Timothy Sexton argues the real Overman is not Doyle's flat 'calculating machine' but Jeremy Brett's Granada Holmes: the sneer with which he frees the Blue Carbuncle thief and the 'I am not retained by the police' outburst show him stepping beyond the herd's good-and-evil after the death of God. Brett's theatrical style, from the pivot before Lady Brackenstall in 'The Abbey Grange' to 'Gentlemen, we can do better than that' in 'The Norwood Builder', enacts Nietzsche's grand art of giving style to one's character, sublimating nihilistic dread into the pleasure of proving superiority. Where Rathbone-era Sherlocks solve crimes for truth, justice and the Victorian Way, Brett's Holmes makes the work its own reward, satisfying Nietzsche's demand that the Overman 'attain satisfaction with himself'.
- ch. 8 "Education never ends Watson. It is a series of lessons with the greatest for" **·** Edmund Gettier, Bertrand Russell, G.E. Moore — The Gettier Problem; Reliabilism; Possible Worlds — J. Solomon Johnson asks whether Holmes's conclusions are knowledge or luck, walking through justified true belief with a Holmesian Gettier case (Watson rightly believing the killer was a former ship hand for the wrong reason), Moore's proof that knowledge entails belief, and Russell's stopped clock as an unsafe belief. BBC Sherlock's fake Vermeer and the 2009 film's 'resurrected' Lord Blackwood illustrate beliefs that fail safety or sensitivity across nearby possible worlds, while 'The Stock-Broker's Clerk' shows Holmes's observation of the scorched slippers making his belief sensitive. The verdict: Holmes is justified by the track record of his own expert methods, a professional billiards player rather than a beginner's-luck fluke, though real-world imitators could never rule out enough alternatives to match him.
- ch. 9 "Birlstone Manor Revisited" **·** Martin Heidegger — Dasein (being-there); Being-Toward-Death — Fiona Tomkinson stages a Watson-Holmes dialogue in which Holmes, reworking The Valley of Fear's Birlstone Manor investigation, defines a thing as a thing of no consequence and an object as a thing transformed into a clue: the half-burned candle proving the witnesses lied, the single dumbbell used to sink Baldwin's clothes in the moat, the wedding ring and the hammer, each read through the human fear and care that moved them. A postscript has an aged Watson in 1926 discover Heidegger's newly published Being and Time and recognize his own friend's method in it: Dasein's care and being-toward-death, the directionality of equipment, and the ready-to-hand versus present-at-hand distinction, joking that Holmes might have sued Heidegger for theft of intellectual property.
- ch. 10 "A Toolbox for Your Holmes" **·** Charles Sanders Peirce, Socrates — Socratic Method (elenchus) — Sami Paavola and Lauri Jaervilehto reconstruct the textbook on detection Holmes never wrote: following Jaakko Hintikka's interrogative (Socratic) model, where the right question cracks the case, as with the dog that did nothing in the night-time in 'Silver Blaze', and Peirce's triad of deduction, induction and abduction, the backward reasoning from effects to causes exemplified by the Watson-just-from-Afghanistan chain in A Study in Scarlet. They add Peirce's categories of Firstness, Secondness and Thirdness to show Holmes succeeds because he fuses imagination and reverie with fieldwork, experiment and exact inference. The chapter closes with a twelve-point practical toolbox distilled from the canon.
- ch. 11 "A DOG REFLECTS THE FAMILY LIFE" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "Final Recommendations" *(no index entry yet)* — Francine Sanders, a former Chicago police-misconduct investigator, rereads the 1939-46 Rathbone films (The Secret Weapon, The Spider Woman, The Woman in Green) against the hard-boiled world of Chandler and Hammett. Holmes's tea-pouring intimacy with Watson, his disguises (book peddler, roughneck sailor, bogus postman after faking his death), his puzzle-obsession rather than femme-fatale obsession with Adrea Spedding, and the closing vigil over a London where 'women can come and go in safety' mark him as the hopeful, partnered opposite of the alienated loner of noir, whose corrupt city always wins.
- ch. 13 "The Postmodern Condition" **·** Jacques Derrida, Friedrich Nietzsche — Deconstruction; Binary Oppositions — Rafe McGregor claims The Hound of the Baskervilles is not a detective story at all: the hound that never bites anyone and Holmes's failure to foresee fog on Dartmoor are, via Derrida's Of Grammatology, the aporia and re-mark where the mystery-horror hierarchy of the text deconstructs. He then applies Noel Carroll's philosophy of horror, the phosphorus-painted hound as a category-crossing monster producing fear plus disgust and Grimpen Mire as horror geography, to reclassify the novel as gothic horror alongside Frankenstein, Jekyll and Hyde and Dracula. The final section ties the book's enduring mass appeal to the postmodern condition, tracing the collapse of certainty from Nietzsche's prophecies about the end of Christian values to Derrida's claim that truth is never finally available, leaving anxiety as the novel's real engine.
- ch. 14 "Chapter 8 - The Case of the Dangerous Detective" **·** Karl Marx, Socrates, Aristotle, René Descartes — Ideology and False Consciousness; Dharma — In a Platonic dialogue, Ronald Green and D.E. Wittkower argue the detective is dangerous because knowledge itself threatens a society's ideology: Oedipus's fatal investigation, the Athenian prosecution of Socrates and Anaxagoras, and Holmes's exposure that genteel Victorian society breeds the same crimes as the slums (while the hard-boiled PI shows official authority cannot deliver), with Aristotle's catharsis re-described as ideological enforcement that teaches audiences not to question social foundations. They then widen to Indian traditions: Vyasa dividing knowledge into the Vedas like an inverted Descartes, Krishna's two paths of inquiry in the Bhagavad Gita, and the Ramayana's dharma, where Rama's trial of Sita upholds cosmic order over truth, compared with the film Raavan, to ask whether ruling by an upheld lie is the greater danger.
- ch. 15 "An Eye for an Eye" **·** Alasdair MacIntyre — Virtues, Practices and Traditions; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Mihaela Frunza and Anatolia Bessemer use MacIntyre's Whose Justice? Which Rationality? to frame Holmes's casual felonies, the disguised-clergyman trick on Irene Adler, freeing Captain Croker after staging a mock courtroom in 'The Abbey Grange', and compounding a felony with Isadora Klein in 'The Three Gables', as one tradition of justice among several with no neutral court of appeal. Against the police's letter-of-the-law tradition stand the criminals' own codes of retribution, above all Jefferson Hope in A Study in Scarlet letting 'the high God judge' between the poisoned and harmless pills, making Holmes and his prey mirror-image vigilantes who prefer restitution or chivalric acquittal to statutory punishment.
- ch. 16 "The Game Is (and Isn’t) Afoot" *(no index entry yet)* — Tom Dowd argues you can never be Holmes: books and films offer only passive immersion, the flow Csikszentmihalyi describes and Marie-Laure Ryan's narrative-as-virtual-reality, with the plot pre-decided, while Holmes video games from The Riddle of the Crown Jewels to Sherlock Holmes vs. Jack the Ripper's Deduction Board supply agency and affordances for shooting and searching but offload actual deduction onto the player, who lacks Holmes's expert domain knowledge catalogued in Watson's 'his limits' list. Hence the genre's sleight of hand: Watson becomes the player's stand-in while Holmes confirms the conclusions, and BBC Sherlock's floating observation text reproduces the same trick on television.
- ch. 17 "But the Contradictions! What about the Contradictions" *(no index entry yet)* — Ivan Wolfe asks what makes the Holmes canon (fifty-six stories and four novels) authoritative, importing the religious vocabulary of canon and apocrypha, plus Star Trek and Star Wars practice, to test borderline texts: the two Doyle tales found only in French editions ('The Man with the Watches' and 'The Lost Special'), 'The Field Bazaar', Queen Mary's Dolls' House story 'How Watson Learned the Trick', and the Gillette play that coined 'Elementary, my dear Watson'. He proposes five canon criteria (by Doyle, published in his lifetime, about Holmes, non-contradictory, prose fiction) and closes by showing Sherlockians handle internal contradictions, Watson's migrating Jezail wound and Holmes's 'Nil' philosophy grade, exactly as believers harmonize scripture: explain, deny, or await further research.
- ch. 18 "I THINK YOU MIGHT WANT A LITTLE UNOFFICIAL HELP" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "Surviving Fusion" **·** Plato, Derek Parfit, Robert Nozick — Philosophy of Love; Personal Identity — Amy Kind asks whether the Holmes who marries Laurie R. King's Mary Russell could still be Holmes, weighing Aristophanes' speech in Plato's Symposium (Zeus split the original spherical humans, and love seeks our lost half) against Derek Parfit's fusion case from Reasons and Persons, in which two people grow into one body, which we would all find horrifying. Against Nozick's account of love as becoming a 'we', Delaney's merger and Gaylin's 'fused identity', she deploys Marilyn Friedman's federation model, lovers as sovereign states forming a flexible third entity, to argue that Holmes and Russell's marriage survives because its fusion reshapes identity without obliterating it: his 'half a creature with two brains and four eyes' and her refusal of the nickname 'Zherlock Mary' show both lovers keeping separate selves.
- ch. 20 "The Best Kind of Friend" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Virtue Ethics (arete); Moral Relativism — Ruth Tallman tests Holmes and Watson against Aristotle's requirement in the Nicomachean Ethics that perfect friendship exists only between the 'alike in excellence': since the two live by irreconcilable moral codes (Holmes's cocaine and burglaries versus Watson's clean living and law-abidingness), Aristotelian moral naturalism denies they can be true friends at all, despite the raw panic in 'The Three Garridebs' proving mutual devotion. Recasting the pair as moral pluralists with different 'good for me's, she argues Holmes is actually the better friend, an 'integrity-promoting' friend who urges Watson to stay home from the Milverton burglary to honor Watson's own code, while the proselytizing Watson, who nags about cocaine yet tags along anyway, repeatedly violates his own integrity.
- ch. 21 "Defiant Male Behavior" **·** Judith Butler — Gender Performativity — Julia Round traces Holmes from Baden-Powell's Scouting for Boys, which told scoutmasters to teach 'Sherlock-Holmesism', through Victorian essentialist masculinity, 'true, cold reason', stoicism under the poison darts of The Sign of the Four, yet violin, moods and the feminized domesticity of Baker Street, to argue Doyle's stories already unsettle gender essentialism. Gregory House of House, built from the same blueprint (221B, a shooter named Moriarty, a lost love named Adler, Wilson as Watson), embodies and mocks both the 1980s 'new man' and the 1990s 'new lad', cooking, soap operas, manipulation, Segways and the 'Rubik's complex', landing in Judith Butler's world where gendered behavior is a performance and masculinity is fallible, immature, and constructed.
- ch. 22 "The Honorable, the Woman" **·** David Hume — Problem of Induction; Objectification — Mona Rocha and James Rocha charge that Holmes's 'deduction' is really Humean induction, and that his inductive shortcuts about women, tricking Mrs. Smith in The Sign of the Four, reading Mary Sutherland's pacing as a love affair, and dismissing Lady Frances Carfax as a 'stray chicken in a world of foxes', are hasty generalizations made dangerous by gender stereotype. Watson is worse: his 'experience of women... over many nations and three continents' reads Mary Morstan's soul off her face and grants full courtesy only to the beautiful intruder of 'The Solitary Cyclist', a feminist case study in objectification. Irene Adler's escape in 'A Scandal in Bohemia', disguising herself as a young man and outwitting the fire ruse, is Doyle's deliberate proof that treating women as a class fails, making her a proto-feminist decades before Poirot's Rossakoff or Spade's O'Shaughnessy.
- ch. 23 "THERE ARE UNEXPLORED POSSIBILITIES IN YOU" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Wrapping Up the Case" **·** Immanuel Kant, Augustine of Hippo, Friedrich Nietzsche — Deontology — Don Fallis organizes the whole canon as a casebook in the epistemology of deception: why characters deceive (concealing crimes like Dr. Roylott's speckled band, committing them like John Clay's Red-Headed League tunnel, Holmes's own smoke-rocket trick on Irene Adler and his faked death at the Reichenbach Falls), how they deceive (Bell and Whaley's hide-the-truth versus show-the-false, unpacked through disguises as masking, repackaging, dazzling, mimicking, inventing and decoying), and how deception is detected, by microexpressions avant la lettre or by inconsistency, as in 'The Problem of Thor Bridge'. Along the way he sorts lying from false implicature (Inspector Baynes's 'I didn't say so'), lies of omission and bald-faced lies, invokes Kant's absolute ban on lying and Augustine's taxonomy of lies, and asks whether Holmes's belief in Moriarty's web, where the absence of evidence counts as evidence, is rational inference or self-deception.
- ch. 25 "Is It All Meaningless" **·** John Stuart Mill, Charles Sanders Peirce, Plato, Aristotle, Socrates, Jacques Derrida, Ludwig Wittgenstein — Rory Kraft adopts the Great Game premise that Watson (not Doyle) wrote the memoirs and shows Watson is an untrustworthy narrator, the Jezail bullet migrating from shoulder to leg, the Tuesday March 4th murder that cannot fit the 1882 chronology, then borrows Socrates' complaint in the Phaedrus that writing 'stands in solemn silence' when questioned, so the texts cannot be cross-examined. He argues Holmes's real method is Mill's System of Logic (the Method of Residues behind 'eliminate the impossible') plus Peirce's abduction rather than deduction proper, and that Aristotle's Metaphysics ideal of truths amassing explains the Holmes brothers' knack. Failed attempts to date 'The Disappearance of Lady Frances Carfax' leave truth underdetermined, nudging toward Carnap's verdict that the unverifiable is 'meaningless' and Wittgenstein's Tractatus silence, while Derrida's 'truth is always that which can be repeated' at least settles one thing: the deerstalker was never worn.
- ch. 26 "That Far-Away Look" **·** Plato — Theory of Forms — Lahr argues that Holmes's crime-solving is an art rather than a forensic science: like his inspiration Oscar Wilde, Holmes is an aesthete whose 'aesthetic sight' perceives the criminal-artist's design in clues, so that Watson the philistine ('What ineffable twaddle!') consistently misses what is self-evident to Holmes. He suggests Plato would say Holmes sees only the perfect Forms behind appearances, and reads the BBC adaptations accordingly: in The Case of the Silk Stocking Holmes's trance-like perception of the victims' pedicured feet reveals a killer with a foot fetish, while Sherlock's 'A Study in Pink' renders his insight as first-person vision with on-screen data. The queer coding (the Diogenes Club, Moriarty's 'hereditary tendencies,' Holmes as Wilde's physical and temperamental double) links Holmes to the first sexologists' puzzle of how marginal men recognize one another at a glance.
- ch. 27 "An Inexact Science" *(no index entry yet)* — Demeter argues that Holmes's official self-image as a cold 'reasoning machine' is an ideology that distorts his actual practice: between collecting facts and eliminating impossible scenarios, Holmes is a creator of stories whose 'narrative imagination' invents possible explanations, a phase deduction cannot account for (Peter Lipton's point that Holmesian 'deduction' is not logically valid). Reading 'The Man with the Twisted Lip,' he shows how the same facts (coins in the coat pockets) become different evidence in different narratives until Holmes reconceives Boone and Neville St. Clair as one person. Holmes's preference for the bizarre over the simple, his warning against theorizing before the data, and his claim that his gift is hereditary ('Art in the blood is liable to take the strangest forms') all show detection is closer to art than science, though the scientific persona lends him professional legitimacy and lets him train Scotland Yard.
- ch. 28 "HOLMES IS A LITTLE SCIENTIFIC FOR MY TASTES" *(front)*
- ch. 29 "The New Man or the Old" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Karl Marx — The Death of God; The Meaning of Life; The End of Grand Narratives — Marks reads Holmes as the paragon Victorian whose faith in reason mirrors his era's confidence and, underneath it, its anxiety: Holmes's outburst in 'The Cardboard Box' ('What is the object of this circle of misery and violence and fear?... That is humanity's great problem to which Reason, so far, has no answer') appears the same year Nietzsche published 'Gott ist tot' in The Gay Science, amid Marx's 'opium of the people' and Darwin's displacement of religion. Reinterpreting the 2009 Ritchie film, he rejects the obvious religion-versus-reason reading of Lord Blackwood: Blackwood's 'magic' is really chemistry and machinery (technocracy), Holmes's science serves the military (dictatorship), and Moriarty (terrorism) defeats both, dramatizing post-9/11 fears about the militarized fruits of Reason. He concludes that Holmes straddles the Victorian and postmodern divide and that replacing religion with science is Rationalism's 'siren song.'
- ch. 30 "Time Enough to Drink the Poison" **·** Gottfried Leibniz, René Descartes, Plato — The Best of All Possible Worlds; Stoicism; The Dichotomy of Control — Domino reads 'The Veiled Lodger' as a drama about hope in a world after God: Holmes's 'Your life is not your own; keep your hands off it' revives Plato's Phaedo argument that we are the gods' possessions, but deist-or-atheist Mrs. Ronder is unmoved, so Holmes falls back on the Leibnizian alternative to the Stoic and Cartesian 'patience without hope' — the example of patient suffering as 'the most precious of all lessons,' grounded in Leibniz's hope that the world is no 'cruel jest.' Jefferson Hope's two pill boxes in A Study in Scarlet literalize the Leibnizian link between hope and divine justice by letting God choose who dies, while Trelawney Hope's gullibility makes the surname ironic. Mrs. Ronder's true hope was reunion with Leonardo, which his death destroyed; what saves her is a new hope founded on Watson's text, since only a writer ('I have made a slight change of name and place') can change the past.
- ch. 31 "This Way Lies Madness" **·** Plato, Gottfried Leibniz, Gottlob Frege, Bertrand Russell, Ludwig Wittgenstein — Franchella takes Holmes's 'I should never marry myself, lest I bias my judgement' as the opening of the emotion-versus-logic question: Andrea Nye's feminist critique warns that casting logic as a genius's superpower underwrites oppression, as with Tonga the 'black cannibal' exhibited like a human zoo attraction in The Sign of Four, while Cellucci and Matte Blanco ground logic evolutionarily and universally in all organisms and everyday reasoning. Holmes's 'reasoning backwards' is the analytic method — the hypothesis-seeking tradition running from Plato's Republic through Cellucci, which Leibniz and Robinson objected requires intuition and divination — and the Wason test shows social, emotional framing can actually improve logical performance, against Frege's ideal of stripping feeling from thought. Via Logicomix's Russell, Wittgenstein, and Godel, and diagnoses of Holmes as bipolar or Asperger's, she suggests logic can be a false harbor from emotion, and that love might have enhanced Holmes's powers rather than clouded them.
- ch. 32 "Our Best Bet" **·** David Hume, Karl Popper — Problem of Induction; Falsificationism — Terjesen argues Mycroft surpasses Sherlock because he truly grasps Hume's Problem of Induction: Sherlock's celebrated eliminations (the three key possibilities for Cadogan West in 'The Bruce-Partington Plans') and his newspaper-ad tests are inductive, Popperian conjecture-testing that can never confirm anything, while Goodman's 'grue' shows the same evidence always supports rival explanations. Watson's failed attempt in 'How Watson Learned the Trick,' the amateur reasoner's wrong solution in 'The Lost Special,' and Holmes's own 'Norbury' failure in 'The Yellow Face' prove that a correct method guarantees nothing. Mycroft, who 'would rather be considered wrong than take the trouble to prove himself right,' implicitly embraces Reichenbach's pragmatic justification — induction is simply our best bet — and therefore hunts longer for the facts that do not fit, acting only when England's fate is at stake.
- ch. 33 "MUSIC AT STRANGE HOURS OR THAT MIXTURE OF IMAGINATION AND REALITY" *(front)*
- ch. 34 "The Essence of Perception Holmes’s Intention and Objects Intended" **·** Edmund Husserl, Martin Heidegger — Intentionality; Phenomenology — Kilroy romanticizes not the drugs but the woodshed: Holmes's cocaine sessions, violin, and clattered study cultivate a Husserlian field of consciousness in which reality is the intercourse of subject and object, so a clue (the Trichinopoly cigar ash, 'Rache' as German for revenge) only appears to a detective whose knowledge, observation, and deduction are unified — Gregson and Lestrade misread the same room in A Study in Scarlet because they theorize before the evidence. Heidegger's distinction between merely present (Vorhandenheit) and usefully present (Zuhandenheit) objects explains what counts as a clue — the lipstick-stained wineglass, not the tablecloth — and Husserl's 'things seen are always more than what we really and actually see' explains the frozen-coaster chair. Watson's see-it-to-believe-it empiricism, drained by the Afghan war, is precisely why he has no 'special powers': he never furnishes his brain-attic with the furniture that lets objects speak.
- ch. 35 "The Seven Percent Conclusion" **·** Martin Heidegger, Blaise Pascal, Søren Kierkegaard, Arthur Schopenhauer, Friedrich Nietzsche — Pendulum Between Pain and Boredom — Malloy names boredom, not Moriarty, as Holmes's true nemesis, sorting his moods through Heidegger's three types: boredom by something (the mind-reading demonstration in 'The Cardboard Box' that bores Holmes but astounds Watson), boredom with everything ('The Noble Bachelor's' 'unwelcome social summonses'), and profound boredom — the 'black moods' behind the seven-per-cent solution, which Heidegger says reveals beings as a whole in remarkable indifference. Against Schopenhauer's pendulum swinging between pain and boredom, and Nietzsche's 'against boredom even gods struggle in vain,' Pascal's and Kierkegaard's verdict that boredom is the root of all evil explains Jeremy Paul's suggestion that Holmes invented Moriarty as an equal opponent to keep the game alive. Religion, Pascal's and Kierkegaard's cure, cannot save the modern Holmes, so work, amusement, and drugs merely treat symptoms of modernity itself.
- ch. 36 "The Game’s Afoot" **·** Socrates, Aristotle — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Virtue Ethics (arete) — Littmann poses Holmes's cocaine habit as philosophy's classic akrasia puzzle: Socrates denies weakness of will, treating it as mis-measured pleasure in which nearer pleasures loom larger — the King of Bohemia risking scandal for Irene Adler's company, Sir George Burnwell's gambling, Holmes's immediate relief of boredom — while Aristotle objects in the Nicomachean Ethics that reason really is clouded by passion, the way 'Black Peter' Carey's murderous violence is clouded by rum, so the cure is habituated practice rather than a science of measuring pleasures. Aristotle's account fits our sense that Holmes, 'the most perfect reasoning and observing machine,' knowingly chooses the lesser good. The verdict is that this is the one case Holmes failed to solve: it was Watson, not Holmes's own reason and will, who 'weaned him from that drug mania.'
- ch. 37 "The Awakened One" **·** The Buddha — Buddhism; Zen Buddhism; Impermanence (anicca) — Callis reads Holmes as a Buddhist practitioner despite the cocaine and the cigars in the coalscuttle: 'You see, but you do not observe' and 'The emotional qualities are antagonistic to clear reasoning' match Vipassana bare attention and the Theravada ideal of the cool, rational, emotionally distant sage, and his improvised violin scraping works like Thich Nhat Hanh's walking meditation — a witness without commentary. The picture is completed by Doyle's Buddhism of Ceylon in The Sign of Four, Holmes's two years 'spending some days with the head lama' in Tibet ('The Empty House'), and his sitting 'like some strange Buddha' in 'The Veiled Lodger.' She maps his method onto the Yoga Sutras' dharana, dhyana, and samadhi — patient attention to the blood-scratched plaster, sustained fixation on the crime scene, ego-surrendering contemplation — making Holmes an 'awakened one' who loves truth for its own sake while Watson lives on autopilot.
- ch. 38 "THE TRACING OF FOOTSTEPS" *(front)*
- ch. 39 "The Adventure of the Time-Traveling Detective" *(no index entry yet)* — Michaels argues that BBC's Sherlock is not a straight adaptation like the Jeremy Brett series but a Fredric Jamesonian pastiche — a hip-hop-style mash-up that samples 'A Study in Scarlet' (Watson's PTSD return from Afghanistan, the 'Rache' clue now reversed into the password 'Rachel'), the video game Heavy Rain (palette, focal blur, on-screen deduction text in the Johnston font), and TV-thriller codes, with 'The Great Game' cramming five bomb-ticking mysteries worthy of 24.
