- ch. 6 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "How to Use this Book in a Philosophy Course" **·** Plato, René Descartes — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Methodological Doubt (evil demon) — Argues philosophy has a public-relations problem and that pop culture can fix it: just as Plato used the ring of Gyges and Descartes imagined a deceitful demon, The Matrix vividly pictures Cartesian deception and South Park's Cartman inheriting a million dollars dramatizes the problem of evil better than dry Jones-and-Brown cases. The chapter then advises instructors on using the chapters to introduce topics, assign summaries, and set reflection papers in intro courses, pointing to fan wikis and pop-philosophy.org so students need not be experts on the shows.
- ch. 8 "Introduction" **·** Socrates — Socratic Method (elenchus); Man Is the Measure (sophistic relativism) — Introduces Part I by casting South Park, The Daily Show, and The Colbert Report as modern Socratic gadflies. It previews Young's comparison of the show's 'corruption of the youth' controversies to Socrates' trial, Arp's use of Johnnie Cochran's Chewbacca Defense to teach logic and fallacies, and Johnson's use of Colbert's 'wikiality' and 'truthiness' to attack relativism and the myth that everyone has a right to their opinion.
- ch. 9 "The Talking Cure for Our Culture" **·** Socrates, Hannah Arendt, Plato — The Banality of Evil; The Unexamined Life; Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — Young argues South Park is perceived as dangerous for the very reasons Socrates was executed — corrupting the youth and impiety — and that like Socrates it is really a gadfly promoting the examined life. Cartman is read through Arendt's Eichmann: evil as thoughtlessness, the inability to think from another's standpoint or ask if one can live with oneself, while Kyle and Stan's dialogues (such as deliberating Stan's grandfather's euthanasia request in 'Death') model the perspective-taking Arendt calls thinking. A final Freudian section explains the show's vulgarity as essential: jokes work like dreams, releasing repressed drives so the culture can talk through what it forbids.
- ch. 10 "The Defense Rests" *(no index entry yet)* — Arp uses 'Chef Aid' — cartoon Johnnie Cochran's 'If Chewbacca lives on Endor, you must acquit' — to introduce the red herring fallacy, then teaches the basics of logic through South Park: Cartman's Tooth Fairy argument as deduction, Towelie's appearances as induction, and episodes like 'The Entity,' 'Weight Gain 4000,' and 'Butt Out' illustrating hasty generalization, slippery slope, false dilemma, appeal to inappropriate authority, and ad hominem. His point is that Parker and Stone deliberately violate logical principles for humor, and that spotting fallacies matters because bad reasoning drives laws, policies, and the beliefs people die for.
- ch. 11 "How to do Philosophy" **·** John Locke, Socrates — Moral Relativism; Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — Johnson argues through Colbert's satire that truth is neither individual ('My Truth') nor cultural ('wikiality' — a Wikipedia entry does not become true by consensus), since relativism is self-contradictory and implies slavery was not wrong before abolition. He deploys Locke's attack on 'enthusiasm' to show 'truthiness' is circular reasoning — sure because one is sure — and dismantles the 'right to my opinion' as a bid to shield beliefs from evidence, closing with Socrates' model: when evidence runs out, admit ignorance and keep doing philosophy.
- ch. 12 "Introduction" **·** Blaise Pascal, René Descartes, Edmund Gettier, William James — Pascal's Wager; Philosophical Skepticism; The Gettier Problem; The Will to Believe — Frames Part II's epistemology chapters. Jacoby's chapter uses Stan Marsh debunking TV psychic John Edward, holistic healers, and Mormon belief to teach the ethics of belief against Pascal's wager; Lawrence's uses The Matrix to pose the skeptical problem and Descartes' response; Silverman's uses Adama's lie about Earth in Battlestar Galactica to raise the Gettier problem and the Clifford–James dispute over believing without sufficient evidence.
- ch. 13 "Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress" **·** Blaise Pascal — Pascal's Wager; Faith and Reason; Philosophical Skepticism — Jacoby reads Stan Marsh as W.K. Clifford's ethics of belief in action: from 'All About the Mormons' ('you better have something to back it up') to 'The Biggest Douche in the Universe,' Stan insists the burden of proof lies with claimants and that faith used as a fallback is no evidence at all. 'Cartmanland' and the story of Job serve to criticize Pascal's Wager — a good God would not eternally torment the virtuous nonbeliever, and the Wager simply assumes its afterlife payoff — while the harms of Miss Information's holistic healers, David Blaine's cult suicide, and Scientology show Clifford was right that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken minds and, as Stan tells John Edward, slow down the progress of all mankind.
- ch. 14 "Skepticism Outside the Matrix" **·** René Descartes, Bertrand Russell — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); The Cogito; Philosophical Skepticism — Lawrence uses The Matrix to walk through Descartes' method of doubt: the dream argument, the evil demon reborn as a machine-run simulation, and invented worse cases ('Neo's Worst Nightmare,' a Matrix-within-the-Matrix that deceives even Morpheus' awakened rebels). The cogito is the only certainty that survives and Descartes' proof of God falls short, so certainty about the external world is unavailable; the chapter then borrows Russell's red-chair analysis of color, texture, and solidity to argue that even outside any Matrix, naive realism is false and we know only appearances.
- ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" **·** Edmund Gettier, Alvin Goldman, William James, David Hume, Alvin Plantinga — The Gettier Problem; Reliabilism; The Will to Believe — Silverman uses Adama's 'true lie' about Earth to motivate the Gettier problem: Starbuck's belief that Earth exists is true and justified by Adama's testimony, yet because that testimony is a lie, her justified true belief is not knowledge — just as Helo's true belief that the woman before him is 'Sharon' rests on mistaking Boomer for Athena. Goldman's reliabilism then questions whether sight, memory, and testimony are reliable belief-formers in a world of humanoid Cylons, weighing Hume's suspicion of testimony against Plantinga's defense of it. Finally Clifford's evidentialism is set against James's will to believe: the Colonials' forced, momentous choice to seek Earth shows that in an uncertain world pragmatic belief can be reasonable — 'so say we all.'
- ch. 16 "Introduction" **·** John Locke, Derek Parfit, Alan Turing — Personal Identity (memory theory); The Turing Test; Compatibilism; Teleporter Paradox (personal fission) — Frames Part III's metaphysics chapters. Lawrence's chapter uses The Matrix to survey dualism and the materialist theories of mind; Southworth's uses Wolverine's amnesia to test Locke's memory criterion and Jamie Madrox's duplicates for Parfit's view of identity; Pierce's asks whether Harry Potter's prophecies leave Harry free, probing compatibilism versus libertarian free will; and Littmann's asks whether Skynet's Terminators could be persons via a Terminator version of the Turing Test.
- ch. 17 "The Role of Matter Biology or Function" **·** René Descartes, John Searle, David Lewis — Mind–Body Dualism; Biological Naturalism / Intentionality — Lawrence asks which theory of mind best fits the Matrix trilogy. Cartesian dualism (with its pineal-gland plug standing in for Neo's headjack) would explain Neo's jackless mind in the Train Station but lacks evidence and faces the interaction problem, so the chapter defends a fully materialist reading — Neo's sentinel-destroying signal and burnt-eye sight reconstrued as Matrix hardware in his skull. It then contrasts reductive and eliminative materialism, Searle's beer-can biological naturalism, and functionalism via Lewis's Martian pain, concluding that the films' sentient machines — Agent Smith's seamless copy into Bane's body — presuppose functionalism.
- ch. 18 "Be Slow to Judge" **·** John Locke, Derek Parfit — Personal Identity (memory theory); Personal Identity; Teleporter Paradox (personal fission) — Southworth tests Locke's memory theory on Wolverine: the Cassandra Nova/Xavier mind-swap shows identity follows mind, not body, and Wolverine's serial memory wipes (Team X, Weapon X, Apocalypse's brainwashing) mean that on Locke's connected-memory view several different people have inhabited his body — with House of M's total recall suddenly loading him with responsibility for all their deeds. Jamie Madrox's duplicates then carry Parfit's objection that shared memories cannot suffice for sameness of person, pushing toward physical continuity and the chapter's deflationary moral: be slow to judge who deserves blame.
- ch. 19 "Time Travel and Fixed Time" **·** Aristotle — Fate and Foreknowledge; The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Compatibilism — Pierce asks what kind of prophecies Trelawney's two 'real predictions' are, starting from Aristotle's problem of future contingents and Alexander of Aphrodisias on self-fulfilling prophecy: Dumbledore's point that Voldemort's choice marked Harry shows the prophecy did not cause its own fulfillment. The Prisoner of Azkaban time travel — later Harry had always cast that Patronus — plus special relativity support a fixed future on which Rowling's denial of destiny amounts only to libertarian openness, and the chapter concludes that the wildly improbable luck fulfilling the prophecies (Polyjuice in Moaning Myrtle's bathroom, the Sword of Gryffindor) makes best sense if some providential being is quietly guiding events.
- ch. 20 "“Cyborgs Don’t Feel Pain. I Do.”" **·** Alan Turing, John Searle — The Turing Test; The Chinese Room; What Is It Like to Be a Bat? — Littmann asks whether Skynet's machines are people, testing three criteria on the Terminator films. The T-101 and T-1000 pass demanding Turing Tests by passing as humans; Searle's Chinese room — recast as a little Austrian inside the T-101 reciting 'Ahll be bahk' without understanding — shows behavior alone cannot prove thought; and feelings are equally unproven by behavior, since the T-101 can smile on command. But the films' first-person 'Terminator's-eye-view' sequences, Littmann argues, display what it is like to be a Terminator and thus prove machine consciousness, so humanity's extinction might not be the end of persons.
- ch. 21 "Introduction" **·** Thomas Aquinas — The Problem of Evil; Faith and Reason — Frames Part IV's philosophy of religion chapters. Johnson's chapter sets Cartman's million-dollar theme park against God's goodness, with South Park characters giving answers echoing Calvin, Hick, and Job; Gallagher's uses Rose's 'I just know' on Lost and Aquinas' distinctions between knowledge, opinion, and faith to argue that faith is not knowledge; and Eberl and Vines' uses Battlestar Galactica's Cylon monotheism versus Colonial religion and atheism to ask whether God can be proven, whether evil disproves him, and whether life is meaningful without God.
- ch. 22 "Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy" **·** Augustine of Hippo — The Problem of Evil — Johnson turns 'Cartmanland' into a survey of answers to the problem of evil: Kyle's hemorrhoid-versus-Cartman's-wealth argument is the logical problem of moral evil; the story of Job fails because Job's continued belief does not rebut the evidence; Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' mirrors Calvin's and Edwards' God-glorifying answer; and Stan's 'Cartman is totally miserable' restores Kyle's faith via second-order goods. The free will defense (via Augustine) handles moral evil but not natural evil, so the chapter closes with John Hick's soul-making theodicy — mirrored by South Park's Jesus saying life is about overcoming problems and growing — before conceding the evidential problem of evil still stands.
- ch. 23 "To Know … and Believe" **·** Thomas Aquinas, Plato — Faith and Reason; The Five Ways; Theory of Forms — Gallagher reads Lost's Rose through Aquinas: faith is 'mid-way between knowledge and opinion,' sharing the certainty of episteme and the imperfection of doxa, so Rose's 'I just know' about Bernard's survival and her island cure confuses what she believes with what she knows. Aquinas' five ways ground natural knowledge that God exists, and the castaways' failures are diagnosed as sins against faith — Charlie's despair is acedia while Rose's certainty is the presumption (praesumptio) of elevating faith to demonstrated knowledge; the lesson is that faith perfects reason without replacing it.
- ch. 24 "“You Have to Believe in Something”" **·** Thomas Aquinas, David Hume, Augustine of Hippo, Bertrand Russell, Blaise Pascal — The Five Ways; The Problem of Evil; The Meaning of Life; Pascal's Wager — Eberl and Vines use Battlestar Galactica to weigh theism against atheism: Baltar's scientific rationalism meets Aquinas' five ways (the universe's ordered structure demands an unmoved, uncaused cause), Six's faith faces the problem of evil answered through Augustine on the perverse will and John Hick's soul-making (Starbuck's mother, 'your life is a testament to pain'), while Hume's faulty-architect analogy presses the atheist case. The chapter concludes with Russell's 'A Free Man's Worship': even in a Godless universe the Colonials find meaning in comradeship and humanity's survival — 'the gods shall lift those who lift each other.'
- ch. 25 "Introduction" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); The Trolley Problem; Tripartite Soul; Utilitarianism — Frames Part V's ethics chapters. Adams' chapter updates Plato's ring of Gyges for Heroes — with Claire's and Sylar's powers, why be moral? — answered by the properly ordered tripartite soul; McAleer's uses The Office to illustrate Aristotle's wit as a mean between buffoonery and boorishness; White's uses the Batman/Joker problem and a Bat-trolley version of Foot's case to argue deontologically that Batman need not kill the Joker; and Loftis' reads Watchmen's Ozymandias and Rorschach as a failed utilitarian and a failed deontologist, pointing to 'who watches the watchmen.'
- ch. 26 "But Isn’t It Only Natural" **·** Plato — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Tripartite Soul; Justice in the Republic; The Golden Rule — Adams answers Plato's ring-of-Gyges challenge with Heroes: even when invisible, wrongdoing corrupts the wrongdoer, because justice is to the soul what health is to the body. Claire's refusal to claim credit for the fire rescue shows thumos (spirit) responsive to logistikos (reason), Sylar's uncontrollable hunger for powers is epithumetikon (appetite) ruling the soul, and Hiro's Vegas cheating shows how injustice makes life spin out of control; Claire's apology to Brody illustrates the Pagan Golden Rule — help your friends, harm your enemies — tempered by Plato's caution that enemies may become friends.
- ch. 27 "Lessons Learned" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Golden Mean; Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Eudaimonia (flourishing) — McAleer maps The Office onto Aristotle's ethics: David Brent is the buffoon who is 'the slave of his sense of humor,' Gareth the literalist boor who cannot take a joke, and Tim the ready wit whose irony responds to the situation — together illustrating that a virtue is a qualitative mean of acting and feeling appropriately, fixed by practical wisdom rather than rules. That humor cannot be codified mirrors the uncodifiability of Aristotelian ethics, and wit's very status as a virtue shows Aristotle's morality is broader than modern duty-and-outcome ethics: it aims at the flourishing (eudaimonia) of the whole person.
- ch. 28 "So, Case Closed – Right" **·** Philippa Foot, Judith Jarvis Thomson — The Trolley Problem; Deontology; Utilitarianism; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — White asks why Batman never simply kills the Joker despite the graveyard he keeps filling, framing the question with Foot's and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant-surgeon variant. Utilitarianism says kill one to save many; deontology says the agent-relative 'do not kill' — but the Batman case differs from the classic dilemmas because the Joker himself endangers his victims, Batman cannot be certain he will kill again (the foggy-track variant), and killing him would amount to the Minority Report-style prepunishment of a crime not yet committed. White, a self-described strict deontologist, concedes the case is genuinely hard and leaves the means-versus-ends debate open.
- ch. 29 "“Who watches the watchmen ”" **·** Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill, Jeremy Bentham — The Categorical Imperative; Humanity as an End in Itself; Utilitarianism; Consequentialism — Loftis argues Watchmen's real target is authoritarianism, with Ozymandias and Rorschach as corrupted rationalizers. Ozymandias calls himself a consequentialist, but his Bentham-Mill utilitarianism cannot survive Dr. Manhattan's 'Nothing ever ends' — an infinite future makes utility sums impossible — and it ignores the rights of the New Yorkers he slaughters as mere means. Rorschach's deontology is hypocrisy (he admires Truman's Hiroshima trade-off and says 'can't make an omelet without breaking eggs'), mistaking Kant's categorical imperative — universalize your maxim, treat humanity never merely as a means — for black-and-white thinking in service of fascist thuggery, while the nonideological Nite Owls embody the lesson that no one should be trusted with such power.
- ch. 30 "Introduction" *(front)*
- ch. 31 "Metallica, Nihilism, and Nostalgia" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Karl Marx — The Death of God; Master and Slave Morality; Ressentiment; Alienation — Peter Fosl reads Metallica's lyrics ("Leper Messiah," "The God That Failed," "One," "To Live Is to Die," "Escape") as extending Nietzsche's and Marx's critiques of Christianity: religion as slave morality born of ressentiment and as opium deadening the oppressed, illustrated by the landmine veteran of "One" pleading with a silent God and Hetfield's abandoned-childhood grief. He argues the band often falls into the "incomplete nihilism" Nietzsche predicted, lamenting God's failure and longing nostalgically for the Christian meaning it can no longer believe in rather than transvaluating values. Yet the defiance of "The Four Horsemen" and "Escape" and the band's creative power show it also working toward an overcoming of Christian nihilism, confirmed for Fosl by Hetfield's post-rehab health.
- ch. 32 "“They Have a Plan”" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Master and Slave Morality; Ressentiment; Immortality and the Soul — Robert Sharp reads the Cylon uprising in Battlestar Galactica as Nietzsche's slave revolt in morality: enslaved by humans, the Cylons react with resentment and overturn their masters' values, just as early Christians did under Rome. The humans keep a master morality (Colonial polytheism, warrior elites, call signs like Apollo and Athena), while Cylon monotheism, doctrines of the soul (Leoben's sermons to Starbuck, Gina's suicidal faith), equality, and consensus government reproduce slave morality's move from bodily weakness to spiritual superiority. The New Caprica occupation debate among the Cavils, Six, and Boomer, and D'Anna's boxing, show the former slaves seeking not just destruction but conversion of their masters to a religion that makes Cylons equal.
- ch. 33 "The Viewer and the Look" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Michel Foucault — The Look (hell is other people); Bad Faith; The Panopticon (surveillance) — Meyer and Schneider use the mockumentary camera of The Office (British and American versions) as Sartre's Look: Pam caught gazing at Jim and Karen in "The Merger" stages shame at being fixed as an object by the Other, while David Brent's bragging over his Inside Paper cover is pride as bad faith, an attempt to control the Other's gaze that requires denying the employee's freedom. Dwight and Angela's furtive affair and the Michael-Jan speakerphone call in "Cocktails" illustrate Foucault's panopticon: the mere possibility of the camera makes characters police themselves. The viewer, positioned behind the lens, becomes complicit in the objectifying Look that constitutes the show's comedy of embarrassment.
- ch. 34 "Determinism and the Dark Knight" **·** Martin Heidegger — Being-Toward-Death; Thrownness (Geworfenheit); Authenticity; Free Will vs Determinism — David Hart uses Heidegger's Being and Time to explain Batman's dedication without reducing it to trauma-determined compulsion: Alfred's butler's-world illustrates being-in-the-world and the thrown-project, and Bruce's confrontation with death, culminating in the bleeding alley scene of Miller's Batman: Year One, is Angst, the recognition of finitude that strips ordinary meanings away. Seen this way, "I shall become a bat" is an authentic, responsible choice of a whole life rather than a mechanical effect of childhood trauma. Hart concludes that Heidegger's analysis dissolves the free will versus determinism debate, since Batman neither blindly follows causes nor chooses from nowhere.
- ch. 35 "You’re Basically “a Stuffed Animal Made by Grandma”" **·** Carol Gilligan — The Ethics of Care; Feminism — Renee Kyle sets House's detached "doctor knows best" medicine against Cameron's practice to argue for Carol Gilligan's feminist ethic of care: Cameron builds trust, refuses to deceive or bully (defending Ezra's control over his body in "Informed Consent"), and sees patients as embedded in relationships, arranging for parents to hold their newborn in "Maternity," where House sees only abstract puzzles. The chapter also presses the standard feminist worry that valorizing care can backfire: Cameron's unresolved grief stops her from telling terminal patients the truth, and by "Que Sera Sera" she secretly injects a patient who wants to leave the hospital, so that caring too much turns her into House.
- ch. 36 "The Price of Existence" **·** Simone de Beauvoir — Woman as the Other; The Male Gaze; One Is Not Born a Woman; Embodiment (the lived body) — Bonnie Mann reads Twilight through Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex: Bella is the "relative being" whose existence has meaning only in orbit around Edward, clumsy, self-sacrificing, carried and watched, living the myth of the eternal feminine in which the masculine gaze confers being on a girl otherwise taught the world is defined without reference to her. She locates the fantasy's pull in the contradictory messages of twenty-first-century girlhood (Pipher, Phillips, Bordo), where being attractive to boys remains the first avenue to existing at all. Yet she also finds a feminist subtext: the vampire transformation returns Bella to the "I can" body, faster and stronger than Edward and saving the day herself, though Meyer ultimately re-sells the old promise that a woman wins existence through self-annihilation for others.
- ch. 37 "Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!" **·** Jean-François Lyotard, Jean Baudrillard, Michel Foucault — The End of Grand Narratives; Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); Power/Knowledge — Jeremy Wisnewski's mock-manifesto uses Family Guy's cutaway gags and taboo jokes (Hitler sausage vendors, Petoria at the UN, Saddam and Khadafi bonding over Seinfeld) to stage postmodernism: Lyotard's "incredulity toward meta-narratives" and Baudrillard's claim that the real is no longer real, since our families are as televisual as the Griffins, who at least know they are cartoons. The danger is that joking about everything breeds cynical passivity, "liberating us from our causes." But Foucault, the 1968 activist and prison reformer, shows through power/knowledge that one can be postmodern and still fight locally, so the Griffins, and the show's satire of religion and politics, get to live.
- ch. 38 "Introduction" *(front)*
- ch. 39 "Gaining Trust from the Past" **·** Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, David Hume — The State of Nature; The Social Contract; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Richard Davies treats the Oceanic 815 survivors' beach as a "framed" state of nature: the stolen water is a tragedy of the commons, Sawyer's "finders keepers" defense of Shannon's inhalers stages Hobbes's war of all against all against Locke's natural rights, and Jack and Sayid's torture of Sawyer marks the first step toward civil society, a claim to punish on another's behalf. He argues no theory of human nature (Rousseau's "Innocence" versus a "Trust No. 1" attitude) is needed to understand the castaways: cooperation grows through iterated prisoner's-dilemma tit-for-tat strategies, which also recasts the real difference between Hobbesian and Lockean states of nature.
- ch. 40 "Downsizing Dreams" **·** Karl Marx, Walter Benjamin — Alienation; Class Struggle; Ideology and False Consciousness — Michael Bray argues the American Office portrays the "salaried masses," a class that exists in denying class: Jim, Pam, and Michael's rationalized, meaningless paper work realizes Marx's account of surplus value and degraded labor (the "run-out-the-clock" truck unloading, Pam's tepid watercolors), while their self-image survives by distinguishing itself from warehouse and prison labor. Episodes like Michael's condo purchase and Pam's "dreams are just dreams" show characters secretly longing for downsizing to force a different life. Against the New Yorker's claim that the show ignores class, Bray reads its comedy as standing on the edge of naming its economic conditions, with Michael's failure to inhabit management-speak making him, via Walter Benjamin, a last glimpse of "authentic humanity."
- ch. 41 "It’s Not That Simple" **·** Utilitarianism; Deontology; Virtue Ethics; Just War Theory — Donal O'Mathuna uses 24 to run the torture debate: the ticking bomb scenario (Syed Ali's nuclear bomb, Miles pressing to torture Audrey) dramatizes the utilitarian case for forward-looking interrogational torture, while Jack slicing off the Russian consul's finger and Morris's broken guilt show torture as a deontological violation that destroys character on both sides and usually fails to extract truth. Against the show's sanitized, banal presentation (Agent Burke as the "kindly torturer"), he sets Abu Ghraib, the systematic training of torturers, and the metastatic spread of torture programs once permitted. Fiction can open the ethical question, he concludes, but must not be mistaken for the reality of torture.
- ch. 42 "Mutants as Racelike" *(no index entry yet)* — Jeremy Pierce asks whether the X-Men's mutants are a race. Biologically they fail: the X-Gene occurs in non-mutants, mutants span every human ancestry (Storm, Banshee, Colossus, Jubilee), and human genetic variation is far too slight to ground racial essences. Socially they could count: like money or political labels, races can be social kinds, and Genosha's mutant slavery and the Days of Future Past camps would push mutants toward becoming one. He concludes mutants are only "racelike," an analogy for real racial treatment rather than a new species ("Homo superior") or race.
- ch. 43 "Introduction" *(front)*
- ch. 44 "“How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons" **·** The Buddha, Dogen — The Four Noble Truths; Karma and Rebirth; Impermanence (anicca); Non-Self (anatman) — James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's sleepless FTL jumps in "33" and Roslin's dwindling survivor counts enact the four noble truths, Leoben's interrogation scenes teach that suffering comes from ignorant attachment, and Dogen's no-self and impermanence frame the show's interdependent characters. Cylon resurrection, D'Anna's serial deaths, and the prophecy that "all of this has happened before" model karma and samsara, while Nishida's kenotic God of Absolute Nothingness makes sense of Six and Leoben's God of love. Because Cylons feel pain, fear death away from a resurrection ship, and act volitionally, McRae concludes they are persons in the Buddhist sense, owed the compassion of the Eightfold Path.
- ch. 45 "House Sitting" **·** Zen Buddhism — Ruff and Barris argue that House's rude, unjustified rhetoric works like Zen koan practice: by refusing to make ordinary sense ("Everybody lies"), he destabilizes everyone's assumptions, including his own, until the real problem reveals itself, as when his irreverent digging shows the faith-healing boy in "House vs. God" is ill because of a concealed affair. This Zen style is simultaneously an ethics of acting without knowing the end (not simple ends-justify-means), a way of stripping politeness to create genuine intimacy, and a method of healing, since on the nondualist view finding the truth of the situation just is healing it. House's equanimity over his fired team at the end of "Human Error" caps the reading.
- ch. 46 "Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat" **·** Laozi, Zhuangzi — Yin and Yang; Wu Wei (effortless action); Taoism (Daoism); The Tao (the Way) — In a fictional interview with the Taoist sage "Bat-Tzu," Mark White explains Taoism through Batman's circle: Bruce's yang-dominated life of vengeance and paranoia needs the yin that Dick and Tim supply, shown by his forgiveness of Zatanna and tenderness toward Helena's baby, while Jason Todd illustrates the fate of the unbalanced who cannot accept death. Alfred emerges as the Taoist sage practicing wei-wu-wei, effortless service like Chuang Tzu's butcher, balancing right and wrong in Bruce, and the Batman-Joker duality shows yin and yang defining each other. Lao Tzu's sayings on balance, complementary opposites, and water-like yielding organize the whole reading.
- ch. 47 "Introduction" *(front)*
- ch. 48 "Reap a Destiny" **·** Martin Heidegger, William James, Aristotle, John Locke — Being-Toward-Death; Authenticity; Immortality and the Soul; Free Will vs Determinism — Jonathan and Jerry Walls read Deathly Hallows philosophically: Harry's willing march into the Forbidden Forest is Heideggerian authenticity, confronting being-toward-death, while Voldemort's horcruxes and the maimed King's Cross stowaway are the inauthentic flight from mortality that ruins the soul. The afterlife scene raises the stakes of this life: by James's "sow a thought... reap a destiny," Aristotle's habituation, and Locke's memory-based identity, Voldemort's lifelong refusal of remorse fixes his character beyond repair, and Kant and Pascal supply reasons why belief in an afterlife transforms morality. Dumbledore's purgatory-like repentance, contrasted with Voldemort's fate, shows that our choices reap a destiny we must live with forever.
- ch. 49 "House and the Life of Reason" **·** Socrates, Aristotle, Plato, Bertrand Russell — The Meaning of Life; The Unexamined Life; Eudaimonia (flourishing); Euthyphro Dilemma — Henry Jacoby takes seriously House's nihilist sound bites ("selfish, base animals," his baiting of Sister Augustine and Foreman's chapel prayer, his clinically dead experiment in "97 Seconds") but argues House actually lives the Socratic examined life and Aristotle's life of reason: his puzzle-solving saves lives, exercises humanity's distinctive function, and issues in eudaimonia. The Euthyphro dilemma shows meaning cannot be grounded in God's plan, and House's refusal of afterlife comfort leaves "our actions here" as all that matters. Against the unexamined life, House's "What's the point in living without curiosity?" makes him a Socratic figure who chooses meaning through reason rather than faith.

## Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry

- ch. 1 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** Socrates, Plato — The Unexamined Life — The editor's Introduction explains why Spider-Man merits a philosophy book: Peter Parker is a self-reflective underdog with a strong moral compass he sometimes fails to follow, so his stories raise lived ethical questions rather than abstract metaphysics. Citing Plato's definition of philosophy as the love of wisdom and a way of life, Sanford frames the whole volume around Socrates' question 'how are you going to live your life?' and lists the questions Peter's life poses: the good life, the obligations attached to talents, friendship, identity over time, the ethics of enhancement, and whether life has meaning.
- ch. 8 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** Epictetus, Viktor Frankl, Thomas Aquinas, Aristotle — Man's Search for Meaning (logotherapy); Stoicism; Virtue Ethics (arete); The Meaning of Life — Mussett asks whether Peter Parker's painful life counts as a good life by testing five philosophers' answers against the comics and films. Kurtz's secular humanism finds Peter wanting in pleasure and acclaim (Uncle Ben dead by his inaction, J. Jonah Jameson's smear campaigns), while Rand's Objectivism condemns Spider-Man as the embodiment of the 'morality of sacrifice' she rejected, noting Steve Ditko's Objectivist devotion. Epictetus scores Peter highly on duty but fails him on self-mastery, since his happiness hinges on attachments to Aunt May and MJ he cannot control; Frankl would see Peter's meaning in his irreplaceable responsibility, evidenced by his refusal of Dr. Judas Traveller's offer of a peaceful life at the cost of innocents (Amazing Spider-Man #402); and Aquinas vindicates Peter's suffering as good pain in a virtuous, charitable life.
- ch. 10 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Emmanuel Levinas, Jacques Derrida, Anselm of Canterbury — The Face of the Other; Teleological Suspension of the Ethical; The Death of God; Forgiveness — Kukkonen reads Peter's never-extinguished guilt over Uncle Ben as an 'infinite debt' modeled on Anselm's atonement theology: no good deed repays the primal transgression, so even the heroic serum rescue for Aunt May in 'The Final Chapter' (Amazing Spider-Man #33) leaves the debt intact. Against the Nietzschean escape into self-sufficient magnanimity (Ben's ghostly blessing in 'Doom Service!'), he argues via Levinas and Derrida that Peter's responsibility extends to every stranger, as when a rescued policeman with Uncle Ben's face calls him back in 'Spider-Man No More!' (#50). Following Kierkegaard's Works of Love, the chapter concludes that Peter's heroics do not pay off but deepen his debt of love, since every choice heeds one call while unavoidably failing others.
- ch. 11 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant — Deontology; The Categorical Imperative; Consequentialism — White analyzes Spider-Man's public unmasking in Civil War as a familiar ethical choice between the right and the good. Peter's promise to Tony Stark and obedience to the Superhuman Registration Act are deontological duties, explicated through Kant's test of universalizing the maxim of promise-breaking, while his worry for Aunt May and MJ pulls him toward consequentialist reasoning whose uncertainty, complexity, and incommensurability the chapter details. Aunt May's 'some things are worth the risk' speech tips Peter toward principle, but the Kingpin's sniper shoots her anyway, and Peter's hellish aftermath — ending in the Mephisto deal of 'One More Day' — shows both the tragedy of doing the right thing and the argument that when consequences are unknowable one should simply do what is right.
- ch. 12 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** The Problem of Evil; Forgiveness — Barkman argues that Spider-Man's ethics, while universal enough for Jews, Platonists, and Confucians, are specifically Christian in emphasis: God creates for friendship, which requires free choice, so 'with great power comes great responsibility' restates Luke 12:48 — the more one is given, the more justice is required, as Peter's refusal of MJ and Octavius's wasted intelligence in Spider-Man 2 show. The free-will solution to the problem of evil (chosen evil, fallen angels, Adam's curse, a law-governed physical world) is read through Peter's questioning God in 'The Big Question' (Peter Parker: Spider-Man #48). The chapter culminates with Spider-Man 3, where the symbiote inflames Peter's grief into revenge against Sandman — a perversion of justice — until Peter forgives Flint Marko, enacting mercy as the perfection rather than the absence of justice.
- ch. 14 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** John Stuart Mill, Alasdair MacIntyre — The Harm Principle — Keeping asks what grounds the claim that great power brings great responsibility and answers through Good Samaritan ethics. Building on MacIntyre's account of human interdependence in family and community, and Mill's point that failing to aid can itself cause harm, he argues that Bad Samaritanism is a blameworthy harm-causing omission, so Spider-Man's rescues of strangers are obligatory negative duties rather than supererogatory favors. His vigilantism is excused because only he can stop supervillains, 'can implies ought' explains why his duties exceed ordinary people's, and his life-risking feats against the Sinister Six and Firelord still go beyond even what his enlarged duty demands.
- ch. 15 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** Bernard Williams, Thomas Nagel, Immanuel Kant, Susan Wolf — Moral Luck; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Tallon uses the problem of moral luck (Williams and Nagel) to ask how blameworthy Peter really is for Uncle Ben's death: the Peter who let the thief go and the counterfactual Peter whose thief was caught at the elevator act identically, yet outcome luck makes the first feel like a murderer, clashing with Kant's Control Principle that only the good will has moral worth. Drawing on Williams's 'agent regret' and Susan Wolf's 'nameless virtue' of taking responsibility for consequences, the chapter separates culpability — Peter is guilty only of letting a thief go, with the intervening agency of the criminal breaking the causal chain — from responsibility for damage. Aunt May's own misguided confession that she caused Ben's death by arguing with him (Amazing Spider-Man #479) shows how virtuous people confuse involvement in a causal chain with guilt.
- ch. 16 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** David Hume, John Locke, Thomas Reid, George Berkeley — Reason Is the Slave of the Passions; Subjective Idealism (esse est percipi); Common Sense Philosophy — Terjesen uses spider-sense to tour early-modern philosophy of perception: against direct realism, Locke's indirect realism and its primary/secondary quality distinction suggest 'dangerousness' is a perceiver-relative secondary quality — bombs threaten Spider-Man but not the Hulk, and Mysterio manufactures danger-experiences — while Berkeley's idealism and Hume's phenomenalism radicalize the resulting skepticism about ever verifying sense data. The decisive clue is that spider-sense fails when Aunt May conks Peter with a vase (Amazing Spider-Man #114) and when his mentor Miles Warren becomes the Jackal: Peter does not fear those he loves. This supports Hume's sentimentalist account of moral judgment, on which vice is found not in the act but in the disapproving sentiment, moderated by Reid's common-sense reply that perception always already contains judgment — so spider-sense is a moralized judgment about what to avoid, not a Geiger counter.
- ch. 18 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** John Dewey, David Hume, Thomas Reid, The Buddha — Pragmatism; Bundle Theory of Self; Non-Self (anatman); Personal Identity — Godwin reads Spider-Man 3's black-suit episode as a question about the self: with the symbiote amplifying his anger, is Peter still Peter? Against Hume's and the Buddha's bundle theories, on which the self is only an imagined aggregate of thoughts and feelings, and Reid's common-sense simple self, she advances the pragmatist 'social self' of Peirce, James, Dewey, and Mead, updated as Engel's biopsychosocial model: Peter's identity is a shifting web of biology, psyche, and relationships (Aunt May, MJ, Harry) expressed in actions and character. Eddie succumbs to the symbiote because, as Dewey says of the slave to his own blind desires, hatred constitutes who he is, while Peter's thicker web of good relations lets him shed the suit at the church bell.
- ch. 19 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Emmanuel Levinas, Thomas Aquinas — Embodiment (the lived body); The Face of the Other; Cardinal and Theological Virtues; Phenomenology — Spencer gives a phenomenological account of bodily transformation in the films: with Merleau-Ponty, Peter's new body changes his world — walls become surfaces to climb — and grants motor knowledge that needs no calculation, while Norman Osborn's deliberately seized powers feed pride and Doc Ock's grief shows how transformation can sweep a weak will into vice. Virtue, on Aquinas's definition as the perfection of a power, develops only through choices and habits worked out across a whole life, so ethics is deeper than rule-following. With Levinas, the call to goodness is experienced bodily: sympathy with others' suffering draws Peter out of himself — he rushes into a burning building even when powerless in Spider-Man 2 — and the Green Goblin lives a self-contradiction by feigning deafness to it, while eros for Mary Jane both distracts from and ennobles the quest.
- ch. 20 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 21 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Nick Bostrom — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Novy asks whether it would be right to deliberately make a Spider-Man. Glaucon's Ring of Gyges challenge from Plato's Republic — that unchecked superpower breeds 'great corruptibility' — is made flesh in Doc Ock, Green Goblin, Lizard, and Morbius, while Bostrom's transhumanism supplies the movement the chapter defends. Against Fukuyama's bio-conservative worries about playing God, destroying equality, and violating a human essence, the chapter notes that Aunt May's bifocals and insulin already make her a cyborg, that Marvel grants personhood by behavior rather than biology (Kree, Skrulls, the Vision), and that the thought experiment of giving Mary Jane a painless 'super smile' shows we are at least sometimes obliged to enhance.
- ch. 22 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** Personal Identity; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Southworth and Timm use the Clone Saga to teach real cloning science: molecular, therapeutic, and reproductive cloning, Dolly's 1-in-277 success rate, the impossibility of clone caskets and inherited memories — while crediting the 1970s writers for correctly making mitochondrial DNA the blood test that distinguishes Peter from Ben Reilly. They then evaluate the characters' reactions: Leon Kass's 'wisdom of repugnance,' which holds that a clone's genotype 'has already lived' and despotically fixes its life's expectations, explains Kane's genocidal self-loathing and Peter's rage and despair when told he is the clone, while Gregory Pence's rebuttal — that such repugnance rests on false expectations, as with twins or children of interracial couples — vindicates MJ's and Ben's insistence that a clone's moral worth lies in what it does, not where its genes came from.
- ch. 23 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** Philosophy of Love — Taliaferro and Little ask whether Spider-Man can champion justice and love Mary Jane at the same time, framed by Mandela's tension between obligations to family and to community. Through paired scenarios — rescuing an endangered coworker at possible mortal cost versus a lover's plea to become a surgeon rather than join a deadly crime-fighting unit — they conclude that justice trumps romance in unforeseen emergencies, while romance can rightly govern the choice of a vocation. For Spider-Man the two fuse rather than conflict, since MJ loves him partly for his commitment to justice, though Gwen Stacy's death on the bridge — where his webbing snapped her neck — shows a hero can lose both at once.
- ch. 25 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Philosophy of Love — Spanakos asks why Spider-Man is called 'friendly' by testing Peter's relationships against Aristotle's three philias (pleasure, utility, virtue) and the proportionality principle that the morally inferior friend should love the superior more — a principle that breaks down for a superhero as godlike as Spider-Man. Peter's secrecy and self-sacrifice block true Aristotelian fellowship with MJ, whose crush on Spidey is mere fantasy-love, and Harry's friendship rests on pleasure and utility, failing every Aristotelian test. Yet against philia the chapter sets Christian agape (St. Basil, John 15, C.S. Lewis's Four Loves): unconditional, self-sacrificial love for the unlovable, which Peter practices toward his betrayers and which Harry finally enacts when he dies saving Peter in Spider-Man 3 — an agape that makes him Peter's equal.
- ch. 26 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Thomas Aquinas — Humanity as an End in Itself; The Categorical Imperative; Doctrine of Double Effect — Robichaud argues Peter actually wronged two of his worst enemies before they became them. Kant's requirement to treat persons as ends, tempered by reflective equilibrium, condemns his years-long deception of best friend Harry about being Spider-Man and about Norman's death — a silence that later explodes Harry into the second Green Goblin — and having unknowingly made the sentient alien symbiote dependent on him during Secret Wars, Peter owed it more caution than blasting it off as dirty laundry. Still, two wrongs don't make a right: Harry may 'Goblinize' only in self-defense, not revenge, and by the doctrine of double effect Spider-Man may ring the bell tower to separate Venom from Eddie Brock even foreseeing the symbiote's destruction and Eddie's breakdown; finally, his special obligations oblige him to seek his friends' reform, not merely their capture.
- ch. 27 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Aristotle, Sigmund Freud, Henri Bergson — Laughter (the comic as mechanical encrusted on the living) — Malloy asks why Spider-Man jokes while fighting for his life. After surveying the superiority theory (Plato, Hobbes's 'sudden glory'), Kant's incongruity theory, and Freud's relief theory, he adapts F. H. Buckley's moral-superiority account: Spidey's quips at the Vulture's boasting, Doc Ock's mercilessness, Kingpin's girth, and J. Jonah Jameson's sourness are moral corrections meant to goad their butts toward the virtues they lack. Aristotle's buffoon/wit distinction saves Spidey from vulgarity — he can be serious after Gwen Stacy's death — and his teasing of allies like the Thing and Captain America teaches social virtues, though the jokes rarely reform anyone.
- ch. 29 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** Virtue Ethics; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — White examines the fan fury over 'One More Day,' in which Peter and MJ trade their marriage to Mephisto to save Aunt May's life. Virtue ethics evaluates people by stable character traits, but situationist psychology (the pay-phone coin experiments, Doris's Lack of Character) argues behavior tracks trivial situational details, not traits — while fictional characters like Captain America and Peter Parker are written with simpler, firmer traits, so making a deal with the devil reads as glaringly out of character and betrays the audience's trust. Since the true agents were editor Joe Quesada and the writers, White asks whether creators owe fans fidelity to a character's established identity, and closes by arguing that even if real character is situational, integrity — being the same person across situations — remains a virtue worth aspiring to, including toward ourselves.
- ch. 30 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Alasdair MacIntyre — Virtues, Practices and Traditions; Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Sanford argues, through the arc of the Raimi trilogy, that Peter becomes good by becoming the narrator of his own life. On Aristotle's Poetics — a story has a beginning, middle, and end, and art imitates life — and MacIntyre's claim that man is a 'story-telling animal' whose life is 'the unity of a narrative quest,' Peter's involuntary obligations (orphanhood, Uncle Ben's death, the spider bite, love for MJ) ground the voluntary ones, and his quest is to use his great powers responsibly. Tracking Aristotle's categories, Peter moves from incontinence (vengeance on Flint Marko, the jazz-club strut in Spider-Man 3) through continence to genuine virtue, and his practice of telling his own story — 'it's the choices that make us who we are' — models how we must get our own stories straight to flourish.
- ch. 31 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 32 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 9 "Who Teaches Philosophy Under the Sea" *(no index entry yet)* — Editor Joseph Foy's introduction recounts SpongeBob's rise from the 1999 Nickelodeon debut to a global staple (seven Emmys, nine million viewers for 'Atlantis SquarePantis', fans from President Obama to a Mexican 'Bob Esponja Presidente' mural), and argues the show's eight-to-eighty appeal comes from philosophical seeds beneath the whimsy: identity and the self, obligations toward others, the individual in community, principles of the marketplace, and environmental ethics. The volume's stated aim is to use the sponge to kindle interest in philosophy's big questions among fans young and old.
- ch. 10 "PART I - I’m Ready, I’m Ready, I’m Ready" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "Why Is It the Best Day Ever" **·** Aristotle — The Golden Mean; Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Nicole Pramik argues SpongeBob is Aristotle's self-mastered man: his daily cheerfulness is eudaimonia, a happiness earned by practicing virtue as the mean between vices of excess and deficiency. The chapter tests each mean with episodes — courage between cowardly isolation ('I Had an Accident') and recklessness ('A Life in a Day'), honor between Patrick's under-the-rock humility and Squidward's Easter-Island vanity, honesty in 'Hooky' and 'Wet Painters', and good temper mended with Patrick in 'New Student Starfish' and 'The Fry Cook Games'. His moderation in pleasure and wealth, contrasted with Mr. Krabs's stinginess, and his F.U.N. Song friendship (Aristotle's greatest external good) show the golden mean served up on a sesame seed bun.
- ch. 12 "How Can I Compete with Geniusness" **·** John Stuart Mill, Socrates — Higher and Lower Pleasures; Utilitarianism; Moral Relativism — Timothy Dunn uses 'Patrick SmartPants', where a brain-coral transplant turns Patrick into a genius who abandons SpongeBob, to ask whether the happy ignoramus or the discontented genius lives better. After sketching a subjectivist defense of Patrick's choice to revert ('knowledge can never replace friendship'), the chapter tests Mill's hedonistic utilitarianism: since competent judges rank higher pleasures qualitatively above lower ones, Mill's dictum that it is better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied condemns Patrick's destruction of his own higher capacities. Dunn then presses two objections — that people's actual lower-pleasure preferences may be genuine rather than socially produced, and that the capacity for higher pleasure seems worthless without its actual experience — leaving Mill's verdict in tension.
- ch. 13 "I Listen to Public Radio" **·** Arthur Schopenhauer — The World as Will; Philosophical Pessimism; Theory of Forms — Natasha Liebig reads Squidward as Schopenhauer made flesh: his endless craving for musical fame and revenge on Squilliam exemplifies the blind, irrational will-to-live whose frustration just is suffering, so even success could never satisfy him and others' joys (SpongeBob and Patrick playing) become his bellum omnium. Yet Squidward's clarinet, self-portraits and dance are Schopenhauer's aesthetic escape — will-less contemplation of universal Ideas, with music the most metaphysical art — granting fleeting moments of peace until his neighbors interrupt. The chapter closes on the irony that Schopenhauer's genius is childlike, so SpongeBob and Patrick's effortless wonder may make them the truer artists.
- ch. 14 "So, You Tried to Kill Me Over a Little New Age Management, Eh" **·** Karl Marx, Aristotle, Adam Smith — Alienation; Commodity Fetishism; Eudaimonia (flourishing); The Unexamined Life — Joseph Foy weighs Mr. Krabs against Ayn Rand's celebration of money-making, Marx's charge that Krabs commodifies his employees — wagering SpongeBob to Plankton in 'Welcome to the Chum Bucket' and working him 43 days without a break in 'Fear of a Krabby Patty' — and Aristotle's and Adam Smith's insistence that wealth is merely instrumental to flourishing. The verdict: Krabs inverts means and ends, fetishizing money until he sells SpongeBob's soul for 62 cents ('Born Again Krabs') and trades his own body for his millionth dollar ('Clams'). His real failing is the unexamined life — he never asks what would actually make him happy — which makes him tragically human rather than simply villainous.
- ch. 15 "After All, Who’s the Toughest Critter in Bikini Bottom" **·** Feminism — Denise Du Vernay argues Sandy Cheeks is the show's one proof of feminist messaging: a liberal feminist who attains equality within the status quo as scientist, bodybuilder and 'smartest one in Bikini Bottom', while a materialist feminist reading would worry most about SpongeBob's exploitation as Mr. Krabs's worker and property ('Welcome to the Chum Bucket'). She reads 'Squirrel Jokes' as a lesson in how stereotypes spread ('stupidity isn't a virus, but it sure is spreading like one'), catalogs the show's tired female stereotypes (nagging Karen, bratty Pearl), and defends SpongeBob and Sandy against Focus on the Family's 2005 gay-panic attacks as the sexualizing of asexual children's characters.
- ch. 16 "That Naive Cube! How Long Must I Suffer This" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Arthur Schopenhauer — Will to Power; The Übermensch; Master and Slave Morality — Nicholas Michaud inverts the show's morality through Nietzsche: Plankton's tenacity, ambition and self-overcoming make him a super-organism driven by the will to power (traced to Schopenhauer's will to live), while Bikini Bottom's lionizing of SpongeBob's mediocrity is slave morality that judges by intentions to keep the strong down. Quoting the lambs and birds of prey from On the Genealogy of Morals and the 'incurably mediocre' passage from Beyond Good and Evil, he argues Plankton is the unsung hero who treats SpongeBob as an equal, Krabs a mere exploiter — and SpongeBob, who makes mediocrity contagious, the true villain.
- ch. 17 "PART II - Welcome to Bikini Bottom" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "An Island of Milk and Honey or Rock Bottom" **·** Robert Nozick, Karl Marx, Aristotle, Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, David Hume — Anarchism; The Minimal State; Ideology and False Consciousness; Utopia and Dystopia — Shaun Young asks whether governmentless Bikini Bottom refutes political philosophy's claim that the good life needs a state: it is not the anarchism of Godwin and Kropotkin (police fines, health inspectors and the Fry Cooks Union constrain liberty), not Marx's communism (Krabs keeps exploiting SpongeBob, whose 'false consciousness' surfaces only briefly in 'Clams'), not the utopias of Plato, Bacon or More (Squidward and Plankton are miserable), and not Nozick's night-watchman state (SpongeBob is arrested for failing to invite police to his party). The lesson he draws: expect neither utopia nor Rock Bottom, because no single theory captures a real (or imaginary undersea) society.
- ch. 19 "The Ideal Candidate" **·** Plato, Aristotle, John Stuart Mill — Democracy; The Philosopher King; On Liberty — Nathan Zook uses the 'Royal Krabby' election from Vote for SpongeBob and the global-warming plot of SpongeBob Goes Green to weigh democracy. Mr. Krabs's rigged election, run only to sell patties, exemplifies C. Wright Mills's power elite manipulating the appearance of popular rule; Plato would bar Producer-class SpongeBob and Squidward from ruling and prefers educated Guardians, while Mill defends each citizen's liberty to choose and democracy's alliance with education (SpongeBob learns about global warming from Sandy). Aristotle's polity — citizens administering the state for the common interest — makes SpongeBob the ideal candidate because he saves Bikini Bottom without claiming power.
- ch. 20 "Yours Is Superior, therefore I Concede to You" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Cardinal and Theological Virtues; Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — Adam Barkman evaluates King Neptune's kingship through Dante's De Monarchia: kingship is God-ordained, justice means treating each being according to its nature, and a true king is a servant-leader who must possess the four cardinal virtues and three theological ones. Neptune ('I'm the king. That's what I do', before executing a crown polisher and smiting at every problem) has courage but lacks prudence and temperance; Triton has prudence without courage; and levelheaded Mindy would be the best ruler, though Dante's tradition would disqualify her because she is female. The chapter concludes neither Neptune nor Triton has enough virtue or political knowledge to be a good king, and reform rather than deposition is the Dantean answer.
- ch. 21 "No Matter How You Flip the Patty . ." **·** John Locke, Thomas Hobbes, David Hume — Labor Theory of Property; The State of Nature; The Social Contract — Michael Dodge asks whether Krabs may guard the Krabby Patty formula, sorting Bikini Bottom's property into collective, communal (Jellyfish Fields) and private, and deploying the tragedy of the commons — Krabs's jellyfish-squeezing factory in 'Jellyfish Hunter' — to show why shared resources get rationally overexploited. Hobbes grounds Krabs's right in sovereign enforcement (without the law, 'Pineapple Fever''s chalk-line household collapses into animals fighting over the fridge), Locke in labor-mixing, with Krabs's identity bound to his patties since 'Help Wanted', and Hume in conventions of justice born of selfishness and scarcity. All three support Krabs's legal and moral right to his secret recipe against Plankton.
- ch. 22 "Friends—Don’t Leave Home without ’Em" **·** Henry David Thoreau, Ralph Waldo Emerson — Transcendentalism; Walden (deliberate living); Wilderness and Nature Aesthetics — Greg Ahrenhoerster places SpongeBob in literary history between Transcendentalism and naturalism: 'Nature Pants' is a failed Walden — SpongeBob gives away his possessions for Jellyfish Fields but his 'jellyfish instincts' fail as badly as self-reliance in London's 'To Build a Fire' — while 'Squidville' shows the industrial city's cold indifference as in Crane's Maggie. 'Jellyfish Hunter' warns that trying to exploit nature (Krabs's jelly factory) invites nature's reprisal, since civilized beings without instinct are at nature's mercy. The naturalist moral, against Transcendentalist solitude, is that we survive only through each other: visit Jellyfish Fields, but bring a friend.
- ch. 23 "PART III - You’re Like a Steamed Vegetable, Only Smarter" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Do I Even Care if I’m Dreaming" **·** René Descartes — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Philosophical Skepticism — Kate Elson Anderson reads 'Sleepy Time' — SpongeBob's tour of his neighbors' dream clouds, from Gary's library to Patrick's quarter-fed kiddie ride to Krabs's Moby Dollar — through Descartes's First Meditation dream argument that no sure mark distinguishes waking from dreaming. Norman Malcolm's claim that one cannot even ask 'Am I dreaming?' while asleep is contradicted by SpongeBob's lucid wandering, and Patrick's mundane dream (he would not even conjure another quarter) proves Descartes's point that dreams can be indistinguishable from reality. SpongeBob's final move — asking the question but never waiting for an answer — leaves Descartes baffled by a truth-seeker immune to skepticism.
- ch. 25 "What You Really Wanted Was Inside You All Along" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Robert Kincaid maps Freud's structural model of the psyche onto Conch Street: Patrick under his rock is the pleasure-principle Id, guilt-administering Squidward the Super-Ego, and mediating SpongeBob the Ego, so 'Mermaid Man and Barnacle Boy IV' becomes the Ego minimizing, rationalizing and literally shrinking its own conscience and desires to dodge guilt over the belt. Episodes missing one member ('Squidville', 'SB-129', 'Big Pink Loser') dramatize egolessness and what each part contributes, and the chapter closes by asking whether Freudian psychic causation — the mind 'outnumbering itself' in 'Squilliam Returns' — undermines moral responsibility for what SpongeBob does.
- ch. 26 "The Future of Sandy Cheeks" **·** Karl Popper, Aldo Leopold — Falsificationism; Ockham's Razor; The Land Ethic — Wilson González-Espada assesses Sandy Cheeks as a portrait of the scientist: she explodes the 'Draw a Scientist' stereotype — female, socially popular, working in an open treedome that mirrors peer review — yet the show muddles the nature of science, calling inventions 'experiments' and a clipboard of math 'science'. The chapter applies Popper's falsifiability to SpongeBob's one-sided evidence that Squidward is a true friend and Newton's principle of parsimony to Sandy's ghost scare, then closes with Aldo Leopold's land ethic, reading 'Jellyfish Hunter' and 'SpongeBob's Last Stand' as environmental parables about habitat and overexploitation.
- ch. 27 "Secret Revealed . . . I Wonder" **·** Plato, Thomas Hobbes, Cicero — Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Robert Vuckovich reads 'The Secret Box' through Plato's Theaetetus — wonder as the birth of philosophy, with Patrick playing Socratic midwife to SpongeBob's desire to know — and Hobbes's diagnosis of curiosity as 'a lust of the mind' that obsesses and torments until satisfied. SpongeBob's masked break-in turns epistemic desire into what Cicero condemns as 'knavery that wears the mask of wisdom', nearly destroying the friendship, while the Charmides ideal of self-knowledge as temperance is exactly what he lacks. The episode ends like a Platonic dialogue in aporia: SpongeBob peeks but does not search, learns nothing, and Patrick still guards the secret.
- ch. 28 "Denizens of the Deep" *(notes)*
- ch. 29 "Index" *(notes)*
