## Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Star Trek and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Federation Council GEORGE A REISCH" *(notes)*
- ch. 6 "Ex Astris, Scientia GEORGE A REISCH" **·** William James, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Plato — The Will to Believe; The Unexamined Life; Allegory of the Cave — The editors' introduction takes Starfleet Academy's motto 'Ex Astris, Scientia' as its frame: Picard handing cadet Wesley Crusher a book by William James shows officers need philosophy, not just ship operations, and the starry-heavens motif runs from Thales and Plato's cave through Kant's 'moral law within and starry heavens above.' It surveys the book's Trek dilemmas (Picard and Dathon's alien language, Data's emotion chip, Khan's vengeance, Riker's Q powers) as 2,500-year-old philosophical problems, and argues Trek's optimism — Picard's 'the acquisition of wealth is no longer the driving force' — restates Aristotle's claim that all humans by nature desire to know. Like philosophy from Socrates on, Trek is presented as 'an entertaining, edifying preparation' for living by one's ideals, a life-education primer sealed with Roddenberry's advice to 'slip in a heavy idea or two.'
- ch. 7 "Starfleet Directive ONE - Seek Out New Ideas Major Philosophical Themes in" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Never Underestimate a TV Writer" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein — Language Games — Cantor argues the TNG episode 'Darmok' dramatizes Wittgenstein's later philosophy of language: Picard first reads Dathon's 'Temba, his arms wide' as naming objects — the Augustinian picture of language Wittgenstein rejects — then realizes on El-Adrel IV that Tamarian utterances mean through their use in a shared activity, as when he and Dathon fight the beast together. The Tamarians speak entirely in citations of their own myths ('Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra', 'Shaka, when the walls fell'), so language is shown to be embedded in a form of life, exactly Wittgenstein's 'if a lion could talk' problem. The chapter then ties this to E.D. Hirsch's cultural literacy — Troi's 'Juliet on her balcony' and Picard's Gilgamesh story show communication presupposes shared cultural knowledge — and concludes that the erudite writers Menosky and LaZebnik made a genuinely philosophic episode of television.
- ch. 9 "“Logic Without Need Is Sterile”" **·** Plato, Mahatma Gandhi, Parmenides — Ahimsa (nonviolence); Non-Self (anatman); The Meaning of Life — Writing as a Vulcan philosophy professor and student of Spock, the chapter reconstructs Vulcan civilization from Surak's Awakening as three interlocking modes of logic — formal logic (whose first law, Kiri-kin-tha's 'nothing unreal exists', parallels Parmenides), ethical logic (the axiom 'the needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few'), and meditative discipline — and maps them onto Patanjali's Yoga: the yamas, meditation, and samadhi's cosmic oneness, with ahimsa linking Surak to Gandhi and King. It then rereads Star Trek: The Motion Picture, where V'Ger's pure logic leaves both it and Spock asking 'Is this all that I am?', and Spock's mind meld with V'Ger becomes a tantric union that integrates feeling with logic after the failure of Kolinahr. The chapter's thesis is that 'logic without need is sterile': logic is 'the beginning of wisdom . . . not the end', and Spock's rebirth culminates in choosing the human thing precisely when it is not the logical thing.
- ch. 10 "“All Good Things Must Come to an End”" **·** Epictetus, Aristotle, Cicero, Seneca — Stoicism; The Dichotomy of Control; The Golden Mean; Preferred Indifferents — Thorsrud casts Spock and Data's exchange in 'Unification, Part II' — Spock dispassionate by choice, Data longing for emotion — as a replay of the ancient debate between Stoics and Peripatetics over whether to eliminate or moderate the passions. The Aristotelian side is built from Data's emotion-chip rage while killing a Borg ('Descent'), his unfelt breakup with Jenna ('In Theory'), and Riker's defense of trust after Ishara's betrayal ('Legacy'): emotions are judgments with pleasure or pain, there is a right amount to feel, and invulnerability costs the 'emotional bonds that make us who we are.' The Stoic reply uses Epictetus's distinction between involuntary impressions and assent (Picard's fear on the Borg ship vs. the holodeck), Cicero's refusal to 'moderate' what is simply a fault, and Seneca on anger, exemplified by Spock's 'quite logical relief' in 'Amok Time', his calculated desperation in 'The Galileo Seven', and his saving the bigot Stiles in 'Balance of Terror' — leaving the Peripatetic conclusion that fortune's goods are not mere indifferents and we may rightly 'smile with so little provocation.'
- ch. 11 "Meaning The Final Frontier" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Robert Nozick — The Übermensch; Ressentiment; The Death of God; Master and Slave Morality — Biderman and Devlin read The Wrath of Khan as a Nietzschean test of whether revenge can ground a meaningful life after the death of God: Kirk, stuck 'flying a goddamn computer console' as an admiral, and the Genesis project seek meaning through creation without God, while Khan, broken by exile on Ceti Alpha V, chooses vengeance. Using Nozick's contrast between impartial retribution and personally satisfying revenge, and Nietzsche's will to power, master-slave morality, and ressentiment, they argue Khan had the superhuman gifts and independence from herd morality of a candidate Overman, but let revenge enslave him — culminating in Genesis turned weapon and his dying 'For hate's sake . . . I spit my last breath at thee,' a resounding No to life. Spock's mirror-image self-sacrifice, which affirms life, is offered as the better Nietzschean Overman.
- ch. 12 "“Condemned to Be a Member of This Lowest of Species”" **·** Plato, John Stuart Mill, Aristotle — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Higher and Lower Pleasures; The Meaning of Life — Arp uses Glaucon's Ring of Gyges from the Republic to ask whether unlimited power must corrupt the just: Q's career of meddling ('Encounter at Farpoint', 'Q Who?', 'The Q and the Grey') shows the corrupted case, while Riker given Q-powers in 'Hide and Q' helps his friends instead, a counterexample Glaucon can resist by pleading insufficient time. He then explains the Q's misery — Quinn's bored suicidal plea in 'Death Wish' — through the hedonistic paradox, refining it with Mill's distinction between bodily lower pleasures and mental higher ones and Aristotle's account of the lasting pleasure of completed states like beating the ship's computer at chess. The conclusion is that Q's 'condemnation' to mortality in 'Déjà Q' reveals the human condition as enviable: it is precisely our lacking unlimited power, pleasure, and immortality that drives the striving for truth, justice, goodness, and love.
- ch. 13 "Starfleet Directive TWO - Go Boldly, Yet Morally Federation Ethics" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "“Sometimes You Just Have to Bow to the Absurd”" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato — Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); Personal Identity; The Übermensch — Eberl weighs genetic enhancement and cloning through Trek's test cases: Julian Bashir's parents' enhancement leaves him feeling 'a fraud' ('You used to be my father. Now, you're my architect'), the Moab IV 'Masterpiece Society' breeds out 'the unknown, self-discovery, things that make life worth living', and the Jem'Hadar show desire itself engineered for control. He argues the right to an open future constrains designing children (B'Elanna's wish to de-Klingonize her baby, Worf pressuring Alexander), defends genetic treatment while rejecting genetic determinism, and uses Kass and Rovane with Picard and Shinzon, the Mariposa clones, and Trip's clone Sim to show clones are numerically distinct persons. Against Malik's Augments quoting Nietzsche — 'mankind is something to be surpassed' — the chapter argues the Übermensch demands self-mastery through philosophy, not eugenic engineering, tracing eugenics from Plato's Guardian breeding scheme through Buck v. Bell to modern prenatal selection.
- ch. 15 "“Make It So”" **·** Immanuel Kant, John Rawls, Michel Foucault, Friedrich Nietzsche — Autonomy of the Will; The Categorical Imperative; Discipline and Docile Bodies — Challans argues Picard is 'Starfleet's conscience' because he exemplifies Kantian moral autonomy — acting on categorical principles like the Prime Directive rather than on orders, authority, or hypothetical imperatives — while the Borg show its total loss: assimilated drones forfeit moral agency, and the Borg Queen's pursuit of collective perfection is at best Rawls's merely 'rational autonomy.' Boétie's dupes and knaves, Nietzsche's herd, Milgram's obedience experiments, and Foucault's institutions producing docile bodies explain how war machines make complicity normal, from Gowron's corrupt Klingon Empire to Browning's 'ordinary men.' Picard passes the twenty-fourth-century Milgram tests — refusing illegal orders in 'Conundrum' and exposing 'The Pegasus', fighting Starfleet itself in Insurrection with 'How many people does it take, Admiral, before it becomes wrong?' — while the chapter closes by charging that America's real war machine now resembles the Borg more than Starfleet.
- ch. 16 "“I’ve Never Been Good at Good-byes”" **·** Immanuel Kant — The Categorical Imperative; Humanity as an End in Itself; Deontology — Lee treats DS9's Cardassian Occupation as a case of transitional justice like post-Holocaust and post-apartheid reckonings, asking whether Odo, security chief on Terok Nor, was a collaborator. Applying Kant's deontology — the good will, both formulations of the categorical imperative, illustrated by Kai Opaka's Kendra Valley betrayal, Quark's smuggling in 'Little Green Men', and Sisko's fraud in 'In the Pale Moonlight' — he judges Odo's letting three innocent Bajorans die in 'Things Past' as negligence, but his years-long cover-up as using the victims merely as means to protect his reputation, and hence genuine collaboration, as was his neglect of duty under the Link's pull in 'Behind the Lines.' Kant's imperfect duty of beneficence then redeems Odo's final departure from Kira: returning to cure and educate the Founders in 'What You Leave Behind' is a moral duty owed to rational beings.
- ch. 17 "“There’s More to Life than Profit”" **·** Adam Smith, Aristotle — The Invisible Hand; The Capabilities Approach — Held argues business ethics stalls because it begins from capitalism's presuppositions instead of asking what we fundamentally value, staging the impasse as Quark versus Rom and as Friedman's stockholder theory against Freeman's stakeholder theory ('The Dogs of War', Zek's reforms, 'Profit and Lace'). He recovers Aristotle's Politics distinction between economics serving the household's good and chrematistics — money-making as sheer accumulation, embodied in Quark's 'pure profit' embezzlement — and corrects the libertarian caricature of Adam Smith: the invisible hand works only within commutative justice and virtue, markets serving welfare rather than profit. Through Sen's capability approach and Quark's own defense of greed as promoting human development in 'Prophet Motive', the chapter concludes profit is only a means to freedom and well-being — 'there's more to life than profit' — and the Rules of Acquisition themselves must stand before the ethical judge.
- ch. 18 "Starfleet Directive THREE - A United Federation Social and Religious Values of" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "“Obviously, the Borg Can’t Hold Their Liquor”" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Baruch Spinoza, Parmenides — Geist (World Spirit); Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura); Being and Changelessness; History Has a Direction — Decker asks 'What's it like to be a Borg?' and tests whether monist metaphysics justify the Collective: Parmenides's changeless, perfect Being matches the Borg's 'bringing them closer to perfection', Spinoza's one substance (God or Nature) makes assimilationist determinism intelligible and finds truth in Seven of Nine's nostalgia for collective harmony, and Hegel's teleological Geist — the whole 'the world, aware of itself' — most closely mirrors the Borg's galactic quest for an Omega-molecule perfection of 'infinite parts functioning as one.' Yet 'I, Borg' shows Hegelian Spirit working through individuals: Hugh's redemption transforms the Enterprise crew's self-understanding, proving nothing is wholly alien and freedom can coexist with collectivity. Via Haraway's cyborgs and against Kass's 'wisdom of repugnance', the chapter concludes the Borg horrify us because the natural/artificial dualism is already obsolete in our technologized lives — 'if we are the Borg, then resistance truly is futile.'
- ch. 20 "“Its Continuing Mission”" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, René Descartes, John Locke — Struggle for Recognition; Master–Slave Dialectic; Democracy — Argues that Star Trek's real subject is Hegelian recognition: a society is worth living in when every member's claims count as reasons and their talents get developed. It reads 'The Measure of a Man' (Data winning legal personhood), 'The Outcast' (Riker defending the J'naii Soren), and DS9's 'Past Tense' Bell Riots as dramas of winning recognition, and maps the Romulan-Reman and Stratos-Troglyte hierarchies onto Hegel's master-slave dialectic, contrasting Descartes's solipsistic cogito with Hegel's claim that self-awareness needs another. Since recognition requires more than non-interference against Locke-style atomism, the Federation's appeal lies in positive liberties — education, open debate, guaranteed basic needs — even though the shows oddly skip elections and democratic politics, a tension the authors flag through Leonard Nimoy's praise of a world with 'no political agenda.'
- ch. 21 "Death on Veridian III" **·** David Hume, Gottfried Leibniz, Aristotle — The Problem of Evil; The Best of All Possible Worlds; The Meaning of Life — Uses the holodeck to re-run the problem of evil: if a safe, painless simulated world like Barclay's fantasy life in 'Hollow Pursuits' is available, why is the painful real one better? Against Hume's Dialogues complaint that a benevolent God should have cut the pain, and Leibniz's best-of-all-possible-worlds optimism, the authors stack Whitehead's 'major beauty' of intensity, Aristotle's tragic magnitude, Swinburne's good of serious responsibility, and Hick's soul-making, reading Moriarty's imprisonment in 'Ship in a Bottle,' Q's humbling in 'Déjà Q,' and Kirk leaving the Nexus because 'nothing here matters' as evidence that intensity, responsibility, and character growth exist only in the real world. Kirk's death on Veridian III in Generations supplies the cautionary counterweight: the real world's goods cost real suffering.
- ch. 22 "“Something to Believe In”" **·** William James, Charles Sanders Peirce — The Will to Believe; Truth as What Works; The Pragmatic Method; The Leap of Faith — Reads Worf's crisis over the clone 'second coming' of Kahless in 'Rightful Heir' as a live, forced, and momentous option in William James's sense, where 'faith creates its own verification.' Peirce's methods of fixing belief — tenacity, authority, and science — explain why Worf cannot accept Koroth's pious fraud once Gowron's DNA test exposes the clone, while Data's own 'leap of faith' in believing he is more than a machine supplies the Jamesian model of believing without evidence. Worf's compromise — telling the Klingon people the truth but installing Kahless-the-clone as spiritual emperor because 'the words are more important than the man' — is offered as pragmatist truth: what works while staying answerable to hard facts.
- ch. 23 "“He’s a Cardassian! That’s Reason Enough”" **·** Jean-François Lyotard — Applies Lyotard's differend and agonistics to the Bajor-Cardassia-Federation triangle around DS9, arguing that 'Duet' dramatizes a dispute where the occupation's horrors are unpresentable in any ruling idiom, so labels like 'Cardassian monsters' and 'Bajoran freedom fighters' frame reality to suit the framer. It follows Aamin Marritza's impersonation of Gul Darhe'el — a guilt-wracked file clerk who wants Bajor's trial to force Cardassia to confess — through Kira's shift from vengeance to forgiveness, and his murder by a Bajoran ('He's a Cardassian! That's reason enough') as proof of totalizing injustice. Federation universalism (Sisko's 'In the Pale Moonlight' compromises, Azetbur's 'Homo sapiens only club' jab, Eddington's 'you assimilate people' speech) appears as one more totalizing standard, with DS9's transgressive characters like Garak pointing past the impasse.
- ch. 24 "Starfleet Directive FOUR - Multiple Enterprises Metaphysical Conundrums from" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "Tomorrow Is Yesterday" **·** J.M.E. McTaggart, Augustine of Hippo, Gottfried Leibniz — The A-Series and B-Series of Time; Augustine on Time; The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Fate and Foreknowledge — Uses the Bajoran Prophets, who experience no linear time ('What is this... time?'), to frame a tour of time's metaphysics: Newton's absolute container versus Leibniz's relationism (the incoherence of a 'temporal vacuum'), Augustine's mind-dependent time (illustrated by 'The Inner Light' and O'Brien's implanted prison years in 'Hard Time'), and McTaggart's argument that neither the A-series nor the B-series can account for change, illustrated by Tasha Yar's death in 'Skin of Evil' and Kirk's Liar-paradox victories over Nomad and Norman. The chapter defends the A-series via tense, then weighs presentism — which would make 'Tomorrow Is Yesterday' and 'Trials and Tribble-ations' impossible — against eternalism, whose fatalism Data embraces when his severed head turns up in 'Time's Arrow' ('It has occurred. It will occur.'), and which finally makes sense of prophets who see the future in 'Destiny.'
- ch. 26 "“I Feel Exactly What You Feel”" **·** John Locke, Derek Parfit — Personal Identity (memory theory); Teleporter Paradox (personal fission); Personal Identity — Runs Star Trek's transporter and android stories as thought experiments on personal identity: the body theory (Kirk rejecting android Korby — 'Dr. Korby was never here' — and Picard telling the resurrected Rishon Uxbridge 'you do not exist'), the brain theory ('Spock's Brain,' Bashir refusing to replace half of Vedek Bareil's brain), and Locke's memory theory as vindicated by the Trill (Lela Dax's 'a person is but the sum of their memories,' the 'Dax' extradition hearing over Curzon's crimes). Riker's transporter double in 'Second Chances' and the Tuvix fusion then break the memory theory through fission and fusion, prompting Parfit's move that psychological continuity, not numerical identity, is what matters in survival. Memory erasure in 'Dagger of the Mind' and Kurn's rebranding after the failed Mauk-to'Vor in 'Sons of Mogh' count as death if we are our memories.
- ch. 27 "Emergentism Now Can Scotty Beam Us Up" **·** René Descartes, John Searle, Thomas Nagel, William of Ockham — Mind–Body Dualism; What Is It Like to Be a Bat?; Biological Naturalism / Intentionality; Ockham's Razor — Tests three theories of mind against Spock's katra transfer in The Wrath of Khan and The Search for Spock and his mind melds with Kirk, the Horta, and Rock people. Descartes's divisibility argument backs the dualism the katra assumes, but the argument from parsimony (Ockham's razor), the problem of mental causation, and the conservation of energy weigh against it; Churchland's eliminative materialism plays by science's rules but runs into Nagel's 'what it is like' objection, dramatized by Geordi failing to describe anger to Data without circularity. The author lands, cautiously, on Searle-style emergentism — mind as an emergent, irreducible feature of neural complexity, as when Nomad and V'Ger exceed their programming — while conceding Kim's charge that it may be dualism in disguise.
- ch. 28 "“Logic Is the Beginning of Wisdom . . . Not the End”" **·** John Searle, Hilary Putnam — Biological Naturalism / Intentionality — Treats Kirk's computer-killing arguments as logic lessons: his valid syllogism forces Nomad to sterilize itself in 'The Changeling,' while the M-5's trial in 'The Ultimate Computer' models inductive hypothesis testing. The Liar paradox ('Everything Harry tells you is a lie' / 'I am lying') crashes Norman in 'I, Mudd' and, via Tarski's T-sentences and the explosion problem, reveals the concept of truth as inconsistent, with three-valued logic offered as a fix that only relocates the paradox. Gödel's incompleteness theorem then grounds the Lucas-Penrose claim that minds outstrip computer programs like Landru — which Putnam's consistency objection rebuts — leaving Searle's point that computers manipulate symbols without understanding them as the residue of Surak's Vulcan logic being the beginning of wisdom, not the end.
