Duty Calls" **·** John Stuart Mill, Jeremy Bentham — Utilitarianism; The Greatest Happiness Principle — Explains Mill-style utilitarianism — rightness fixed entirely by consequences for overall pleasure and pain, counting every sentient being (a cat may enjoy tuna but not Watchmen) — and applies it: Clark Kent must rescue the failing plane over the Daily Planet press conference, and you must give the jeans money to charity. Since adopting a role is obligated whenever it produces the most overall good, anyone with superpowers has a duty to become a superhero, so Peter Parker's misery in Spider-Man 2 is morally beside the point: utilitarianism says he must remain Spider-Man.
- ch. 92 "Aw, C’mon! Do I Have to Save the Day" **·** Utilitarianism; Consequentialism — Presses four objections to utilitarianism through superhero cases: a weakened Jean Grey dying to save Juggernaut's bus victims shows utilitarianism obliterates supererogation — she would be blameworthy whichever way she chose; Ares' demand that Wonder Woman kill an innocent girl to avert global biowar forces her against her character; Batman refusing to let an innocent-of-this-crime Joker die in The Joker: Devil's Advocate shows the theory sacrificing justice; and the Green Goblin accidentally doing great good by dragging a would-be mass shooter down Fifth Avenue shows consequences alone cannot make an intended wrong right.
- ch. 93 "I’m a Lover, Not a Fighter!" **·** Immanuel Kant — Humanity as an End in Itself; The Categorical Imperative; Deontology — Turns to Kantian nonconsequentialism: persons must be treated as ends in themselves and never merely as means, from duty rather than consequences, with negative duties (not harming) stronger than positive duties (aiding) — so Reed Richards may not kill a pedestrian for organs to heal Doctor Doom's victims, though a utilitarian would require it. Since neither becoming Spider-Man nor refusing to violates any negative duty, being a superhero is supererogatory: 'with great power comes great responsibility' is at most a duty not to misuse power, and precisely because heroes don't have to do what they do — as Clark Kent's Superman II choice shows — their choosing it is what makes them praiseworthy.
- ch. 94 "I Fought the Law and the Law Won" **·** Socrates, Immanuel Kant — Deontology; Utilitarianism — Argues that Batman's warrantless raids, intimidation and evidence-free arrests violate negative duties that bind everyone regardless of role, so producing good (the utilitarian reply) cannot justify them, and superpowers earn no legal exemptions that we would deny police. When Spider-Man evades NYPD warrants, the chapter applies Socrates' argument in Plato's Crito that citizens owe the law their obedience even when wrongly accused, though it concedes that keeping a secret identity safe from villains who would torture or kill loved ones can override the duty to submit, a move consistent with non-Kantian nonconsequentialism since Kant could not abide any lie.
- ch. 95 "But It’s Just a White Lie!" **·** Immanuel Kant — Deontology; Respect for Persons — Asks whether superheroes may deceive the people they love, testing Kant's absolute duty not to lie against resolvable conflicts of negative duties: Peter may deceive Aunt May only because telling her would seriously harm her. But the chapter rejects the paternalistic silence Clark keeps from Lois and Peter from MJ, arguing that assuming the women cannot keep secrets or would crumble under worry fails to treat them with the respect owed to persons, so superheroes owe their loved ones the truth about who they are.
- ch. 96 "Chapter 15 - Why Be a Superhero Why Be Moral" *(front)*
- ch. 97 "The Problem for Spider-Man" **·** Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Ethical Egoism — Sets up the chapter's question through the Spider-Man film: after the promoter cheats him, Peter lets the armed robber go with the taunt "I missed the part where that's my problem," and the robber's escape gets Uncle Ben killed. The scene turns Uncle Ben's "with great power comes great responsibility" into the classic question "Why be moral?" — why not use superpowers for "great personal satisfaction," an egoist's super life, when no payoff for virtue is guaranteed.
- ch. 98 "Phony Answers" *(no index entry yet)* — Interrogates the tendency to assume the strongest or overriding reasons always favor doing one's moral duty, imagining an all-powerful malevolent deity who eternally torments the virtuous and rewards the wicked to show that moral reasons could fail to be overriding. Whether morality is rational on this score is left as the live question the Spider-Man narrative will be used to answer.
- ch. 99 "Reasons to Be Moral" **·** Plato, Immanuel Kant, Aristotle — Tripartite Soul; Virtue Ethics (arete); The Categorical Imperative; Ring of Gyges (why be moral?) — Extracts two candidate answers from Spider-Man — Reason One, that immorality rebounds on you (Uncle Ben's death), tested and weakened by the Ms. Poore poverty-theft case, and Spider-Man's agonized "Because it is right" to the Green Goblin, the Kant-and-Bradley motive of duty — and finds both insufficient to show morality is rational. It then tests Plato's answer that only the moral have harmony of soul (reason governing appetite and spirit) against Flash Thompson and self-forgiving sinners, and Aristotle's "virtue is its own reward" against the thought experiment of virtuous Arachnid-Girl rotting in prison while the fraudulent Norm Osborne flourishes.
- ch. 100 "In It for the Long Run" **·** Immortality and the Soul; Karma and Rebirth — Adds Reason Five — being moral always pays in the long run, where the long run includes life after death — arguing that a perfectly good and all-powerful God would not set up a moral order that penalizes virtue, so Peter Parker's virtue is guaranteed its reward beyond this life. It notes that Eastern reincarnation-plus-karma makes the same promise (the more virtuous this life, the better the next), and that since Peter, Uncle Ben and Aunt May would never water morality down, the morally serious are pushed toward these metaphysical guarantees.
- ch. 101 "Superheroes, Duty, and the Biggest of Big Pictures" **·** The Watchmaker Argument (design); Karma and Rebirth — Argues that non-theistic karma undermines itself: the impersonal moral laws connecting each soul's deeds to its circumstances in the next life would be enormously complex and would serve the moral end of justice, and order that intricate serving a moral end demands an intelligent cause, so reincarnation becomes evidence for God. It closes the chapter by comparing the universe's moral order to a superhero's origin story — it would have to begin with something like a God.
- ch. 102 "Swinging from One Idea to Another" *(interlude)*
- ch. 103 "Chapter 16 - Superman and Kingdom Come The Surprise of Philosophical Theology" **·** Immortality and the Soul — Opens the philosophical-theology chapter by mapping Superman onto Christ: Kal-El sent by his father Jor-El from dying Krypton in a rocket parallels Jesus sent by the Father to Bethlehem, both alien saviors raised as small-town boys. It announces eschatology — final things, ultimate outcomes, whether the hope for justice is an empty utopian dream — as the lens through which the graphic novel Kingdom Come will be read.
- ch. 104 "The Background of Kingdom Come" *(no index entry yet)* — Explains the Kingdom Come title from the Lord's Prayer and the book's Revelation allusions, then recounts its premise: the retired heroes idle while vicious new "heroes" who "no longer fight for the right" run rampant and Batman rules Gotham by fear. Via Maggin's line "The superhero is Everyman," it turns Superman's despair in the Fortress of Solitude into the reader's own predicament when facing pervasive injustice.
- ch. 105 "Hope, Obligation, and the Big Picture" **·** Bertrand Russell — The Meaning of Life; Immortality and the Soul — Argues whether Wonder Woman's "must" really binds Superman — whether he is obliged to leave the Fortress and fight again — depends on one's eschatology or big-picture worldview. It contrasts Christian theism's purposeful culmination with naturalism, whose outlook is fixed by Bertrand Russell's "unyielding despair" passage: accidental collocations of atoms, no preservation beyond the grave, and all human achievement buried beneath the debris of a ruined universe, heroism included.
- ch. 106 "Gloom, Doom, and Morality" **·** Immanuel Kant, Bertrand Russell — Immortality and the Soul; Faith and Reason — Works out naturalism's moral cost: no purpose behind our existence, no blueprint for life, Russell's hope that sensitive souls can love the tragic beauty of it anyway, and the Wilson-Ruse claim that ethics is "an illusion fobbed off on us by our genes," which loses its grip once seen through — like Macbeth's dagger. Against this it sets Kant's moral faith: morality makes rational sense only if we postulate God and immortality so virtue is finally rewarded, and the chapter concludes naturalism offers no deep basis for the life-risking duties a hero like Superman faces.
- ch. 107 "Worldviews, Values, and Superheroes" **·** Socrates, Friedrich Nietzsche — Moral Relativism — Argues that in a naturalist universe of particles and force fields nothing grounds objective good and evil, so a defiant Superman who fights evil just because he wants to prizes sympathy while downplaying truth. Wonder Woman's challenge — "Truth and justice" — raises whether they are in league: Socrates and the classic tradition held truth, beauty and goodness are one, while Nietzsche, godfather of postmodernism, snarls that "Truth is ugly," leaving naturalism a dilemma between believing in ultimate justice or accepting that it is an illusion.
- ch. 108 "A Theological Basis for Super-Heroics" **·** Immortality and the Soul; Faith and Reason — Proposes that Christian theism's doctrines of heaven, hell and Christ's return resolve the truth/justice tension by grounding moral obligation in God's perfectly moral nature and guaranteeing that justice prevails. It rebuts Maggin's claim that faith in a power greater than ours breeds inaction: God works through human co-creators, so Superman still has a duty to do what he can, and the objective hope of ultimate justice is exactly the corrective that despairing Superman and tyrannical, fear-ruling Batman in Kingdom Come both lack.
- ch. 109 "Hope and the Human Challenge" **·** Faith and Reason; Immortality and the Soul — Reads Superman's return — "Up in the sky!", the crowd hailing "the second coming of Superman" at the UN — as the enacted theology of Kingdom Come: hope in a greater power revives a world "hungry for hope" and draws the other heroes back to the fray. The Spectre's charge to the preacher Norman McCay, "you exist to give hope," voices the chapter's conclusion that a supernatural eschatology holds hope, truth, and individual responsibility together in a way naturalism's unyielding despair cannot.
- ch. 110 "Part Four - Identity and Superhero Metaphysics" *(front)*
- ch. 111 "Chapter 17 - Questions of Identity Is the Hulk the Same Person as Bruce Banner" **·** Personal Identity — Frames the chapter with a San Francisco criminal trial in which Bruce Banner's lawyer argues the Hulk — a large green figure — literally was not the same individual who now stands small and pale before the judge. Ruling requires criteria for "continuity of personal identity over time": what makes you the same person today as ten years ago, applied here to whether Banner should answer for the Hulk's rampage.
- ch. 112 "The Hulk’s Bodily Identity" **·** Personal Identity; Ship of Theseus — Tests the everyday bodily criterion of identity: the Hulk's body contains far more atoms than Banner's, but since all our cells turnover anyway — the "Stan Lee Schooner" has every part replaced yet stays the same boat, the Ship of Theseus problem — and the organ-donor case of "Herb Trimpe" shows a body with greater physical continuity to Kinghorn than to its owner, bodily continuity cannot be what personal identity consists in.
- ch. 113 "The Mental Realm of the Hulk" **·** John Locke, Thomas Reid — Personal Identity (memory theory); Personal Identity — Applies Locke's memory theory: the shape-shifting Martian Manhunter and the irradiated Fantastic Four stay the same people through mental continuity, and the early comics' Banner-minded Hulk meets Locke's criterion — but the later "Hulk smash!" Hulk, who recognizes Betty Ross yet lacks Banner's memories, fails it. The chapter then breaks the criterion itself with Reid's brave-officer objection (the general both is and is not the flogged boy), Alzheimer's and Doc Ock's amnesia attack on Spider-Man, and the circularity of distinguishing genuine from false memory (the deluded fan who "remembers" starring in Adventures of Superman).
- ch. 114 "A Causal Account of the Hulk’s Identity" **·** Personal Identity; Teleporter Paradox (personal fission) — Proposes that the Hulk is Banner because Banner "Hulks out" — the monster state develops causally from Banner's body and mind through radiation, danger and anger, rather than one person being swapped for another. But a mad scientist's cloning accident that splits Banner into two simultaneous rampaging Hulks breaks the account, since both would be causally derived from Bruce yet could not both be the one person — the fission-style counterexample that afflicts every theory so far.
- ch. 115 "Is There No Way to Tell" **·** Derek Parfit — Teleporter Paradox (personal fission); Personal Identity — Presents Derek Parfit's challenge to the whole enterprise: just as there need be no answer to whether a repaired machine is "the same" machine, Parfit's divided-brain case — each half housed in a new body — suggests a person can "survive as two different people without implying that I am these people," so identity questions may lack answers. Kinghorn resists the leap: difficulty finding the truth does not show there is none.
- ch. 116 "The Hulk’s Relational Identity" **·** Personal Identity — Defends a relational account: a person's identity persists through continuing relationships with others (like a marriage or a corporation), against our post-Enlightenment fixation on private attributes. Objections — severed relationships, the castaway, others' biased projections — are answered by positing a God who relates to every person without distortion and guarantees each identity, and who, since divine power cannot do the logically impossible, could not make Banner identical with two numerically distinct Hulks at once.
- ch. 117 "What Should We Conclude" **·** Personal Identity — Renders the verdict in the Banner trial: Bruce is the Hulk, because their relationships continue — when David Banner phones to say Betty Ross will be eliminated, Bruce forms the protective intention the Hulk then executes by destroying the three mutant poodles, and Betty, David and General Ross all relate to the Hulk as Bruce. Physical, mental and causal indicators are mere cues to the deeper continuity of relationships that constitutes who someone is.
- ch. 118 "Chapter 18 - Identity Crisis Time Travel and Metaphysics in the DC Multiverse" *(no index entry yet)* — Opens with Sherlock Holmes continuity errors — Watson's war wound migrating from shoulder to leg — and Conan Doyle's forced resurrection of Holmes, defining "corrections": later installments that change what is true of earlier ones. Unlike the finished Holmes serial, comics permit genuine correction across different authors, which is the machinery behind the retcons Crisis on Infinite Earths performs.
- ch. 119 "The DC Comics Multiverse" **·** Possible Worlds — Recounts how DC resolved its Silver Age continuity mess: rather than treat Jay Garrick's adventures as a fiction-within-a-fiction, Flash #123 has Barry Allen cross into Earth-2 and meet Garrick — and one cannot meet a merely fictional character — so the multiverse is born. As alternative histories multiplied and heroes routinely world-hopped, the only correction strategy left was postulating yet another world, setting up 1985's Crisis.
- ch. 120 "Crisis on Infinite Earths The Story Unfolds" **·** The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Possible Worlds — Summarizes Crisis: Krona's forbidden experiment splits one universe into a multiverse plus an antimatter universe whose Anti-Monitor devours worlds; the Monitor self-sacrifices to pocket five Earths; heroes and villains travel to the dawn of time, where the Spectre's intervention leaves a single positive-matter universe. The aftermath — Superman of Earth-2 mourning a Lois who "never existed," three Supermen on one Earth — sets up the two metaphysical conjectures, time travel and multiverse, to be examined.
- ch. 121 "Time Travel and Wishful Thinking" **·** The Metaphysics of Time Travel — Distinguishes changing the past from affecting it: a fan killing Marv Wolfman in 1984 contradicts what happened, while Superboy #85's failed rescue of Lincoln — Superboy immobilized by time-traveling Lex Luthor's red Kryptonite, so Booth shoots on schedule — is coherent because Luthor only "helped make history." Crisis instead rewrites cosmic history wholesale, and Hanley notes the irony that time-travel theorists usually save coherence precisely by postulating multiple timelines: travelers don't change the world, they change worlds.
- ch. 122 "More Things in Heaven and Earth" **·** David Lewis — Possible Worlds — Surveys real multiverse arguments: the Everett-Wheeler many-worlds reading of quantum mechanics, fine-tuning explained by every possible initial condition existing somewhere rather than by God, and David Lewis's modal realism, on which every way the world could have been is a causally isolated world — it was possible to write a shorter chapter because in some world Hanley did. Tegmark's physics multiverses round out the menu before the question: does any of this fit Crisis?
- ch. 123 "A Multiversity" **·** David Lewis — Possible Worlds; The Metaphysics of Time Travel — Rules out Lewis's modal realism for the DC multiverse (DC worlds interact; Lewis's are causally isolated) and standard branching many-worlds too, then proposes "hypertime," a second time dimension that makes sense of a traveler arriving in another timeline's "1984." Since Crisis speaks of the multiverse becoming one "at the dawn of time" — something that cannot happen in plain time or hypertime — Hanley posits a six-dimensional cosmos with "supertime" and superhistories.
- ch. 124 "Does Anything Change, or Not" **·** The Metaphysics of Time Travel — Argues the superhistory picture still under-delivers: Joe only exchanges histories rather than making Crisis never exist, and the Anti-Monitor may well live on in the not-quite-native hyperhistory. What Crisis's writers really envisaged — Wonder Woman de-aging out of existence to be reborn with a different life — is "dynamic change," making it so no history contains the event, and that, Hanley says, is incoherent.
- ch. 125 "Identity in Crisis" **·** Personal Identity; Possible Worlds — Poses the persistence problem through Superman-1 and Superman-2: are they strictly identical? Perdurantism — persons as four-dimensional space-time worms made of temporal parts — makes them distinct worms with no parts in common, so Superman meeting his counterpart is no stranger than you meeting a friend; endurantism, with wholly present strict identity, could identify them across timelines but balks at the impossibility of Superman meeting himself.
- ch. 126 "Endurantist Past-Changing" **·** The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Personal Identity — Chases the endurantist bullet: if one thing can differ across timelines, one and the same timeline can exist differently in different hyperhistories, letting Joe's murder of Wolfman make 1984 "not the way he remembers it." Yet even this yields only switching, not the dynamic change Crisis dramatizes, so the six-dimensional cosmos stands; Hanley closes with Wolfman's own secret plot device for bringing back the killed Barry Allen Flash.
- ch. 127 "Chapter 19 - What’s Behind the Mask The Secret of Secret Identities" *(no index entry yet)* — Opens with the Lone Ranger, Zorro and the Princess Bride's masked heroes to ask why superheroes wear masks at all — Tom Morris noting the little raccoon masks fool no one at the office. The puzzle of what the point of disguise could be for heroes doing only admired, nonlethal good deeds sets up the more generic phenomenon of dual identity to be analyzed.
- ch. 128 "Dual Identities" **·** Personal Identity — Lists the classic hero/normal identity pairs (Batman/Bruce Wayne, Spider-Man/Peter Parker, plus Woody Allen's joke alias) and separates costume as role-transition — the Fantastic Four's public uniforms, doctors' scrubs, Bob's garage shirt — from costume as tool, Batman's fear-theater aimed at "a superstitious and cowardly lot" and the female heroes' calculated "gawk factor." What most superheroes do is the distinct third thing, masking: personas from the Latin for mask, keeping Peter's Spider-Man and Matt Murdock's Daredevil secret in both directions.
- ch. 129 "Keeping Secrets" **·** Deontology — Takes up the objection that secret identities require the deception superheroes condemn, and answers that skillful deception within a legitimate context — quarterback fakes, a painter's perspective tricks — is acceptable, while even a lie bad in itself can be morally right or obligatory when needed to prevent great harm to the innocent. So Spider-Man's secrecy about being Peter Parker is justified, even praiseworthy, because a slipped secret would hand his enemies leverage over Aunt May and his friends.
- ch. 130 "Superman’s Interesting Motivation" **·** Blaise Pascal — The Meaning of Life — Argues Superman inverts the usual identity rule: Kal-El's powers precede any civilian persona, so Superman is the real identity and Clark Kent the ruse. Drawing on Pascal's point that celebrity otherness is a function of imagination — a movie star at your cafeteria table changes everything — and on Krishna's disguise as Arjuna's chariot driver in the Bhagavad-Gita and Christ's messianic secret, Morris reads Clark Kent not as operational cover but as Superman's quest to live the human condition from within, loved into humanity by the Kents and refusing to be an isolated "Aristotelian God."
- ch. 131 "Switching Identities" **·** Aristotle, Plato, William James, Blaise Pascal — Virtue Ethics (arete); Authenticity; Theory of Forms — Maps Superman and Batman onto Plato and Aristotle — the otherworldly philosopher of the heavenly Good versus the this-worldly master of logic and applicable science — then argues that Bruce Wayne's years of intentional self-transformation may have swapped the mask, making Batman the core identity and Bruce the disguise. With Mark Waid, he sees Superman inwardly embracing his alien otherness as the path of authenticity, both cases yielding a fused "heterosis" of identities; Aristotle, Pascal and William James back the closing lesson that who we are is a matter of what we repeatedly do, so every mask may eventually become the face.

## Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "i" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "ii" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "It’s About Damn Time" *(no index entry yet)* — The editor's introduction argues that the fans' endless Batman-vs-Superman fight is never really about who is stronger or richer but about who is the better hero — who we should try to be like, raise our children to resemble, and model our future on. Recalling learning sacrifice from Batman and total self-giving from the Death of Superman storyline, it frames the book's debate format as a choice between hopeful faith that humanity will succeed and cynical suspicion that everyone is one lab accident from villainy, and hands the verdict to the reader.
- ch. 8 "Pre-Fight Warm-Up Battle of the Billennium" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "1. Where Have All the Supermen Gone" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Übermensch; The Apollonian and the Dionysian; The Death of God; Will to Power — Holdier tests each hero against Nietzsche: Superman looks like the Übermensch but his mild-mannered Clark Kent pose is slave morality that would turn Nietzsche's stomach, while Batman's will-forged heroism (his Year One vow, 'what does not kill me makes me stronger') seems more overman-like until his self-loathing in Hush ('deep down, I'm not [a good person]') disqualifies him too. Neither qualifies; instead Superman embodies the Apollonian sun-god force of The Birth of Tragedy and Batman the Dionysian, so their Dark Knight Returns clash is the inevitable but never-final friction of art's twin poles — and the readers are the ones who win the fight.
- ch. 10 "Round One Decision—Superman! The Son Shines Bright" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "2. Sure We’re Criminals" **·** Socrates, Plato, Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, David Hume, Robert Nozick — The Social Contract; Civil Disobedience; Anarchism — Alloy uses the problem of political obligation to split the heroes: against Plato's Crito, where Socrates refuses escape because even bad laws bind, Bruce Wayne simply flees arrest in Bruce Wayne: Murderer?/Fugitive, treating law as a tool of his war. He tests consent theory through Superman's chosen handcuffs in Man of Steel and Darkseid's Apokolips as Hobbes's 'mortal god' versus Locke's natural-rights standard, lets Hume's objection sink tacit consent (Red Son Superman cannot really emigrate, and Batman would never leave Gotham), rejects gratitude theory via the Kents' adoption of Kal-El, and dismantles Batman's 'I'm not wearing hockey pads' defense with Nozick's Batman-lottery — concluding Superman's law-conforming restraint protects the public from him becoming Luthor's 'alien overlord', while answerable-to-no-one Batman remains a force of chaos.
- ch. 12 "3. Darwin in Metropolis" **·** Herbert Spencer — Social Darwinism; Existential Risk — Springett applies evolutionary biology to the debate: natural selection, fitness (Batman edges it by one child, Damian Wayne), morphospace reasoning, and biological altruism, which technically Batman satisfies better since invulnerable Superman cannot lower his own fitness. But judged as an effective helper at species scale — Gould's catastrophes, asteroids, alien invasions — Superman protects the fitness of the whole species and planet where Batman guards one city, so a closing three-premise argument crowns Superman the superior Superhero, and his habit of saving the less fit makes him a living counterexample to Social Darwinism.
- ch. 13 "4. A Cape and a Code" **·** Virtue Ethics — Farrell traces the heroes to medieval knighthood and evaluates them by C.S. Lewis's 'The Necessity of Chivalry': both live the double demand of fierceness and meekness (Batman brutalizing the Joker in The Dark Knight yet gifting a boy his surveillance gear; Superman turning back time for Lois yet rescuing a girl's cat), and both must achieve knightly character 'by art, not nature'. The decisive difference is restraint: Superman's Pa Kent lessons and the Smallville 'Red' red-kryptonite episode show the mighty man choosing self-control, making Kal-El the truer chivalric knight, where Lewis's examples (Achilles, triumphant generals) show power without meekness is no heroism.
- ch. 14 "5. How Heroes Argue" **·** Aristotle, Friedrich Nietzsche — Virtue Ethics — LaBauve opens with an imagined Justice League showdown over a Joker hostage where Batman sways the crowd with pathos (fear of failing the innocent) and Superman wins them back through ethos — years of trusted character — to stage the chapter's claim from Aristotle's On Rhetoric. Superman alone balances all three appeals: Batman's pathos is all too human (Nolan's tormented Bruce) and his logos is master-detective method, but pure pathos risks Hitler-style demagoguery and pure logos is inhuman, while Superman's surpassing ethos — reinforced by the Kill Bill Vol. 2 monologue that Clark Kent is the costume — makes him the virtuous exemplar who 'must win'.
- ch. 15 "Round Two Decision—Batman! More Human than a Superman" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "6. The God We Need Now" **·** The Death of God — Ketcham frames a fictional 1939 memoir asking which god a god-forsaken age gets: Depression-era America needed Superman as a messiah (Siegel and Shuster as gospel-writers, DC's clerics redrawing him all-good like the church editing the New Testament), but a jaded modern America, he argues, now worships the dark billionaire as a Hades figure — Wayne Manor's hidden underworld with Alfred as Cerberus, the rich sacrificed to like Greeks propitiating Zeus. Superman is dismissed as unattainable alien fiction while Bruce Wayne is the self-made god of the American dream, with the essay ending on the prospect of a cybergod for his grandchildren.
- ch. 17 "7. How Batman Cowed a God" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Master and Slave Morality; Ressentiment; The Übermensch — Reider reads Batman as Nietzsche's aristocratic 'good' man — pagan wrath and vengeance without shame, his no-kill rule in Under the Red Hood mere pride, like Achilles dragging Hector's body — and Superman as the unwitting pawn of slave morality, his Kent-farm humility, guilt, and protect-the-weak ethos the very values the resentful revolt installed. The provocation: a god whose morality favors the weak may secretly wish to be overcome, so the imagined confrontation where Batman growls 'follow the plan or I'll take you out myself' lets Superman feel happily, honestly human again — which is also why Wonder Woman pursues Batman and Clark pines for the domineering Lois.
- ch. 18 "8. Saints and Superheroes" **·** Peter Singer, Susan Wolf — Utilitarianism; Deontology; The Drowning Child (obligation to aid) — Alloy uses supererogation — Urmson's saints-and-heroes puzzle — to separate the heroes: utilitarianism (via Singer's Famine, Affluence, and Morality, where even Clark's novelty glasses are stolen from charity) and deontology both erase acts that are good but not required, and Susan Wolf's moral saints show where that lands — a Bruce Wayne with no hobbies, friends, or life, like Astro City's Samaritan. Alloy's own Raz-style fix (requirements overridden by moral permitting reasons) yields the verdict: Batman risks his life by choice and so is a true hero, while Superman, facing no real danger, merely does what his powers make morally required — 'a good person with the powers of a living god'.
- ch. 19 "9. Masks, Hearts, and Superheroes" **·** Aristotle, Plato — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Golden Mean; Ring of Gyges (why be moral?) — Dupree and Fuš argue from identity statements: Bruce Wayne is 'just a mask' for Batman, while Clark Kent is in his heart Superman, so only an essentially human character can be a true superhero. On their Aristotelian definition — virtue ethics, the golden mean, flourishing through self-developed excellence — Batman's no-kill rule (sparing even the Joker), his planned avoidance of lethal force in Gotham Knights #31, and his balance against extremes make him the true hero, whereas Superman's given god-powers (killing Zod in Man of Steel, tyrant in Red Son) mirror power rings as Gyges's ring: possession without earned virtue.
- ch. 20 "10. Gods Are Overrated" **·** David Hume, Friedrich Nietzsche — The Problem of Evil; The Death of God; Immortality and the Soul; The Meaning of Life — Michaud runs Hume's problem of evil against a Superman who is nearly all-powerful, all-knowing, and good yet takes dates with Lois while animals and children suffer pointlessly — and unlike God he cannot hide behind mystery, only laziness. God-like protectors breed excuses ('Superman is our great excuse' for doing nothing about homelessness or starving children), and belief in afterlife and divine rescue cheapens this life; following Nietzsche's death of God, the chapter argues we should stop believing in saviors, face the infinite night, make our own meaning, and be more like Batman — self-reliant people who try to save others themselves.
- ch. 21 "Round Three Decision—Superman! The Best Man for Tomorrow" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "11. Of Bats and Supermen" **·** Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Thomas Nagel — Embodiment (the lived body); What Is It Like to Be a Bat?; Social Darwinism — Springett argues Superman, not Batman, is the right goal for a transhumanist future: through Merleau-Ponty's embodied cognition (Lois's deadline nausea, Alfred recovering a thought by redoing his posture, real-life 'Subway Superman' Wesley Autrey's gut-level rescue) he shows bodies shape thought and morality, so a super-body means a super-mind. Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' becomes 'what is it like to be Superman' — a problem of superhero minds, with Doctor Manhattan's indifference as the cautionary case — while Superman's rescues of the less fit show transcendence need not slide into eugenics or Social Darwinism.
- ch. 23 "12. Vigilante Wanted" **·** Forgiveness; The Ethics of Political Violence — Ketcham writes a fictional Dust Bowl kid's 1940 diary: facing bank foreclosure, he weighs which comic to keep as the vigilante who would burn down the bank — Superman, the Kansas farm boy gone Metropolis-insider, or Batman, rich like the bankers yet a fellow avenger who only fights 'carnival freaks'. Testing each against Hamlet's paralysis, Henry V at Agincourt, Tom Joad's 'I'll be ever'where' promise, and a Lex-Luthor pact with the devil, he burns the Batman comics and keeps Superman — realizing he is really giving up his own hate and the preacher's unforgiveness, though even Superman begins to fade 'like dust in that wind'.
- ch. 24 "13. Time to Choose" **·** John Stuart Mill, Immanuel Kant — Consequentialism; Deontology; Moral Luck; Utilitarianism — Goldberg and Gavaler read Superman's first-year Action Comics adventures (reforming the Blakely Mine owner, demolishing slums, buying back swindled stock) as consequentialism on Millian lines, and Batman's Detective Comics year (letting the Joker's victims die while 'the time isn't ripe', the batarang deflected by invisible glass) as a dark, vengeance-based cousin of Kant's duty ethics. Moral luck is the pivot — deontology ignores it, consequentialism is hostage to it — but Superman's powers cancel luck, and in the opening Luthor/Joker two-bomb scenario Superman defuses while Batman chases the villain, so the chapter rules Superman's 'super consequentialism' the superior code.
- ch. 25 "14. Who Watches the Justice League" **·** David Hume, Karl Popper — Consequentialism; Reason Is the Slave of the Passions; Utilitarianism — Judges the two heroes by negative consequentialism (attributed to Hume and Popper): the better hero is the one who best prevents future suffering, including suffering he might cause himself. Superman qualifies because he hands the League—Batman above all—the means to defeat him (as in Injustice) and kills himself with gold kryptonite after executing Mr. Mxyzptlk in 'What Happened to the Man of Tomorrow?', while Hume's reason-is-slave-of-the-passions reading explains the Zod neck-snap in Man of Steel as passion-driven necessity. Batman's countermeasures in 'Tower of Babel' and Justice League: Doom stop every Leaguer except Batman himself ('My failsafe is the Justice League'), an arrogance that loses him this round.
- ch. 26 "15. Infinite Environmental Crisis" **·** Karl Marx — Anthropocentrism; Climate Ethics — A scripted Lois Lane–Batman interview argues that the Batmobile/Batwing upgrade cycle and Wayne Enterprises' multinational production enact Marx's 'metabolic rift' (via John Bellamy Foster): both take from nature and return unprocessable waste faster than the planet can replenish, so protecting Gotham's way of life perpetuates an infinite environmental crisis of consumption. Solar-powered Superman wins the environmental showdown on lifestyle impact, but Batman counters that Krypton's ecological suicide makes Superman an 'environmental refugee,' not a model. The chapter's real verdict is Bruce's line 'We are all Bruce Wayne': human consumers must rebalance the human–nature relationship before finite resources like fresh water run out.
- ch. 27 "16. You Made Me First" **·** William James, Arthur Schopenhauer — Free Will vs Determinism; The Will to Believe — Starting from the Joker's 'You made me' / Batman's 'You made me first' exchange in Tim Burton's Batman, the chapter argues origin stories fix character: Bruce's witnessed trauma destines him to darkness (and we expect his death to match), while Kal-El is sent to Earth as an act of hope that the chapter reads through William James's will-to-believe—belief itself makes success possible, like Bruce's ropeless leap in The Dark Knight Rises. Against 'I can do whatever I want' free will it deploys Schopenhauer's 'we can do what we will, but we cannot will what we will': Bruce cannot will away his vengeance, and Red Son's Soviet-raised Superman shows biology and upbringing determining who Clark becomes. Superman still wins because his origin story permits the hope that Bruce's cannot.
- ch. 28 "Round Four Decision—Batman! It’s Always Darkest Before the Knight" *(front)*
- ch. 29 "17. Batman’s Mask in Aristotle’s Drama" **·** Aristotle, Plato — Authenticity — Reads Batman's defining difference—the mask—through Aristotle's Poetics: Batman is mimesis, a theatrical performance (the prosopon) engineered to produce pity, fear, and suspense, while unmasked, transparent Superman is the more Platonic figure who wants the Mirror of Truth in All-Star Superman to confirm Clark Kent is his real self. Batman's acting literally beats Superman in The Dark Knight Returns, where the fight is won by a staged death from a fake-heart pill, and his 'Feat of Clay' interrogation shows him performing cruelty to weaponize criminals' imaginations. Because the role is imitable—Robin, Batman Incorporated, the Sons of Batman—'Batman is an idea' anyone can become, whereas Eco's 'Myth of Superman' explains why the unimitatable alien preserves rather than changes his world.
- ch. 30 "18. Superman the Super Dick" **·** Harry Frankfurt, Peter Singer — The Drowning Child (obligation to aid); On Bullshit — Borrowing Harry Frankfurt's move of philosophically defining a colloquial term (as Frankfurt did for 'bullshit'), it defines a 'dick' as someone who willfully disregards others' needs and argues Superman is one: the vending-machine thought experiment shows he could rescue a sinking school bus in less time than it takes Clark to buy a chocolate bar, so saving people at little or no cost to himself is obligatory, not supererogatory. Peter Singer's famine-and-affluence argument extends the same obligation to the affluent reader, while the SuperBat arc of Superman/Batman #53–56—in which Batman temporarily gains Superman's powers and empties every city's jails in one night—proves Superman could do vastly more than he does. Batman, who risks his mortal life and seeks out strangers to save, is 'not a dick' and wins the round.
- ch. 31 "19. Overpower versus Empowerment" *(no index entry yet)* — A game designer explains why roughly a hundred Batman games include acclaimed ones while no good Superman game exists: flow (Csikszentmihaly's balance of challenge and skill) is impossible with a hero who is either omnipotent or wholesale nullified by kryptonite, whereas Batman's trainable skills and acquirable, losable equipment—like Samus Aran's suit in Metroid—give designers levers for escalation, and the player can even supply the detective's brain. Superman's 'heart,' the willpower that unleashes his full might (as in Saint Seiya's unadaptable Cosmo), cannot be tested through a controller. Playing journalist Clark Kent's investigations and no-win dilemmas is sketched as the one route to a decent Superman game.
- ch. 32 "20. What It Takes" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau — The Problem of Evil — Argues Batman is more heroic than Superman because heroism requires supererogation and replicability: Wesley Autrey's subway rescue, done without obligation, outranks Sullenberger's 'just what we're trained for,' and unlike otherworldly Superman, Batman's human abilities let the rest of us imagine imitating him—heroism begets heroism, as Gordon's coat around young Bruce's shoulders helped make Batman. Batman is framed as the answer to the problem of evil in Susan Neiman's secular form: Rachel Dawes' challenge that good people do something, on the Rousseau side of the Enlightenment debate that morality must make evil intelligible (against Voltaire's refusal). Superman's overwhelming power makes relying on reason superfluous, so he becomes a symbol of what we can't be, while the Dark Knight models what we can.
- ch. 33 "21. Batman Is Superman" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Übermensch; The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Eternal Recurrence; The Death of God — Argues that Christian Bale's Batman, not the alien Superman, embodies Nietzsche's Übermensch: a mortal, flawed, lonely hero whose identity is forged in the unreconciled struggle between Dionysian vengeance and Apollonian reason across Nolan's trilogy. Batman Begins enacts eternal recurrence as Bruce repeatedly relives and integrates the well, the opera, and his parents' murder; The Dark Knight's Joker is Batman's Janus-faced shadow whose ferry experiment nearly proves the herd's 'gravity of madness,' and Dent's fall shows what Batman resists becoming. Superman II's temporarily mortal Superman is beaten by a truck driver and retreats to invincibility, proving the immortal alien can never overreach mortal limits as the Übermensch must.
- ch. 34 "Post-Fight Analysis Superhero Truthers Speak Out!" *(front)*
- ch. 35 "22. Unmasking the World and Its Heroes" **·** Plato, Socrates — Allegory of the Cave; Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know); Existence Precedes Essence — Claims the Superman-vs-Batman debate misses the point: both heroes are cave-escapers who must first see beyond appearances—Bruce renouncing vengeance on Joe Chill and then shaking Gotham from apathy (the ferries refusing the Joker's detonators), Clark learning from Jonathan and Jor-El that his powers are not for touchdowns but to lead humanity out by example. Masks serve the Socratic warning of the Apology that the just man must act privately to survive—Jonathan Kent dies keeping Clark's secret—yet risk becoming their own trap, from Smallville's Red Kryptonite ring to Batman's sonar surveillance that Lucius Fox calls too much power for one person. The chapter closes on Socratic ignorance and Man of Steel's genesis chambers: a hero, like Socrates, knows his wisdom is worth nothing, and anyone who chooses can be one.
- ch. 36 "23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep" **·** The Buddha, David Hume, Mahatma Gandhi — The Four Noble Truths; Impermanence (anicca); Non-Self (anatman); Karma and Rebirth — A Fight Club-style Arkham case study: a patient's hallucinated Superman companion is diagnosed by a Buddhist psychiatrist who explains the three marks of existence—impermanence, non-self, and dissatisfaction—arguing superheroes impose order and a fabricated second self on a world that resists both, so Superman's super-intellect and even flight are distractions (levitation should be ignored; the Buddha-eye beats x-ray vision) while Batman's violence and psychosis, compared to American Psycho's Patrick Bateman, make awakening impossible—both are victims of Mara. A robber literally named David Hume objects that the heroes' law and order is grounded on what ought to be rather than what is, and a Gandhi quote on preferring one's own bad government explains why Batman finally kryptonites his alien 'friend.' The verdict inverts the book's debate: conquering the deceiver within is the only superpower worth having.
- ch. 37 "24. The Fifty-Third Card" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Written in the Joker's voice, it plays the fifty-third card no other contributor considered: maybe both 'heroes' are the villains—Superman's public saves are attention-seeking ego when he could help unseen, and Batman selfishly pours billions into Bat-toys instead of donating it to save millions of dying children. Its deeper target is our hypocrisy: the Dark Knight ferry scene is unbelievable because in reality we would climb over each other to push the button, since we are only as moral as our circumstances allow while buying sweatshop chocolate and bacon and calling ourselves good. The genuine 'super-man' would drop the pretense of morality altogether, live by his own lights before dancing with the devil, and laugh as the world burns.

## Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits

- ch. 1 "Globalization and Contemporary Art" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 6 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Written in the voice of the GhostFacers mourning their slain intern Alan Corbett, the introduction presents the volume as their covert infiltration of 'the industry of philosophy.' It reports that philosophy derives from the Greek philosophia, 'loving wisdom,' and jokes that the philosophers it recruited all 'readily admitted that they knew nothing' yet kept pursuing it, with a running gag about whether knowledge itself might be a tulpa. It frames the following essays as the GhostFacers' manifesto of truth about what exists in the Supernatural universe, ghosts and demons included and the Winchester 'Wine-chesters' excluded.
- ch. 7 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Nathan Stout uses P.F. Strawson's account of moral responsibility through 'reactive attitudes' to ask when Sam and Dean are justified in killing what they hunt. Monsters sort into three groups: low-functioning animal killers like the wendigo and 'Heart''s werewolf Madison, intelligent but conscienceless 'antisocial' monsters like demons and leviathans, and 'moral monsters' like the cow-blood-drinking vampires of 'Bloodlust' and the kitsune Amy from 'The Girl Next Door,' who can understand and be motivated by moral reasons. Because Group 3 monsters are members of the moral community, Dean's 'if it's supernatural, we kill it' bigotry and his secret killing of Amy make the supposedly good hunters morally suspect, since killing a fellow member of the moral community ought to weigh on them.
- ch. 9 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Potentiality and Actuality; Speciesism — Foresman and Tobienne deploy Aristotle's apparatus of essence and accident, the ten categories, and actuality versus potentiality to define the monster and explain the show's appeal. They test candidates against canon: whether hunting is essential or accidental to Sam after Azazel's kills, what John Winchester in 'Dead Man's Blood' treats as essential to vampire substance, and Madison's transformation in 'Heart' from actual human and potential werewolf into actual monster, concluding that monstrosity lies in thought and action rather than appearance, as the human-hunting but human Benders confirm. Tracing 'monster' to the Latin monstrum, a sign or omen, they argue monsters are monsters only through their relation to human self-importance, so our 'speciesist' prejudice is exactly why we love watching them hunted, and why we love Supernatural.
- ch. 10 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Just War Theory; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Shannon Ford reconstructs the Winchesters' ethics of killing: self-defense and defense of others justify lethal force, as when Sam kills Jeremy in 'Dream a Little Dream of Me' and Andy shoots Ansem to save Dean in 'Simon Said,' while Dean's refusal of Ruby's virgin-sacrifice spell in 'Jus in Bello' and sparing the disarmed Pa Bender mark lines they will not cross even when the math favors killing. Killing possessed innocents like Meg is treated as permissible only under necessity and with regret. The chapter then argues that once the brothers hunt to banish all demons from the world, their conflict is war rather than hunting, so just war theory (jus ad bellum and jus in bello) might license killings ordinary morality forbids, a slippage dramatized by Gordon's enjoyment of killing and Dean's unjustifiable killing of Amy.
- ch. 11 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, David Hume — Free Will vs Determinism; Bad Faith; Compatibilism — Ralston and Applegate read the Winchesters' contested destiny through the free will debate: the angels' case for determinism runs from a cupid arranged to couple John and Mary, through Azazel's deal and Mary's death, to Zachariah and Michael's claim that 'free will is an illusion' and the brothers must say yes as vessels. Sartre supplies the response: with no pre-given essence, the Winchesters are radically free and responsible, Dean admirably resisting 'bad faith' while Sam's early rebellions are self-deceptive until he stops blaming family expectations. Hume's point that free choices must still flow from the agent's character and values grounds a two-stage model of free will used to argue that soulless Sam, lacking the moral filter of the soul, has more options but is less free and less responsible.
- ch. 12 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Jeremy Bentham, Immanuel Kant — Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Utilitarianism — Foresman asks what would make Hell a justified punishment for the souls claimed by crossroads deals, like Mary, John, and Dean trading damnation to bring a loved one back to life. Using Joel Feinberg's expressive account of punishment, he argues that souls in Hell through stupid deals suffer mere bad consequences rather than punishment, because no message of moral condemnation reaches someone who never knew the rule. Bentham's utilitarian test fails to justify Hell, since a Hell nobody takes seriously deters nobody and nothing there is rehabilitated, and Kantian retributivism fails too because no finite wrong can deserve eternal torment, leaving Crowley's endless-queue Hell as at least better proportioned to desert.
- ch. 14 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Hobbes — The State of Nature; The Social Contract — Dena Hurst reads Heaven's civil war through Hobbes's Leviathan: with God absent there is no common power, so the angels fall into a state of nature that is a state of war, complete with natural equality, competition over the same prize, and glory-seeking, as when Zachariah's faction lets Lilith break the seals to force the Apocalypse. God ruled as sovereign by acquisition and proves 'a lousy king' not for demanding obedience but by vanishing without designating a successor, dissolving civil society and with it justice, since where there is no law there is no injustice. Meanwhile Hell under Crowley and the leviathans under Dick Roman display Hobbesian legitimacy from opposite directions: demons join by covenant-like contracts, making Hell a rough democracy, while the leviathans' unified hierarchy enacts the Leviathan itself.
- ch. 15 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Karl Marx — Alienation; Class Struggle; Ideology and False Consciousness — Canode reads 'It's a Terrible Life' as Marx's alienation of labor: Dean Smith's corporate existence at Sandover Bridge & Iron is Zachariah's ruse, and the American dream, like the promise that one more hunt will finally let the brothers quit, is the ideology that keeps workers laboring for owners who profit from them. Sam and Dean become the proletariat and the angels the owners of the means of production, and their refusal of Heaven's plan enacts the Communist Manifesto's line that the bourgeoisie has forged the weapons of its own destruction. The closing meta-turn applies the critique to the audience: fans who watch, buy DVDs, and attend conventions are the bourgeoisie whose demand keeps the Winchesters hunting.
- ch. 16 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill — Objectification; Humanity as an End in Itself; Utilitarianism — Brace applies Kant's prohibition on using persons merely as means to the women of Supernatural: Bobby helping willingly is not objectification, demonic possession and Azazel's forcing Ellen's gun to her own head are, and Zachariah's 'fornicate with women' pitch reduces women to objects. She reads Mary, Ellen, and Jo as warrior mothers whose duty and sacrifice, following Jean Bethke Elshtain, the brothers most respect, while Mill's utilitarianism explains the lovers (Jessica, Lisa, the djinn-dream Carmen) each brother sacrifices to the mission. The 'Jus in Bello' virgin-sacrifice debate exposes the tension, since Dean invokes Kantian respect yet ignores Nancy's free choice to die, and the killings of female monsters like Amy and Emma show objectification running in both directions.
- ch. 17 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Utilitarianism; Deontology; Just War Theory — Browning shows that 'Jus in Bello' is built from Romero's Night of the Living Dead: the besieged police station is a 'survival space' (a form he traces to Matheson's I Am Legend), Henricksen takes Ben's role and Nancy Barbra's, and the massed possessed townspeople mirror the shuffling zombie horde. Inside that space the show stages a clash of values, Ruby's utilitarian spell requiring Nancy's heart against Dean's absolute refusal to kill an innocent ('your choice is not a choice'), resolved by the rock-salt-and-exorcism plan that kills no one. The survival space works as a proving ground for its occupants' values, and the ending, where Lilith slaughters Nancy anyway, indicts the heroes' scruples and asks what the body count says about the viewers who enjoyed it.
- ch. 18 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** The Problem of Evil — Haas uses Dean's stubborn refusal to believe in God, even after meeting Castiel, escaping Hell, and visiting Heaven, to run through the problem of evil. Casey's challenge in 'Sin City' states the logical problem; the free-will theodicy answers it but falters before Supernatural's designed horrors like the rugaru, a creature God built to suffer an irresistible hunger that ends with it eating its spouse. Dean's real objection is the evidential problem, that the amount and severity of apparently pointless evil makes the omni-God unlikely, and neither a 'natural order' defense (Dick Roman humanely farming humans for food) nor John Hick's soul-making theodicy explains suffering far beyond what character formation requires.
- ch. 20 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Aquinas, William Paley — The Problem of Evil; The Watchmaker Argument (design); The Five Ways; Ockham's Razor — Curry argues that angels like Anna and Castiel can reasonably be atheists, because a higher perspective confers no epistemic advantage about God: Anna admits only four angels have seen him and the rest 'take it on faith.' Aquinas's cosmological argument, illustrated by the endless causal chain behind the Impala, yields at most an uncaused first cause rather than an omnipotent, omnibenevolent one, and Paley's design argument, an Impala in the desert implies a designer, is undermined by Darwinian natural selection, which Castiel himself witnessed ('Don't step on that fish'). The free-will theodicy fails against natural evils like famine and childhood cancer, and the principle of parsimony tells angels to expect a natural explanation for their own existence, so Uriel's 'There is no will. No wrath. No God.' turns out to be rational.
- ch. 21 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Baruch Spinoza, George Berkeley, René Descartes, Immanuel Kant, John Locke — Subjective Idealism (esse est percipi); Forgiveness; Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura) — Chaib takes Ruby's line that Hell is 'forgetting what you are' and reads God's character through early modern philosophy: Descartes' supremely real being and deceiving demon frame Castiel's delusion of godhood and Ruby's manipulation of Sam, Spinoza's denial that evil exists (it is 'inadequate knowledge') explains the comprehensible motives of Crowley and Lucifer, Berkeley's claim that things persist only because God perceives them makes a dead God an existential threat, and Kant's 'moral theism' rebuts dogmatic atheism. With Hegel and Fromm, Hell becomes self-forgetting and communion with God becomes self-knowledge achieved through knowing others, the opposite of Ruby's Hell. The chapter concludes via Locke that closing Hell's gates would deny once-human demons the redemption tied to our very idea of God, so the brothers' forgiving love, unlike Michael and Lucifer's rigidity, reflects God's nature.
- ch. 22 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes, W.V.O. Quine — Mind–Body Dualism; The Cogito; Methodological Doubt (evil demon) — Blackmon and Foresman ask what makes ghosts, spells, and holy water supernatural, rejecting definitions based on fiction, disbelief, or weirdness, and using Quine's point about the circularity of dictionary definitions to show lexicography cannot settle the question. Definitions keyed to current science or to the causal nexus fail because ghosts in Supernatural and in Hamlet causally interact, Bobby's ghost talks, moves objects, and possesses a maid, so the authors define the supernatural as what can on occasion transcend the world of material interaction. Descartes' interactionist substance dualism supplies the model: the cogito (even a djinn cannot make you falsely believe you exist), the pineal gland as the soul's point of causal contact, and a testable hypothesis that makes the supernatural scientifically investigable and implies that we, as spirits, are supernatural too.
- ch. 24 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Isaiah Berlin, Aristotle, Plato, Simone de Beauvoir, Friedrich Nietzsche — Two Concepts of Liberty; Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Philosophy of Love — Goguen reads the Winchesters through two masculine ideals: the warrior (Dean and Michael, chivalric protection culminating in Dean's 'protecting Sam... it's who I am') and the sovereign (Sam and Lucifer, whose freedom is analyzed with Isaiah Berlin's negative and positive liberty, with nods to Hobbes's absolute sovereign and Nietzsche's Übermensch). The show's stoic culture, where 'baring my soul like a freaking girl' is an insult, keeps the L-word unspoken, making Ellen's dying 'I will always love you, baby' to Jo a foil the brothers cannot match. Plato's Symposium, via Aristophanes' myth of split soulmates, and Aristotle's claim that the purest love is between virtuous male friends make sense of the 'psychotically, irrationally, erotically codependent' bond, and the chapter concludes that true masculinity requires embracing the seemingly supernatural: love.
- ch. 25 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** The Problem of Evil — Evolutionary biologist Graves applies naturalist method to the Supernatural universe: assume natural explanations first, as the Catholic Church does before granting an exorcism, and only posit the supernatural where naturalism fails. He builds a naturalistic phylogeny in which souls behave like genetic codes (50,000 new souls when Balthazar unsinks the Titanic), and demons, ghosts, and most monsters derive from human souls, which explains why mundane salt, iron, fire, and burned bones work on them, while pagan gods killable by wooden stakes and dog's blood are 'more akin to monsters' than gods. The framework yields rules and predictions about the Colt, holy water, and the Croatoan virus, and even suggests God and Death may be natural beings obeying laws lesser beings do not share.
- ch. 26 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 27 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward

- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 6 "The Devils Get Their Due" *(no index entry yet)* — Editor Ben Dyer's introduction argues that supervillains have effectively 'won' as comics matured: since the 1970s-80s turn (O'Neil/Adams Green Lantern, Miller's Dark Knight Returns, Watchmen), heroes like Batman, Superman, and Spider-Man acquired broken psychologies while villains like Magneto, Ra's al Ghul, and Lex Luthor were humanized until hero and villain barely contrast. Citing Stan Lee's claim that the supervillain is the most important character, Dyer announces the volume's project: to restore that contrast by analyzing the villain's relation to morality and society, asking whether tyranny can serve a good cause, whether an all-powerful being is limitless, whether anyone can truly desire evil, and why good henchmen are so hard to find.
- ch. 7 "4" **·** Plato, Hannah Arendt, Aristotle, Thomas Hobbes, John Rawls, Niccolò Machiavelli, Cicero — Allegory of the Cave; The Banality of Evil; Aristotle on Friendship (philia); The State of Nature — Four 'Phase One' essays. Dyer reads Mark Millar's Wanted through Plato's cave: Wesley Gibson escapes a pathetic life like the freed prisoner, but like Adolf Eichmann (via Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem) he murders his conscience, so the Fraternity's consequence-free world leaves him numb and unable to value anything - a descent deeper into the cave, ending in the banality of evil. Novy explains why henchmen betray using Aristotle's utility/pleasure/complete friendship distinction (Big Cheese, Henchmen Muenster and Feta): supervillain gangs are Hobbesian pirate crews with no enforcer, so a modus vivendi of self-interest collapses under interrogation and only Machiavellian fear secures loyalty. Foresman applies Goodman and Rawls's reflective equilibrium as a 'cheat' to rank Apocalypse, Magneto, Luthor, the Joker, and Bizarro, concluding the 'best of the worst' is judged on evil ends (or evil means, as with Magneto) and even on glorious failure. Arinder and Milton, in a staged descent-into-madness frame, diagnose mad science in Victor Frankenstein and Dr. Doom as science that denies value-laden theory choice - impossible because data underdetermine theory - breeding the hubris that dehumanizes the scientist.
- ch. 8 "8" **·** Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill, J.L. Mackie, Thomas Aquinas, William of Ockham, Jeremy Bentham — Humanity as an End in Itself; Utilitarianism; Higher and Lower Pleasures; Moral Relativism — Four 'Phase Two' essays on the nature of evil. Arp argues that in V for Vendetta V is a utilitarian user of persons just like the fascist Norsefire state - using Dascombe as a shield and torturing Evey 'for her own good' - so Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means condemns the hero-as-villain, though 'moral autonomy' Kantians complicate the verdict. Poon stages the Aquinas-Ockham debate over will and intellect as Magneto reprograms Sentinels against New York (Ultimate X-Men #05), arguing the will cannot choose against the intellect's judgment, so supervillains like Magneto, Ra's al Ghul, and Apocalypse act for what seems good to them with a deeply flawed conception of the good. Robichaud uses Superman Returns, Civil War, and Captain America vs the Red Skull to test Mackie's error theory, prescriptivism, expressivism, and moral relativism, defending moral objectivism against the Modern Age's gray morality. Sylvia IV and Walters use Bentham, Mill's higher and lower pleasures with competent judges, and Railton's ideal-advisor moral realism to dismantle Mojo's defense that his Spineless Ones' ratings-driven bloodsports are just desire-satisfaction, indicting our own reality TV.
- ch. 9 "12" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Philippa Foot, John Stuart Mill, Augustine of Hippo, Jeremy Bentham, Arthur Schopenhauer — The State of Nature; Virtue Ethics (arete); Utilitarianism; Just War Theory — Four 'Phase Three' essays on world conquest. Terjesen asks whether Doctor Doom's magnanimity (Aristotle's great-souledness, contra the unity-of-virtues thesis Aquinas held and Philippa Foot qualified) makes him less villainous than The Authority, whose purely consequentialist paternalism - like Doom's Emperor Doom or Ozymandias's plot - usurps a free choice no mere power can justify. Barringer reads Marvel's Civil War through Hobbes: the Stamford explosion and unrestrained superpowers recreate the state of nature, the Registration Act is the surrender of freedom to a sovereign, and Stark, Richards, and Pym repeat Hobbes's flawed faith in 'scientific' deductive politics, sealed by the clone-Thor killing of Goliath. Hillerbrand and Sandburg pit Rorschach's Kantian deontology (no compromise, not even to save the world) against Ozymandias's utilitarian murder of three million New Yorkers in Watchmen, arguing via Laplace's Demon that even Dr. Manhattan - nihilist or Schopenhauerian recluse - cannot verify the outcome, so watchmen can be trusted only by knowing their limits. Ostrander's fictional NSC interview has Amanda Waller's Suicide Squad defended with Benthamite utility, the rejection of natural rights as 'nonsense on stilts,' and the Augustinian just-war criteria of just cause, right intent, and proportionality, while the interviewer exposes how conveniently those limits bend.
- ch. 10 "15" **·** Albert Camus, Friedrich Nietzsche, Immanuel Kant, Jean-Paul Sartre, Elizabeth Anscombe — The Absurd; Amor Fati (love of fate); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Existence Precedes Essence — Three 'Phase Four' essays. Moseley reads the Joker across Batman #1, The Killing Joke, The Dark Knight, A Death in the Family, and Dark Knight Returns as a 'moral monster' who knowingly does evil - and, following Anscombe and Scanlon's guise-of-the-good analysis, pursues aesthetic 'higher values' in a Camus-like affirmation of the absurd, embracing the irrationality Batman's rational moral order cannot fathom. Levin uses X-gene biology (Beast's explanation in Astonishing X-Men, genotype vs phenotype, M-Day) to strip Magneto's Homo sapiens superior claim of any genetic or phenotypic basis, then argues via the moral community of rational persons (Kant's criterion) that mutants and humans share one moral community, condemning both the Registration Act and mutant separatism. O'Neil's prose piece traces Harvey Dent from Calvinist certainty through the acid that scars him to cosmic doubt - quantum randomness, many worlds, Sartre's condemnation to freedom - until Nietzsche's amor fati lets him embrace duality and let the scarred two-headed coin decide good and evil.
- ch. 11 "19" **·** Harry Frankfurt, Plutarch, Daniel Dennett, René Descartes, Andy Clark — Compatibilism; Ship of Theseus; Personal Identity; Embodiment (the lived body) — Four 'Phase Five' puzzle essays. Lindahl-Urben and Taliaferro use Secret Wars to test omnipotence: the Beyonder, Doom, and Galactus cannot do the logically impossible (no spherical cubes, no stone too heavy to lift), two omnipotent beings collide, and a truly omnipotent being has no desires - so villains can never climb to the top they crave. Matthewson and Wall use Frankfurt cases and reasons-responsive source compatibilism to explain why Eddie Brock is responsible for Venom's villainy (he voluntarily bonded and endorses the symbiote's adjusted psychology) while Anne Weying, horrified by what the symbiote made her do, bears only minimal blame. Pickavance reconstructs the Ship of Theseus with Sandman's 'mansand': combining part exchange with materialism lets Norman Osborn reassemble a duplicate Sandman from his scattered remains, and since neither principle nor soul-dualism comes free, personal identity through material change remains unsolved. Loader argues Brainiac's reinvention as a 'facts and logic' computer embodies disembodied Cartesian AI, so the frame problem (Dennett's exploding robots) and embodied cognition (Clark's Tetris, Dreyfus) suggest his detachment from body and world would make him less, not more, intelligent than the humans he scorns.
